explanation.summary: On any antipsychotic the RANZCP monitoring schedule sets metabolic bloods at baseline, 12 weeks, then at least yearly, plus weight and waist at every review. Early weight gain on olanzapine is a specific trigger to repeat glucose/HbA1c and fasting lipids and to consider a switch.
key_points: Baseline, 12 week and at least annual fasting glucose/HbA1c and lipids on all antipsychotics.
Weight and waist every review; >=7% weight gain triggers intervention.
Prolactin and ECG are agent-specific, not universal.
explanation.pearls: Olanzapine and clozapine carry the highest metabolic burden; the 12 week bloods catch early dysglycaemia before overt diabetes.

options.rationale: Prolactin is checked when there are hyperprolactinaemia symptoms or on high-prolactinaemia agents (risperidone, amisulpride); it does not replace glucose and lipid surveillance which is the priority on olanzapine (Source: eTG Psychotropic; AMH).

12 week bloods are a specified checkpoint on all antipsychotics; deferring to 12 months misses early-onset dysglycaemia and dyslipidaemia which are highest risk on olanzapine (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG).

HbA1c is explicitly recommended in the RANZCP monitoring schedule alongside fasting glucose; either can be used to screen and both are covered by MBS for this indication (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG).

Baseline and follow-up ECG is only routine for certain agents (e.g. ziprasidone, high-dose haloperidol, clozapine); troponin has no role in routine metabolic monitoring for olanzapine (Source: eTG Psychotropic).

RANZCP and eTG Psychotropic recommend fasting glucose or HbA1c and a fasting lipid profile at baseline, 12 weeks, then at least yearly on any antipsychotic; weight and waist are checked at every review with early rise on olanzapine a specific trigger for lifestyle intervention and consideration of agent switch (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Schizophrenia; eTG Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Persistent >7% weight gain and worsening lipids and glucose on olanzapine, despite lifestyle intervention, is a trigger to switch to a metabolically neutral antipsychotic such as aripiprazole. Cross-titration protects the stabilised illness while lifestyle measures continue.
key_points: Metabolic switch threshold: >7% weight gain, worsening lipids or dysglycaemia after adequate lifestyle trial.
Aripiprazole has the most favourable metabolic profile among SGAs.
Clozapine is not a metabolic-neutral alternative.
explanation.pearls: Adjunctive metformin is second-line to a switch when the current agent cannot be changed (e.g. clozapine responder).

options.rationale: A weight gain of >7% with progressive metabolic drift plus a first-degree family history of type 2 diabetes triggers active management rather than watchful waiting (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG).

Aripiprazole has the most favourable metabolic profile among second-generation antipsychotics; switching after failed lifestyle intervention in a patient with >7% weight gain and worsening lipids is the recommended step, with a cross-titration to preserve symptom control (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG; eTG Psychotropic).

Adjunctive metformin has modest evidence for attenuating antipsychotic-induced weight gain but is considered when a switch is not feasible; here the primary lever is agent switch given her preferences and progressive drift (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG).

Dose reduction of olanzapine has an inconsistent effect on weight and risks relapse of a stabilised psychosis; switching to a metabolically neutral agent addresses the mechanism more reliably (Source: eTG Psychotropic).

Clozapine is reserved for treatment-resistant illness and carries an equal or greater metabolic burden than olanzapine; it is not indicated as a metabolic-friendly switch (Source: eTG Psychotropic; AMH).

explanation.summary: Symptomatic hyperprolactinaemia on risperidone (galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea) is best managed by switching to a prolactin-sparing antipsychotic such as aripiprazole, then reassessing prolactin. MRI is reserved for persistent elevation off the offending drug or for red-flag features.
key_points: Risperidone, paliperidone, and amisulpride are the highest prolactin agents.
Aripiprazole is prolactin-sparing and can also be added at low dose to lower prolactin without switching if needed.
MRI pituitary if prolactin remains elevated after switch or if red-flag features.
explanation.pearls: Dopamine agonists in patients on antipsychotics can trigger relapse; avoid unless endocrine consultation.

options.rationale: MRI is reserved for prolactin above ~2500 mIU/L after drug cessation or when clinical features suggest a pituitary lesion; imaging first is not the appropriate initial step when a plausible drug cause is present (Source: eTG Endocrinology).

Risperidone-induced prolactin elevation is often persistent even at lower doses and dose reduction risks symptom relapse; switching to a prolactin-sparing agent is more reliable (Source: eTG Psychotropic).

Dopamine agonists risk destabilising the psychosis by pharmacological antagonism of the antipsychotic; they are not first line in drug-induced hyperprolactinaemia in patients with schizophrenia (Source: eTG Psychotropic).

Symptomatic drug-induced hyperprolactinaemia is best managed by switching to a prolactin-sparing agent such as aripiprazole; prolactin normalises within weeks and reassessment then determines whether MRI is needed (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG; eTG Psychotropic).

Oestrogen replacement is only considered after the drug cause has been addressed and hypogonadism persists; it is not the first response to symptomatic drug-induced hyperprolactinaemia (Source: eTG Endocrinology).

explanation.summary: Long-term lithium monitoring is trough level every 3-6 months once stable, plus renal function, thyroid function and corrected calcium every 6-12 months. This catches nephropathy, hypothyroidism, and hyperparathyroidism early.
key_points: Trough level = 12 h post dose.
Prophylaxis target 0.6-0.8 mmol/L (0.8-1.0 for acute mania in some).
Corrected calcium is first-line; PTH is second-line if calcium elevated.
explanation.pearls: Any acute illness with vomiting, diarrhoea, dehydration, new NSAID, ACEi/ARB, or diuretic warrants an ad hoc lithium level.

options.rationale: Yearly-only lithium levels miss subclinical drift; renal function must be tracked routinely because chronic lithium nephropathy is often silent and irreversible if missed (Source: eTG Psychotropic).

eTG Psychotropic and RANZCP mood disorders CPG recommend trough lithium every 3-6 months once stable, plus renal function, thyroid function and calcium at 6-12 monthly intervals for the duration of therapy (Source: eTG Psychotropic; RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG).
Corrected calcium is the standard first-line surveillance for lithium-induced hyperparathyroidism; PTH is checked only if calcium is elevated (Source: eTG Psychotropic).
6-weekly levels are used during dose titration; 24 hour urine is not routine and is triggered by polyuria or polydipsia (Source: eTG Psychotropic).
Lithium does not require FBC surveillance and does not replace TFTs, which detect hypothyroidism in around a quarter of long-term users (Source: eTG Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Chronic lithium toxicity with neurological features (ataxia, confusion, nystagmus) plus impaired renal function meets EXTRIP criteria for haemodialysis even at levels below the classical 4.0 mmol/L threshold. ACEi and volume depletion are recognised precipitants.
key_points: Haemodialysis: level >4.0 OR level >2.5 with neurological features/renal impairment OR unable to excrete due to renal failure.
Chronic toxicity presents with neurology at lower levels than acute overdose.
Charcoal does not bind lithium.
explanation.pearls: Whenever an ACEi, ARB, thiazide, or NSAID is started in a lithium patient, check a level within 1-2 weeks.

options.rationale: IV saline alone is inadequate for chronic toxicity with neurological features and level >2.5-3 mmol/L range; renal replacement therapy is the definitive treatment when neurological signs are present with impaired clearance (Source: eTG Toxicology; Australia and New Zealand Poisons Information Centres).
Charcoal does not bind lithium; it has no role in lithium toxicity of any severity (Source: eTG Toxicology).

Chronic lithium toxicity with neurological features (ataxia, confusion, nystagmus) and impaired renal function meets EXTRIP consensus criteria for haemodialysis regardless of the precise level; ACEi and dehydration precipitated toxicity by reducing lithium clearance (Source: EXTRIP lithium recommendations; eTG Toxicology).
Sodium polystyrene sulfonate is not indicated for lithium; forced alkaline diuresis increases sodium load without improving lithium clearance and risks fluid overload (Source: eTG Toxicology).
Continuing lithium during established toxicity risks worsening neurotoxicity even with dose reduction; the drug must be withheld and clearance actively enhanced (Source: eTG Toxicology).

explanation.summary: Any woman of childbearing potential remaining on valproate must be in the TGA Pregnancy Prevention Program: annual specialist counselling, a highly effective contraceptive method (IUD or implant preferred), and documented acknowledgement of teratogenic risk.
key_points: Valproate: ~10% congenital malformation, ~30-40% neurodevelopmental impairment.
Highly effective contraception = LARC (Cu-IUD, LNG-IUD, etonogestrel implant) or DMPA.
Combined oral contraceptive is user-dependent and less preferred here.
explanation.pearls: If she conceives, valproate is a Category D drug and pre-conceptual switch (usually to lamotrigine) is planned with psychiatry.

options.rationale: Carbamazepine is also Category D with an appreciable neural tube defect risk and enzyme-induction interactions; substituting one Category D agent for another does not solve the problem (Source: AMH).

Condoms alone do not meet the highly effective threshold required by the TGA program; the risk of unplanned pregnancy with a Category D teratogen is unacceptable (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Program).

Folate does not mitigate the specific teratogenic risk of valproate (neural tube defects, cognitive impairment, autism spectrum) which persists despite supplementation; contraception is the primary intervention (Source: AMH).

The TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Program requires documented annual counselling, use of a highly effective contraceptive method (LARC preferred: IUD or implant), and signed acknowledgement in any woman of childbearing potential remaining on valproate (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Program; AMH).

She has already failed lithium and abrupt discontinuation of a stabilising agent risks manic relapse; the priority is safe contraception on her current effective regimen (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG).

explanation.summary: First trimester valproate carries the highest teratogenic and neurodevelopmental risk of the mood stabilisers. Cross-titrating to a previously tolerated safer agent (usually lithium) minimises cumulative exposure while maintaining relapse prevention; folic acid dose is escalated to 5 mg daily.
key_points: Valproate: 10% major malformation, 30-40% neurodevelopmental effects.
Lithium: ~0.1% Ebstein anomaly, requires close level monitoring especially peripartum.
Abrupt cessation of a mood stabiliser in bipolar I is a high-risk event.
explanation.pearls: The postpartum period is the highest-risk window for bipolar relapse; medication planning must include a postpartum plan.

options.rationale: Abrupt cessation of valproate risks acute manic relapse; a cross-titration to an agent she has previously tolerated is safer than sudden switch to olanzapine monotherapy without a proven personal record on that agent (Source: RANZCP Perinatal CPG).

Continued valproate exposure across the pregnancy compounds the teratogenic and neurodevelopmental burden well beyond the first trimester; switching earlier still reduces cumulative risk (Source: RANZCP Perinatal CPG).
Carbamazepine is also Category D with neural tube defect risk and enzyme-induction interactions and is not a safer alternative during pregnancy (Source: AMH).

Continuing valproate confers ~10% major malformation risk and neurodevelopmental impairment; cross-titration to a mood stabiliser with demonstrable prior tolerability and lower teratogenic burden (lithium ~0.1% Ebstein anomaly) is recommended, with high-dose folate and specialist monitoring (Source: RANZCP Perinatal CPG; AMH).

Psychological therapy is not adequate mood stabilisation for bipolar I disorder with prior severe mania; the risk of unmedicated relapse is high, particularly in the postpartum (Source: RANZCP Perinatal CPG).

explanation.summary: QRS >100 ms in TCA overdose predicts seizure and ventricular arrhythmia. Hypertonic sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mmol/kg bolus is titrated to narrowing of the QRS and arterial alkalisation. Class I/III antiarrhythmics and flumazenil are contraindicated.
key_points: QRS >100 ms predicts seizure; >160 ms predicts ventricular arrhythmia.
R wave in aVR >3 mm supports diagnosis.
Benzodiazepines for seizures; hyperventilation and hypertonic saline are adjuncts.
explanation.pearls: Lipid emulsion therapy is a rescue option for refractory cardiovascular collapse in severe TCA toxicity.

options.rationale: Charcoal is appropriate within 1-2 hours in an alert cooperative patient but is unsafe here given reduced GCS and seizure risk without airway protection; and it does not address the established cardiotoxicity (Source: eTG Toxicology).
Flumazenil is contraindicated in mixed or TCA overdose because it can precipitate seizures and unmask arrhythmias; it has no role here (Source: eTG Toxicology).
Phenytoin shares sodium channel blockade with TCAs and can worsen cardiotoxicity; benzodiazepines are the anticonvulsant of choice in TCA poisoning (Source: eTG Toxicology).
Class Ia/Ic and class III antiarrhythmics prolong QT and can precipitate torsades in TCA toxicity; amiodarone is contraindicated (Source: eTG Toxicology).

QRS >100 ms with hypotension and seizure indicates significant sodium channel blockade in TCA toxicity; hypertonic sodium bicarbonate is the first-line antidote and is titrated to QRS narrowing and arterial pH 7.45-7.55 (Source: eTG Toxicology; Australia Poisons Information Centre).

explanation.summary: Varenicline is the most effective single-agent smoking cessation pharmacotherapy in Australia. The EAGLES trial found no excess neuropsychiatric events versus NRT or placebo in stable patients with or without prior psychiatric illness; the FDA black box warning was subsequently removed, though monitoring remains prudent.
key_points: First-line: varenicline or combination NRT (patch plus fast acting).
Bupropion is second-line; contraindicated with seizure disorder, eating disorder, or acute alcohol/benzo withdrawal.
Nicotine vaping products are for those who have failed first-line therapy.
explanation.pearls: Prescribe varenicline for 12 weeks minimum; a further 12 weeks reduces relapse in responders.

options.rationale: Combination NRT is effective but varenicline has superior evidence for sustained abstinence in heavy smokers, and the historical EAGLES trial showed no excess neuropsychiatric risk in stable patients (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines).

Varenicline is the most effective single agent and the RACGP guideline reaffirms it as first-line in stable patients regardless of past depression; the black box warning was downgraded after EAGLES demonstrated no excess neuropsychiatric events in stable patients but routine safety monitoring is still advised (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines; AMH).

Bupropion is a valid second-line option but reduces the seizure threshold and is less effective than varenicline; it is not first-line where varenicline is safe (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines).
Nortriptyline is third-line for smoking cessation, used only when first- and second-line options are contraindicated or have failed (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines).

Nicotine vaping products are reserved for patients who have failed first-line pharmacotherapy; they are not the initial choice in a treatment-naive patient with an effective option available (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Bupropion is contraindicated in seizure history and in current or past eating disorder. Varenicline is first-line where NRT alone has failed and there are no contraindications. Combining pharmacotherapy with behavioural support doubles quit rates.
key_points: Bupropion absolute CIs: seizure disorder, eating disorder, acute alcohol/benzo withdrawal, MAOI.
Varenicline: safe in seizure and eating disorder history; monitor for neuropsychiatric symptoms.
NRT combination (patch + fast-acting) is equivalent to varenicline in many meta-analyses.
explanation.pearls: Pregnancy: NRT is first-line; varenicline and bupropion are not recommended.

options.rationale: Bupropion is contraindicated in patients with a seizure history and in current or past eating disorder; both are absolute contraindications on the Australian PI (Source: AMH; RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines).
Nortriptyline is third-line, reserved for those who have failed or cannot tolerate first- and second-line therapy (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines).
Monotherapy NRT is less effective than combination NRT or varenicline and is not preferred in a patient who has already failed a single nicotine product (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines).

Varenicline is a first-line effective option with no seizure or eating-disorder contraindication and is appropriate here where bupropion is contraindicated and gum alone has failed (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines; AMH).

Combining behavioural support with pharmacotherapy roughly doubles quit rates compared with either alone; withholding pharmacotherapy in a motivated patient is not appropriate (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines).

explanation.summary: In NSW, Schedule 8 psychostimulants require a stimulant authority under the Poisons and Therapeutic Goods Regulation. GPs can co-prescribe under a shared care model with the initiating specialist. Driving is generally permitted on stable therapeutic stimulant dosing per Austroads.
key_points: NSW stimulant authority is required before dispensing any Schedule 8 stimulant.
Baseline BP, HR, ECG when indicated, and screen for cardiovascular disease before starting.
Austroads permits private driving on stable stimulant dosing without cognitive impairment.
explanation.pearls: Substance use disorder is a relative contraindication to stimulants; consider atomoxetine or guanfacine as non-scheduled alternatives.

options.rationale: ADHD itself is not a mandatory notification condition; notification is required only if the patient continues to drive against medical advice with an unsafe condition (Source: Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive).

Any prescriber of a Schedule 8 psychostimulant in NSW must hold or share a stimulant authority; a specialist assessment does not exempt the GP from the regulatory requirement (Source: NSW Health Stimulant Authority).

NSW GPs can prescribe under a shared care or delegated authority arrangement once the specialist has initiated and the authority is granted; sole specialist prescribing is not required (Source: NSW Health Stimulant Authority).

Austroads criteria permit private driving on stable therapeutic stimulant dosing without cognitive or behavioural impairment; blanket licence surrender is not required (Source: Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive).

In NSW a stimulant authority under the Poisons and Therapeutic Goods Regulation is required to prescribe Schedule 8 psychostimulants; this can be a co-prescribing arrangement with the specialist, but must be in place before dispensing; driving is generally permitted on stable therapeutic stimulant dosing (Source: NSW Health Stimulant Authority Guidelines; Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive).

explanation.summary: In adult ADHD with a history of stimulant use disorder in stable remission, non-stimulant pharmacotherapy is preferred first-line. Atomoxetine is TGA-approved for adult ADHD, has no misuse potential, and takes 4-6 weeks for full effect.
key_points: Atomoxetine and guanfacine are non-stimulant options.
Long-acting stimulants (lisdexamfetamine, methylphenidate MR) are preferred over IR when stimulants are used.
Baseline BP, HR, and cardiac history for all stimulant candidates.
explanation.pearls: Atomoxetine carries a rare warning for suicidal ideation in young adults and hepatotoxicity; monitor mood and consider LFTs if symptomatic.

options.rationale: Immediate-release stimulants have the highest misuse liability and are least preferred in a patient with a history of stimulant use disorder; a long-acting agent or non-stimulant is preferred (Source: RANZCP ADHD Position Statement; eTG Psychotropic).
Bupropion has limited evidence in adult ADHD and is not a first-line agent in Australian guidelines; it is used when other options are contraindicated (Source: RANZCP ADHD Position Statement).

Atomoxetine is a non-stimulant selective noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor with no misuse potential and is preferred first-line in adults with ADHD and a personal history of stimulant use disorder in stable recovery (Source: RANZCP ADHD Position Statement; eTG Psychotropic).

Lisdexamfetamine's prodrug status lowers but does not eliminate misuse risk; RANZCP still lists non-stimulants ahead of stimulants when there is a personal history of stimulant use disorder (Source: RANZCP ADHD Position Statement).
Modafinil is not an approved or evidence-based first-line ADHD pharmacotherapy in Australia and is not TGA indicated for ADHD (Source: AMH).

explanation.summary: DSM-5-TR duration thresholds: brief psychotic disorder <1 month, schizophreniform 1-6 months, schizophrenia >=6 months. Delusional disorder requires absence of prominent hallucinations, disorganised speech, or negative symptoms. Schizoaffective requires a concurrent major mood episode.
key_points: Duration separates brief psychotic disorder, schizophreniform disorder and schizophrenia.
Delusional disorder: single non-bizarre or bizarre delusion, no other psychotic features.
Schizoaffective: mood episode concurrent with active psychosis plus >=2 weeks of pure psychosis.
explanation.pearls: Diagnosis is often provisional and may evolve; document trajectory to allow revision at 1 and 6 month marks.

options.rationale: DSM-5-TR brief psychotic disorder requires at least one positive symptom lasting >=1 day but <1 month with eventual full return to premorbid functioning; at 3 weeks she meets duration criteria for brief psychotic disorder pending resolution (Source: DSM-5-TR; RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG).
Schizophreniform disorder requires 1-6 months of continuous symptoms; at 3 weeks she does not yet meet the minimum duration (Source: DSM-5-TR).
Schizophrenia requires >=6 months of prodrome or active symptoms; first-rank symptoms are neither necessary nor sufficient in DSM-5-TR (Source: DSM-5-TR).

Delusional disorder requires >=1 month of one or more delusions without prominent hallucinations, disorganised speech, negative symptoms, or grossly disorganised behaviour; the prominent hallucinations and disorganised speech here rule it out (Source: DSM-5-TR).

Schizoaffective disorder requires a major mood episode concurrent with the active phase of psychosis and >=2 weeks of psychosis without prominent mood symptoms; there is no persistent mood disturbance here (Source: DSM-5-TR).

explanation.summary: Delusional disorder is characterised by one or more delusions of >=1 month duration with function otherwise largely preserved, no prominent hallucinations, disorganised speech, negative symptoms, or grossly disorganised behaviour. Jealous type has spousal infidelity as the delusional content.
key_points: Subtypes: erotomanic, grandiose, jealous, persecutory, somatic, mixed, unspecified.
Function is preserved apart from the impact of the delusion.
Treatment: antipsychotic (often modest doses), engagement often limited.
explanation.pearls: Rule out organic causes (dementia, alcohol, medication-induced) and rule out mood disorder with psychotic features before diagnosing.

options.rationale: There is no depressed mood, anhedonia, or neurovegetative disturbance; delusion of jealousy is not a mood-congruent feature (Source: DSM-5-TR).

Schizophrenia requires additional active-phase symptoms (hallucinations, disorganised speech, negative symptoms) that are absent here, and functional impairment; these are not present (Source: DSM-5-TR).

DSM-5-TR delusional disorder requires >=1 month of one or more delusions with function otherwise preserved and no other prominent psychotic symptoms; jealous type describes the delusional infidelity content and duration criteria are exceeded (Source: DSM-5-TR).
There is no history of substance use; alcohol-induced psychotic disorder requires temporal relationship to intoxication or withdrawal (Source: DSM-5-TR).
bvFTD would show progressive personality change, executive dysfunction, apathy, or disinhibition; MoCA of 28/30 and preserved function make bvFTD unlikely (Source: DSM-5-TR).

explanation.summary: Synthetic cannabinoid receptor agonists (SCRAs, "K2", "Spice") are full CB1 agonists (unlike THC partial agonism), producing severe sympathomimetic toxicity, agitation, psychosis, and rhabdomyolysis. Standard urine cannabinoid immunoassay does not detect them - a negative result does not exclude the diagnosis.
key_points: SCRAs cause more severe toxicity than THC because they are full agonists.
Standard immunoassay does not detect SCRAs; specific testing required.
Management: benzodiazepines for agitation, cooling, IV fluids for rhabdomyolysis.
explanation.pearls: "Bath salts" (synthetic cathinones) are the sympathomimetic parallel to SCRAs; a similar toxidrome with a negative amphetamine screen.

options.rationale: Synthetic cannabinoids (SCRAs, e.g. "K2", "Spice") are full CB1 agonists producing tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia, agitation and psychosis, often with rhabdomyolysis; standard immunoassay does NOT detect them, so a negative cannabinoid screen does not exclude the diagnosis (Source: eTG Toxicology; NCETA Synthetic Cannabinoid Fact Sheet).

Serotonin syndrome usually shows hyperreflexia, clonus (especially lower limbs), and ocular clonus; these classical features are not described and MDMA would typically be detected on immunoassay (Source: eTG Toxicology).

The autonomic hyperactivity, hyperthermia, and rhabdomyolysis are inconsistent with primary schizophrenia; toxidrome features and temporal relationship to inhalation of the SCRA drive the diagnosis (Source: DSM-5-TR).

Anticholinergic toxidrome features dry mucous membranes, urinary retention, absent bowel sounds, and flushed dry skin; this patient is diaphoretic which is against anticholinergic aetiology (Source: eTG Toxicology).

Alcohol withdrawal requires a background of sustained heavy drinking; 3 beers is inadequate substrate and the timeframe of 4 hours from last drink is too short for withdrawal (Source: eTG Toxicology).

explanation.summary: For acute behavioural disturbance in an adult with known psychosis and after failed de-escalation, IM olanzapine 5-10 mg is first-line per RANZCP and NSW Health. Do NOT combine parenteral olanzapine with parenteral benzodiazepines because of respiratory depression risk.
key_points: IM olanzapine 5-10 mg first-line; onset 15-45 min.
Do not co-administer parenteral olanzapine with parenteral benzodiazepine.
IM droperidol or IM haloperidol + promethazine are alternatives where olanzapine is unavailable.
explanation.pearls: Post-sedation observations: pulse, BP, respiratory rate, SpO2, and level of consciousness every 15 minutes until fully alert.

options.rationale: Lorazepam monotherapy is an option but does not treat the underlying psychosis; IM olanzapine is preferred first-line in a known psychotic patient not on regular antipsychotic (Source: RANZCP Acute Behavioural Disturbance Guideline).

Concomitant parenteral olanzapine and benzodiazepine carries a significant risk of respiratory depression and hypotension; TGA and RANZCP warn against this combination (Source: TGA olanzapine PI; RANZCP Acute Behavioural Disturbance Guideline).

High-dose IM haloperidol without ECG carries a substantial QTc and torsades risk and is not recommended as first-line; IM olanzapine or lower-dose haloperidol with promethazine is preferred where available (Source: RANZCP Acute Behavioural Disturbance Guideline).

Ketamine is reserved for pre-hospital or code-black-style acute severe agitation and requires airway management readiness; it is not first-line for in-hospital psychiatric agitation (Source: RANZCP Acute Behavioural Disturbance Guideline).

RANZCP and NSW Health guidance recommend IM olanzapine 5-10 mg as first-line for acute behavioural disturbance in an adult without benzodiazepine coadministration due to respiratory depression risk; onset ~15-45 min; monitor sedation and vitals (Source: RANZCP Acute Behavioural Disturbance Guideline; NSW Health Management of Adults with Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance).

explanation.summary: DBT crisis survival skills are the immediate intervention when emotional arousal is very high (>=7/10). TIPP (Temperature via cold water dive reflex, Intense exercise, Paced breathing, Paired muscle relaxation) rapidly reduces sympathetic drive within minutes.
key_points: DBT four modules: mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation, interpersonal effectiveness.
Crisis survival skills (TIPP, ACCEPTS, self-soothe, IMPROVE the moment, pros and cons) sit within distress tolerance.
Interpersonal and emotion regulation skills come AFTER arousal is reduced.
explanation.pearls: TIPP temperature = cold water immersion of the face (dive reflex); avoid in cardiac disease or eating disorder with bradycardia.

options.rationale: DEAR MAN is an interpersonal effectiveness skill best used when arousal is manageable; at 9/10 urge intensity, distress tolerance must precede interpersonal engagement (Source: Linehan DBT Skills Manual 2nd Ed).

TIPP is Linehan's crisis survival skill within distress tolerance, designed for very high emotional arousal (>=7/10) to rapidly reduce sympathetic activation via the dive reflex, aerobic exertion, and paced breathing; onset within minutes and appropriate to bridge the next hour (Source: Linehan DBT Skills Training Manual 2nd Ed; RANZCP Personality Disorders CPG).
Radical acceptance is a reality acceptance skill for longer-term suffering, not the acute crisis survival skill needed when the urge to self-harm is 9/10 (Source: Linehan DBT Skills Manual 2nd Ed).
Check the facts is an emotion regulation skill useful once arousal has been reduced; at very high arousal, distress tolerance skills come first (Source: Linehan DBT Skills Manual 2nd Ed).
Mindfulness skills are foundational but not sufficient at 9/10 acute urge; crisis survival distress tolerance is the immediate need (Source: Linehan DBT Skills Manual 2nd Ed).

explanation.summary: The NHMRC BPD Guideline recommends structured psychological therapy as the primary treatment for BPD. No medication has robust evidence for core BPD symptoms; polypharmacy is common and harmful and should be systematically deprescribed. Benzodiazepines are contraindicated.
key_points: Structured psychological therapy (DBT, MBT, schema, TFP) is first-line.
Medication has a role only for comorbid conditions (MDD, PTSD) or short-term crisis.
Avoid benzodiazepines; deprescribe polypharmacy systematically.
explanation.pearls: Comorbid conditions (MDD, PTSD, ADHD) are treated on their own merits; do not medicate BPD itself as if it were a mood disorder.

options.rationale: Continuing unnecessary polypharmacy is not neutral; metabolic side effects and dependence risk accumulate without symptom benefit (Source: NHMRC BPD Guideline).

Escalating quetiapine adds metabolic and sedation burden without robust evidence for BPD core symptoms; deprescribing and prioritising psychotherapy is the guideline direction (Source: NHMRC BPD Guideline).

The NHMRC BPD Guideline states that no medication has robust evidence for treating core BPD symptoms; polypharmacy in BPD is common and harmful and should be systematically deprescribed while ensuring access to structured psychological therapy (DBT, MBT, schema therapy) (Source: NHMRC BPD Guideline; RANZCP Personality Disorders CPG).
Cochrane and NHMRC reviews (including the LABILE trial) found lamotrigine no more effective than placebo for BPD symptoms; substitution is not supported (Source: NHMRC BPD Guideline; LABILE trial).
Scheduling benzodiazepines creates dependence and worsens impulsivity and self-harm risk in BPD; both drug class and pattern are contraindicated (Source: NHMRC BPD Guideline).

explanation.summary: Clozapine-induced myocarditis peaks in the first 4 weeks of titration. Active surveillance is standard in Australian services with weekly troponin, CRP, and clinical review. Any two of: persistent tachycardia >100, troponin above upper limit, CRP >50, or new symptoms (fatigue, fever, dyspnoea) mandates cessation and cardiology consultation.
key_points: Highest myocarditis risk is weeks 2-3 of titration.
Australian surveillance: weekly troponin and CRP plus symptom review for first 4 weeks.
Cessation is required at threshold; rechallenge is specialist-led with cardiology approval.
explanation.pearls: Neutropenia surveillance is a separate weekly requirement; both toxicities have distinct thresholds and neither can be substituted for the other.

options.rationale: Active clozapine myocarditis surveillance criteria (typically Ronaldson protocol adopted by Australian services) are met: tachycardia and troponin above local upper limit with CRP >50 during the first month; the response is immediate cessation, cardiology consultation, and echocardiogram (Source: NSW Health Clozapine Guideline; Ronaldson clozapine myocarditis protocol).

In active surveillance during the high-risk 4 week window, tachycardia plus rising troponin and CRP meets Australian clozapine myocarditis criteria and requires immediate cessation and cardiology assessment (Source: NSW Health Clozapine Guideline for the Management of Physical Health; Ronaldson et al. protocol).

Dose reduction does not reverse an inflammatory myocarditis and steroids are not routinely indicated as an outpatient response; cessation and cardiology-led management are required (Source: NSW Health Clozapine Guideline).

Rate-controlling a compensatory tachycardia risks masking clinical deterioration; the priority is to establish or exclude myocarditis, not to blunt vital signs (Source: NSW Health Clozapine Guideline).

The clinical picture with troponin and CRP rises in the first month on clozapine is myocarditis until proven otherwise; presumptive antibiotics for a clear chest do not address the diagnosis (Source: NSW Health Clozapine Guideline).

explanation.summary: Akathisia is a drug-induced sense of inner restlessness with observable psychomotor manifestations (foot-tapping, weight-shifting), typically emerging days to weeks after starting or dose-escalating a D2 antagonist. First-line management is reduction of the causative agent plus propranolol.
key_points: Akathisia: inner restlessness + observable movement; distinguish from anxiety by the physical compulsion to move.
Onset days to weeks after starting/increasing D2 antagonist; worse with higher potency agents.
First-line: dose reduction + propranolol 20-40 mg BD-TDS; second-line: benzodiazepines, mirtazapine, cyproheptadine.
explanation.pearls: Akathisia is associated with medication non-adherence and elevated suicide risk in first-episode psychosis; recognise and treat early.

options.rationale: Akathisia is best managed by dose reduction of the causative agent plus beta-blockade (propranolol 20-40 mg BD-TDS is the first-line treatment per eTG Psychotropic and Barnes Akathisia Scale-guided practice); onset within days is characteristic (Source: eTG Psychotropic; Barnes Akathisia Rating Scale references).
The picture is akathisia; increasing the causative D2 antagonist will worsen it, not improve it (Source: eTG Psychotropic; RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG).

Anticholinergics such as benzatropine are first-line for acute dystonia and drug-induced parkinsonism, not akathisia; they are unreliable for akathisia and add anticholinergic burden (Source: eTG Psychotropic).

Benzodiazepines can be adjunctive if beta-blockade is contraindicated, but they are not first-line; anchoring on "anxiety" misses the drug-induced mechanism and delays reduction of the D2 antagonist (Source: eTG Psychotropic).
Haloperidol has a higher rate of extrapyramidal side effects including akathisia; switching to a higher-potency typical worsens the mechanism, not improves it (Source: AMH).

explanation.summary: Medical admission in anorexia nervosa is driven by objective instability, not weight alone. ANZAED and RANZCP list bradycardia below 40, postural hypotension with symptomatic drop, hypothermia below 35.5 degrees Celsius, potassium below 3.0 mmol/L, phosphate below 0.75 mmol/L, and hypoglycaemia below 3.5 mmol/L as individually sufficient triggers. Stabilisation happens on the nearest suitable medical or adolescent ward; specialist ED beds follow.
key_points: Any single instability criterion triggers medical admission.
Refeeding syndrome risk peaks in the first 5-7 days; monitor phosphate, potassium, magnesium daily.
Thiamine 100 mg IV or oral before glucose delivery in severe malnutrition.
explanation.pearls: The MARSIPAN threshold of pulse below 40 supine has the highest positive likelihood for imminent cardiac arrhythmia in adolescent anorexia.

options.rationale: Bradycardia below 40, postural drop over 20 mmHg systolic, hypothermia and hypokalaemia each independently trigger inpatient medical admission under RANZCP and NSW ANZAED criteria; outpatient management is unsafe here (Source: RANZCP Eating Disorders CPG).

Refeeding in a severely malnourished young person must occur in a monitored inpatient setting with electrolyte replacement to avoid refeeding syndrome; ambulatory refeeding under these vitals is unsafe (Source: NSW Health Eating Disorders Toolkit).

Specialist eating disorder beds have long wait lists and she is medically unstable now; medical stabilisation on the nearest paediatric or adolescent ward with cardiac monitoring takes precedence over transfer (Source: NSW Health Eating Disorders Toolkit).

A four hour observation does not address her severe malnutrition or refeeding risk; medical instability in anorexia nervosa mandates admission rather than brief ED observation (Source: RANZCP Eating Disorders CPG).

Multiple ANZAED/RANZCP medical instability criteria are met (bradycardia below 40, postural drop over 20 mmHg, hypothermia below 35.5, potassium below 3.0, phosphate below 0.75, glucose below 3.5); the priority is a monitored medical bed for stabilisation and structured refeeding before any specialist eating disorder placement (Source: ANZAED/RANZCP Practice and Treatment Guide for Eating Disorders; NSW Health Eating Disorders Toolkit).

explanation.summary: Refeeding syndrome is driven by insulin surge after starvation, causing intracellular shift of phosphate, potassium and magnesium and expansion of extracellular fluid. Prophylaxis is thiamine before any carbohydrate, staged energy advancement, and daily monitoring in the first week. Australian practice has moved away from ultra-low starting calories toward monitored moderate starts.
key_points: Highest risk: BMI below 14, intake below 500 kcal/day for over a week, prior low electrolytes.
Thiamine 100-300 mg IV or oral before glucose in severe cases.
Daily phosphate, potassium, magnesium for the first 5-7 days.
explanation.pearls: A drop in phosphate to below 0.32 mmol/L in the first 72 hours of refeeding is the hallmark biochemical trigger for refeeding syndrome.

options.rationale: Contemporary refeeding guidance in severe restriction starts at around 20 kcal/kg/day (about 900 kcal for this patient), advances every 24-48 hours as electrolytes tolerate, with prophylactic thiamine 100-300 mg daily and daily phosphate, potassium and magnesium monitoring for the first week (Source: NSW Health Eating Disorders Toolkit; RANZCP Eating Disorders CPG).

5 kcal/kg/day is below current MARSIPAN and ANZAED guidance and risks underfeeding syndrome; the trend has moved to higher starting energy with daily electrolyte checks rather than very low calorie starts (Source: NSW Health Eating Disorders Toolkit).

50 kcal/kg/day at BMI 14.9 with prolonged restriction risks classical refeeding syndrome with rapid drops in phosphate, potassium and magnesium; energy should be advanced gradually with daily monitoring (Source: RANZCP Eating Disorders CPG).
Prolonged starvation on the ward worsens catabolism; electrolyte replacement and cautious refeeding should proceed together rather than waiting (Source: RANZCP Eating Disorders CPG).

Intravenous glucose without thiamine can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy in the malnourished, and IV dextrose is not the primary refeeding modality; oral or nasogastric enteral feeding is preferred (Source: AMH).

explanation.summary: The Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale is used at every perinatal contact under Australian universal screening. A score of 13 or above indicates probable depression and prompts a diagnostic interview, while any positive response to item 10 mandates immediate risk assessment regardless of total score. Australian first line for mild to moderate perinatal depression is structured psychological therapy with pharmacotherapy for moderate to severe illness.
key_points: EPDS 13+ = probable depression, prompt assessment.
Item 10 above 0 triggers immediate safety review regardless of total.
Sertraline is the preferred SSRI when pharmacotherapy is indicated in breastfeeding.
explanation.pearls: Antenatal EPDS at booking and third trimester and postnatal 6-12 weeks is the COPE-recommended schedule for universal perinatal screening in Australia.

sources.label: NSW Health Perinatal and Infant Mental Health

options.rationale: COPE guidance treats EPDS scores of 13 or higher as suggestive of probable depression requiring further assessment, not routine reassurance and delayed repeat screening (Source: COPE Perinatal Mental Health Guideline).

COPE and RANZCP recommend acting on a positive EPDS at 13 or above with a diagnostic interview at the same visit rather than delaying two weeks for a repeat screen (Source: COPE Perinatal Mental Health Guideline).

SSRI monotherapy is appropriate for moderate to severe illness, prior severe episodes, or where therapy is unavailable or declined; psychological therapy is the recommended first line for mild to moderate perinatal depression (Source: RANZCP Perinatal CPG).

Mother and baby unit admission is reserved for severe depression, postpartum psychosis, or active safety concerns; an EPDS of 14 with no risk features is manageable in the community (Source: NSW Health Perinatal and Infant Mental Health).
source_refs: NSW Health Perinatal and Infant Mental Health

options.rationale: EPDS 13 or above triggers a full clinical assessment for a mood disorder; first line management of mild to moderate perinatal depression in a woman without prior severe illness is structured psychological therapy (CBT or IPT) with early review, escalating to pharmacotherapy if inadequate response or worsening (Source: COPE Perinatal Mental Health Guideline; RANZCP Perinatal CPG).

explanation.summary: Sertraline and paroxetine are the SSRIs with the lowest relative infant dose via breast milk and are preferred first line in lactation. Prior good response to a specific SSRI is a strong argument for restarting the same agent given individual pharmacogenomic variability. Continued breastfeeding is compatible with effective maternal treatment and is protective for infant attachment.
key_points: Sertraline: relative infant dose <2%, extensively characterised in breastfeeding.
Avoid fluoxetine at initiation in lactation (long half life, norfluoxetine).
Restart the SSRI that previously worked when tolerability was good.
explanation.pearls: Sertraline's relative infant dose sits around 0.5% of the weight-adjusted maternal dose, well below the 10% conservative safety cut off used in lactation pharmacology.

options.rationale: Agomelatine has minimal lactation safety data and requires LFT monitoring; it is not recommended in the perinatal period as a first line antidepressant (Source: AMH).

Fluoxetine has a long half life and its active metabolite norfluoxetine accumulates in breastfed infants; sertraline or paroxetine are preferred when initiating an SSRI in a lactating woman (Source: eTG Psychotropic).

Citalopram is compatible with breastfeeding but is not preferred over sertraline when there is a prior positive sertraline response and better infant exposure data for sertraline (Source: RANZCP Perinatal CPG).

Venlafaxine is reserved for treatment resistant depression or as second line where an SSRI trial has failed; it is not first line in a woman with previous SSRI response (Source: RANZCP Perinatal CPG).

Sertraline has one of the lowest infant plasma to maternal plasma ratios of the SSRIs, well characterised safety data in breastfeeding, and her prior good response makes it the rational first choice; the RANZCP and eTG both list it as first line for perinatal depression in a woman who wishes to continue breastfeeding (Source: RANZCP Perinatal CPG; eTG Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Postpartum psychosis has an incidence around 1-2 per 1000 births, peaks in the first 2 weeks postnatally, and carries a suicide rate around 2 per 1000 and infanticide risk around 4%. It is treated as a psychiatric emergency with urgent admission, ideally to a mother and baby unit to preserve the maternal-infant relationship. Family history of bipolar disorder confers up to 20-fold increased risk.
key_points: Emergency admission is the default; involuntary if capacity impaired or refusing.
Prefer mother and baby unit when available; otherwise nearest acute bed.
Antipsychotic plus mood stabiliser typical; ECT for rapid response.
explanation.pearls: Around 20-25% of women with a personal history of bipolar I develop postpartum psychosis after childbirth, making prophylactic lithium in the immediate postpartum period a considered option in specialist care.

sources.label: NSW Health Perinatal and Infant Mental Health

options.rationale: Separating mother and infant is often harmful and unnecessary when a mother and baby unit can safely admit both; child protection notification is a parallel duty but does not replace maternal psychiatric admission (Source: NSW Health Perinatal and Infant Mental Health).
source_refs: NSW Health Perinatal and Infant Mental Health

options.rationale: Community management of postpartum psychosis with active safety concerns and infant risk is unsafe regardless of medication; inpatient care with mother and baby is the standard (Source: RANZCP Perinatal CPG).

Partner supervision cannot substitute for inpatient containment when there is a rapidly evolving psychosis with concrete infant risk behaviours; 72 hour delay is unsafe (Source: RANZCP Perinatal CPG).

Postnatal wards are not equipped for acute psychosis containment; she also lacks capacity to consent to informal admission given active delusional beliefs about the doctors (Source: NSW Mental Health Act 2007).

Postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency with high risk of infant harm and maternal suicide; when the mother refuses voluntary admission, section 19 or 20 scheduling under the NSW Mental Health Act 2007 with transfer to a mother and baby unit (or nearest acute psychiatric bed) is indicated (Source: NSW Mental Health Act 2007; RANZCP Perinatal CPG).

explanation.summary: ECT is highly effective for severe melancholic depression, psychotic depression, catatonia, treatment resistant depression, and severe mania. In NSW consent is either given by the patient with capacity or authorised by the Mental Health Review Tribunal on application; substitute decision makers cannot consent to ECT. Two consultant certificates support the application and course length must be specified.
key_points: Response rates 70-90% in melancholic and psychotic depression.
Bilateral ECT is faster but more cognitive impact than right unilateral.
Anaesthetic workup: airway assessment, cardiac and dental review.
explanation.pearls: In NSW the Mental Health Review Tribunal authorises a specified number of ECT treatments (typically up to 12) per application; further courses require reapplication.

options.rationale: In NSW ECT cannot be authorised by a substitute decision maker; the NSW Mental Health Act requires either the patient's own informed consent or an application to the Mental Health Review Tribunal for a specific number of treatments (Source: NSW Mental Health Act 2007).

Her nihilistic delusion impairs capacity to weigh risks and benefits, so relying on next-day consent risks proceeding without valid consent; a tribunal pathway is required (Source: RANZCP Position Statement on ECT).

Emergency ECT in NSW still requires either patient consent, tribunal authorisation, or in a genuine emergency the Chief Psychiatrist's approval; the doctrine of necessity does not itself authorise ECT (Source: NSW Mental Health Act 2007).

Under Chapter 4 Part 2 of the NSW Mental Health Act 2007, where a patient is incapable of consenting to ECT the treating team must apply to the Mental Health Review Tribunal for an order authorising a specific number of treatments; the two consultant certificates support the application (Source: NSW Mental Health Act 2007; RANZCP Position Statement on ECT).

She has already failed adequate trials of three antidepressants and has severe melancholic depression with nihilistic delusions and refusal of intake; ECT is a first line rather than salvage option in this presentation (Source: RANZCP Position Statement on ECT).

explanation.summary: Cognitive impairment is the main side effect of ECT and includes acute post-ictal confusion, anterograde amnesia during the course, and variable retrograde amnesia. Older age, bilateral placement, brief pulse (compared with ultra-brief), higher charge, and closer inter-treatment spacing all increase burden. Switching to right unilateral ultra-brief pulse is the primary risk mitigation without abandoning ECT.
key_points: Bilateral fastest response, greatest cognitive impact.
Right unilateral ultra-brief pulse preferred where cognition is a concern.
Retrograde amnesia most often around the course itself and improves over months.
explanation.pearls: Ultra-brief pulse widths (0.3 ms or less) reduce cognitive side effects while maintaining efficacy in most trials of right unilateral ECT.

options.rationale: Right unilateral ultra-brief pulse ECT has substantially less anterograde and retrograde amnesia than bilateral ECT with only modestly slower response; switching modality is the standard response to significant cognitive burden mid-course (Source: RANZCP Position Statement on ECT).

Cholinesterase inhibitors are not routine adjuncts during ECT and do not address the mechanism of ECT related cognitive impairment; reducing the cognitive dose of ECT is the first step (Source: RANZCP Position Statement on ECT).

Stopping a working ECT course after only four sessions in a responding psychotic depression risks relapse; modifying to a less cognitively burdensome technique preserves response (Source: RANZCP Position Statement on ECT).

Reducing frequency without changing placement does reduce cognitive burden but at the cost of slower recovery in a patient who is now responding; unilateral ultra-brief is a better trade-off (Source: RANZCP Position Statement on ECT).
Higher propofol doses raise seizure threshold and reduce ECT efficacy without addressing the underlying cognitive burden of bilateral stimulation (Source: RANZCP Position Statement on ECT).

explanation.summary: Serotonin syndrome and NMS share fever, autonomic instability and altered mental state but differ in tempo and neurology. Serotonin syndrome develops within hours of a serotonergic change and features clonus (especially lower limb), hyperreflexia and mydriasis. NMS develops over days on dopamine blockade with lead-pipe rigidity, hyporeflexia, high CK and normal pupils. Antidotes differ: cyproheptadine for serotonin syndrome; bromocriptine and dantrolene for NMS.
key_points: Clonus and hyperreflexia = serotonin syndrome; lead-pipe rigidity = NMS.
Hours after serotonergic change vs days on antipsychotic.
Benzodiazepines first for agitation in both; avoid antipsychotics in serotonin syndrome.
explanation.pearls: Tramadol added to any SSRI, SNRI, MAOI or triptan is a leading Australian trigger for serotonin syndrome and appears on the AMH interaction alert list.

options.rationale: Continuing the precipitating serotonergic combination will worsen the syndrome; paracetamol does not lower hyperthermia driven by increased muscle activity in serotonin syndrome (Source: eTG Toxicology and Toxinology).

Dantrolene is used in malignant hyperthermia and considered in severe NMS with muscle rigidity; the clonus and hyperreflexia pattern here is serotonin syndrome, where cyproheptadine is the specific antidote (Source: eTG Toxicology and Toxinology).

Bromocriptine is a dopamine agonist considered for NMS to counter dopamine blockade; NMS classically causes lead-pipe rigidity and much higher CK, not lower limb clonus with hyperreflexia (Source: eTG Toxicology and Toxinology).

The clinical picture (lower limb clonus, hyperreflexia, mydriasis, autonomic hyperactivity within hours of adding tramadol to an SSRI) is serotonin syndrome by Hunter criteria; management is withdrawal of the offending agents, benzodiazepines for agitation and hyperthermia, and cyproheptadine as a 5-HT2A antagonist for moderate to severe cases (Source: eTG Toxicology and Toxinology; AMH).
Haloperidol worsens autonomic instability and is contraindicated for agitation in serotonin syndrome; benzodiazepines are the correct sedative (Source: eTG Toxicology and Toxinology).

explanation.summary: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is a rare but life threatening reaction to D2 blockade, most often within the first 2 weeks of starting or escalating a high potency antipsychotic. Mortality is 5-20% mainly from renal failure secondary to rhabdomyolysis, aspiration, and arrhythmia. Recovery takes 7-10 days after cessation of the offending agent.
key_points: Tetrad: hyperthermia, rigidity, autonomic instability, altered mental state.
Stop the antipsychotic; supportive care in a monitored bed.
Consider bromocriptine, amantadine or dantrolene in severe cases.
explanation.pearls: CK over 1000 U/L in the context of new antipsychotic initiation with fever and rigidity is a diagnostic anchor for NMS in Australian ED practice.

options.rationale: Anticholinergics like procyclidine treat drug induced parkinsonism but do not resolve NMS; continuing the antipsychotic is dangerous once NMS is recognised (Source: eTG Toxicology and Toxinology).

The picture (recent dose escalation of a high potency D2 blocker, hyperthermia over 38.5, lead-pipe rigidity with hyporeflexia, autonomic instability, CK over 1000, leucocytosis) is NMS; management is stopping the antipsychotic, aggressive supportive care in a monitored bed, and adding a dopamine agonist such as bromocriptine or amantadine (Source: eTG Toxicology and Toxinology; AMH).

A lorazepam challenge is appropriate for catatonia but does not address life threatening hyperthermia and rhabdomyolysis; NMS needs immediate supportive care and specific pharmacological reversal (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG).

There are no serotonergic agents on board and the neurology (rigidity with hyporeflexia, not clonus and hyperreflexia) is against serotonin syndrome; cyproheptadine is not the answer (Source: eTG Toxicology and Toxinology).

Dantrolene is an option in severe rigidity but must be combined with cessation of the antipsychotic and monitored bed level care; the offending drug must always be stopped (Source: eTG Toxicology and Toxinology).

explanation.summary: Symptom triggered diazepam guided by CIWA-Ar is the preferred inpatient regimen for uncomplicated alcohol withdrawal in Australia. Diazepam's long half life provides an inherent taper. Parenteral thiamine (300 mg IV daily for 3-5 days) is given before glucose to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy. Fixed dose regimens are reserved for higher risk patients or where symptom scoring cannot be done reliably.
key_points: Symptom triggered = less total benzodiazepine, shorter withdrawal.
Fixed dose reserved for prior seizures/DTs or unreliable scoring.
Lorazepam preferred in significant hepatic impairment.
explanation.pearls: In NSW the CIWA-Ar action threshold is typically 10; scores above 20 with rising trend or hallucinations should prompt consideration of transfer to a higher acuity bed for delirium tremens.

options.rationale: Lorazepam is reserved for significant hepatic impairment given hepatic first pass; diazepam self-tapers due to long half life and is preferred when liver function is preserved (Source: eTG Addiction Medicine).

Fixed schedule benzodiazepines are reserved for patients with prior withdrawal seizures or DTs, unreliable scoring, or where nursing capacity for symptom triggered dosing is limited; symptom triggered is preferred here (Source: NSW Health Alcohol Withdrawal Guidelines).

Symptom triggered diazepam titrated to CIWA-Ar (dose typically 10-20 mg orally when score above 10) is the preferred Australian regimen for uncomplicated alcohol withdrawal in patients without prior seizures or DTs, using less total benzodiazepine than fixed schedules and with earlier detection of worsening (Source: NSW Health Alcohol Withdrawal Guidelines; eTG Addiction Medicine).
Chlordiazepoxide is used in some UK regimens but Australian guidelines prefer diazepam; scheduled dosing without CIWA-Ar risks under or overdosing (Source: NSW Health Alcohol Withdrawal Guidelines).
A CIWA-Ar of 12 already meets the threshold for symptom triggered diazepam; waiting to CIWA-Ar 20 delays treatment and risks seizures and DTs (Source: NSW Health Alcohol Withdrawal Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Wernicke encephalopathy classically presents with any of the triad of encephalopathy, ophthalmoplegia (nystagmus, sixth nerve palsy) and ataxia, but only one is needed in a chronically undernourished heavy drinker to justify treatment. IV thiamine 500 mg three times daily for 2-3 days followed by 250 mg daily and then oral maintenance is the Australian regimen. Magnesium is a cofactor and must be replaced.
key_points: Any one of triad + chronic alcohol use = treat empirically.
Thiamine before any glucose to prevent precipitation.
500 mg IV three times daily for 2-3 days; taper as symptoms improve.
explanation.pearls: Anaphylactic reactions to IV thiamine occur at rates below 1 per 100 000 doses; resuscitation equipment should be available but the treatment is not withheld for that reason.

options.rationale: 100 mg once daily is inadequate for suspected Wernicke; treatment doses in Australia are 500 mg IV three times daily; magnesium repletion is required for thiamine to function (Source: AMH).
Oral thiamine has poor bioavailability in dependent drinkers; giving dextrose before adequate parenteral thiamine can precipitate or worsen Wernicke encephalopathy (Source: eTG Addiction Medicine).

Wernicke encephalopathy is likely (encephalopathy, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia in a chronically undernourished heavy drinker); Australian guidance is high dose parenteral thiamine (500 mg IV three times daily for 2-3 days then taper), correction of magnesium (a cofactor for thiamine dependent enzymes), and any dextrose given only after the first thiamine dose to avoid precipitating or worsening Wernicke (Source: eTG Addiction Medicine; AMH).

Serum thiamine is not required to justify treatment; empirical high dose parenteral thiamine is given whenever Wernicke is suspected because the cost of delay is a Korsakoff amnestic syndrome (Source: eTG Addiction Medicine).

IM thiamine 100 mg daily is prophylaxis dosing (used in dependent drinkers without Wernicke features), not treatment; her signs meet Wernicke criteria and warrant IV treatment doses (Source: eTG Addiction Medicine).

explanation.summary: Buprenorphine is a high affinity partial mu agonist that displaces full agonists and can precipitate withdrawal if given too early. NSW OST induction requires objective moderate withdrawal (OOWS 5+ or COWS 12+) at least 12 hours after last short-acting opioid or 24-48 hours after methadone. Combination buprenorphine-naloxone is preferred for community use; long-acting depot (subcutaneous buprenorphine) is an option once stabilised on sublingual dosing.
key_points: Wait for moderate withdrawal to avoid precipitated withdrawal.
Start 4/1 mg sublingual, review 2 hourly, titrate as needed on day one.
Long-acting depot buprenorphine available once stabilised.
explanation.pearls: Sublocade depot buprenorphine (100-300 mg subcutaneously monthly) requires prior stabilisation on transmucosal buprenorphine of at least 8-24 mg/day for 7 days before first depot injection.

sources.label: NSW Opioid Treatment Program Clinical Guidelines

options.rationale: Standard buprenorphine induction requires objective moderate withdrawal (OOWS 5 or above) at least 12 hours after last short-acting opioid or 24-48 hours after methadone to avoid precipitated withdrawal, then starting at 4/1 mg with titration by symptom review over the first day (Source: NSW Opioid Treatment Program Clinical Guidelines; RACGP Prescribing Drugs of Dependence).
source_refs: NSW Opioid Treatment Program Clinical Guidelines

options.rationale: Objective withdrawal is still mild (OOWS 4) and short-acting opioids clear over 12-24 hours; starting buprenorphine at this point risks precipitated withdrawal because buprenorphine displaces full agonists from the mu receptor (Source: RACGP Prescribing Drugs of Dependence; NSW Opioid Treatment Program Clinical Guidelines).
source_refs: NSW Opioid Treatment Program Clinical Guidelines

options.rationale: Methadone induction starts at 20-30 mg with cautious titration over days because of the risk of accumulation and death during induction; 40 mg is not a safe starting dose and switching against her preference isn't warranted (Source: NSW Opioid Treatment Program Clinical Guidelines).
source_refs: NSW Opioid Treatment Program Clinical Guidelines

options.rationale: Naltrexone in an actively opioid dependent user precipitates severe withdrawal and is contraindicated without a fully documented opioid free period of at least 7 days; it is also not aligned with her stated OST preference (Source: RACGP Prescribing Drugs of Dependence).

Combination buprenorphine-naloxone is the preferred agent for community induction because of reduced injection diversion; starting with mono product without indication and delaying until reaching adequate withdrawal is standard, regardless of formulation choice (Source: NSW Opioid Treatment Program Clinical Guidelines).
source_refs: NSW Opioid Treatment Program Clinical Guidelines

explanation.summary: Take-away doses in the NSW Opioid Treatment Program balance patient stability and quality of life against risks of diversion, overdose in third parties, and paediatric accidental exposure. Stability criteria include a minimum period on the current dose, negative UDS for illicit substances, absence of diversion or overdose risk, secure storage, and stable social circumstances. Take-aways are increased incrementally with review.
key_points: Minimum around 3 months on methadone before first take-aways.
Start 1-2 take-aways/week; review at each escalation.
Secure lockable storage and safety plan mandatory.
explanation.pearls: NSW OTP allows up to 4 unsupervised methadone take-aways per week for highly stable patients, with any weekly plan requiring specialist consultation and documented dispensing at the authorised pharmacy.

sources.label: NSW Opioid Treatment Program Clinical Guidelines

options.rationale: NSW OST take-away doses are increased incrementally as stability is demonstrated; jumping straight to four take-aways bypasses the graded pathway and safety review at each step (Source: NSW Opioid Treatment Program Clinical Guidelines).
source_refs: NSW Opioid Treatment Program Clinical Guidelines

options.rationale: NSW OST guidance allows take-aways on a graded basis once stability is documented (minimum 3 months on methadone for the first take-aways, sustained abstinence from illicit drugs, no diversion risk, adequate storage); starting with 1-2 take-aways per week with structured review is standard (Source: NSW Opioid Treatment Program Clinical Guidelines; RACGP Prescribing Drugs of Dependence).
source_refs: NSW Opioid Treatment Program Clinical Guidelines

options.rationale: There is no 12 month minimum in NSW; the minimum is around 3 months of stable dosing on methadone with the other stability criteria met (Source: NSW Opioid Treatment Program Clinical Guidelines).
source_refs: NSW Opioid Treatment Program Clinical Guidelines

options.rationale: Buprenorphine-naloxone take-aways still require the same graded stability assessment and NSW OTP approvals; switching a stable methadone patient against his preference for administrative reasons is not appropriate (Source: NSW Opioid Treatment Program Clinical Guidelines).
source_refs: NSW Opioid Treatment Program Clinical Guidelines

options.rationale: Depot buprenorphine is a reasonable long term option but is not the immediate next step for a stable methadone patient asking for a small number of take-aways; his stated preference and current stability support a graded methadone take-away plan (Source: NSW Opioid Treatment Program Clinical Guidelines).
source_refs: NSW Opioid Treatment Program Clinical Guidelines

explanation.summary: OCD requires higher SSRI doses and longer trials than depression, typically 10-12 weeks at target dose before deciding response. First line pharmacotherapy is an SSRI (sertraline, fluoxetine, escitalopram) with ERP; clomipramine is second line. Augmentation with low dose risperidone or aripiprazole is considered after failed adequate SSRI trials.
key_points: OCD needs higher SSRI doses (sertraline 150-200 mg, fluoxetine 40-80 mg).
10-12 week trial at target dose before non-response.
ERP is essential; medication supports rather than replaces therapy.
explanation.pearls: The Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale (Y-BOCS) is the standard Australian measure of OCD severity and treatment response, with a 25-35% reduction after 10-12 weeks considered a meaningful medication response.

sources.label: RANZCP Anxiety and Related Disorders CPG

options.rationale: Fluvoxamine is effective in OCD but has substantial CYP interactions (including with the combined oral contraceptive) making it a less convenient first choice; sertraline is preferred here (Source: eTG Psychotropic; AMH).

OCD responds to SSRIs at doses at the upper end of the antidepressant range; sertraline 150-200 mg/day is a first line Australian regimen with a favourable interaction profile in a woman on combined oral contraceptive (Source: eTG Psychotropic; AMH; RANZCP Anxiety and Related Disorders CPG).
source_refs: RANZCP Anxiety and Related Disorders CPG

options.rationale: Clomipramine is effective in OCD but is reserved for SSRI failure due to anticholinergic burden, weight gain, seizure risk at higher doses and ECG monitoring; it is not first line (Source: eTG Psychotropic).

Benzodiazepines have no place in the maintenance treatment of OCD and can undermine ERP by suppressing anxiety exposure; dependence risk over months is significant (Source: RANZCP Anxiety and Related Disorders CPG).
source_refs: RANZCP Anxiety and Related Disorders CPG

options.rationale: Antipsychotic augmentation of an SSRI is reserved for OCD that has failed adequate SSRI trials at high dose; using it before any SSRI trial is not appropriate (Source: RANZCP Anxiety and Related Disorders CPG).
source_refs: RANZCP Anxiety and Related Disorders CPG

explanation.summary: SSRIs are first line for panic disorder alongside CBT. Starting at low doses and titrating slowly reduces the classic early jitteriness that can otherwise be misattributed by patients to worsening panic and lead to premature discontinuation. Adequate trials require 6-8 weeks at target dose. Benzodiazepines are reserved for short bridging use and are generally avoided due to dependence risk.
key_points: Halve the antidepressant starting dose in panic disorder.
Assess response at 6-8 weeks at target dose.
CBT is at least as effective as medication and durable long term.
explanation.pearls: Alprazolam is a Schedule 8 restricted benzodiazepine in Australia requiring specialist authority; short and intermediate acting benzodiazepines are avoided in panic disorder because of high dependence and rebound risk.

sources.label: RANZCP Anxiety and Related Disorders CPG

options.rationale: Alprazolam causes tolerance, rebound anxiety and dependence in panic disorder and is no longer S8 available in Australia without specialist authority; it is not a first line long term treatment (Source: RANZCP Anxiety and Related Disorders CPG).
source_refs: RANZCP Anxiety and Related Disorders CPG

options.rationale: Starting at 100 mg risks initial anxiety worsening and jitteriness in panic disorder; a low start with slow titration is the recommended approach (Source: eTG Psychotropic).

In panic disorder starting SSRIs at half the usual antidepressant starting dose (sertraline 25 mg, escitalopram 5 mg, fluoxetine 10 mg) reduces the risk of initial anxiety exacerbation; titration to target dose over 2-4 weeks with response assessed at 6-8 weeks is standard (Source: eTG Psychotropic; RANZCP Anxiety and Related Disorders CPG).
source_refs: RANZCP Anxiety and Related Disorders CPG

options.rationale: Beta blockers may attenuate autonomic symptoms in performance anxiety but do not prevent panic attacks in panic disorder and are not first line monotherapy (Source: RANZCP Anxiety and Related Disorders CPG).
source_refs: RANZCP Anxiety and Related Disorders CPG

options.rationale: Mirtazapine can be considered second line in panic disorder, particularly with insomnia or weight loss, but SSRIs are first line with the largest evidence base (Source: eTG Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Autism spectrum disorder in adult women is under-diagnosed because of camouflaging: internally driven behavioural adaptation that hides autistic traits in social settings. Presentations often include a long history of anxiety and depression with partial treatment response, exhaustion after socialising, routine dependence, sensory sensitivities, and family history. Australian diagnostic pathway is multidisciplinary using ADOS-2 and ADI-R with a developmental informant.
key_points: Masking is common in women and delays diagnosis into adulthood.
AQ-50 is a screen, not a diagnostic tool.
Multidisciplinary assessment includes ADOS-2, ADI-R and informant history.
explanation.pearls: Adult women referred for autism assessment have a mean age at diagnosis around a decade later than men and are more likely to have prior misdiagnoses of borderline personality disorder or treatment resistant depression.

sources.label: National Guideline for Autism Assessment and Diagnosis

options.rationale: Successful academic and vocational function does not exclude autism, particularly in women who mask; the developmental screens of the era often missed autism in girls and cannot be used to rule out a current diagnosis (Source: National Guideline for Autism Assessment and Diagnosis).
source_refs: National Guideline for Autism Assessment and Diagnosis

options.rationale: The RANZCP and Australian Autism Alliance guideline recommends multidisciplinary diagnostic assessment using ADOS-2 (semi-structured observation) and ADI-R (developmental history interview with an informant), particularly important for women who mask; an elevated AQ warrants specialist assessment rather than treatment change (Source: A National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorders in Australia; RANZCP Position Statement).
source_refs: National Guideline for Autism Assessment and Diagnosis

options.rationale: ADHD and autism can co-occur but starting a stimulant without a diagnostic assessment is not appropriate; her presenting features (routine dependence, sensory sensitivities, social masking) are more suggestive of autism than of ADHD (Source: eTG Psychotropic).

The AQ-50 is a screening tool and cannot substitute for structured diagnostic assessment; a positive screen indicates the need for referral, not diagnosis (Source: National Guideline for Autism Assessment and Diagnosis).
source_refs: National Guideline for Autism Assessment and Diagnosis

options.rationale: Deferring diagnostic assessment misses the opportunity to reframe her difficulties, access supports, and tailor mental health care; her AQ-50 warrants specialist assessment now (Source: RANZCP Position Statement on Autism).

explanation.summary: Conduct disorder is defined by repetitive violations of the rights of others or major age-appropriate rules across four domains: aggression to people/animals, destruction of property, deceit/theft, and serious rule violations. Childhood-onset (before age 10) and adolescent-onset subtypes have different prognoses, and the limited prosocial emotions specifier identifies a subgroup with a higher risk of persistent antisocial trajectory. Early intervention (parent management training, multisystemic therapy) improves outcomes.
key_points: ODD = defiance and irritability without rights violations.
Conduct disorder = rights and rules violations across 4 domains.
Limited prosocial emotions specifier identifies higher-risk subgroup.
explanation.pearls: Parent management training and multisystemic therapy are the evidence-based first line interventions for conduct disorder; pharmacotherapy is reserved for comorbid ADHD, mood disorder, or aggression that has not responded to psychological therapy.

options.rationale: ODD centres on angry/irritable mood, argumentative/defiant behaviour and vindictiveness, but does NOT include serious violations of others' rights or major rules; his behaviours have progressed beyond ODD to violations that meet conduct disorder criteria (Source: DSM-5-TR; RANZCP Child Adolescent CPG).

DMDD requires chronic severe irritability with frequent temper outbursts in a child before age 10 and is not diagnosed alongside conduct disorder; his hallmark features are rights violations, not sustained irritability (Source: DSM-5-TR).

He meets criteria for conduct disorder (aggression to people, destruction of property including fire setting, serious rule violations, deceit/theft over 12 months) with onset of the serious behaviours after age 10 (adolescent onset) and the limited prosocial emotions specifier (lack of remorse); classification directs prognosis and intervention (Source: DSM-5-TR; RANZCP Child Adolescent CPG).
Antisocial personality disorder requires age 18 or older with a prior conduct disorder diagnosis; at 13 he is too young for that diagnosis (Source: DSM-5-TR).
No substance use has been identified; a substance-induced diagnosis requires temporal linkage to substance use, which is absent here (Source: DSM-5-TR).

explanation.summary: The EPPIC (Early Psychosis Prevention and Intervention Centre) model, developed at Orygen in Melbourne, is now delivered nationally through headspace Early Psychosis and state early psychosis services. It targets young people aged 12-25 with first episode psychosis, providing low dose antipsychotic, CBT for psychosis, family work, vocational and educational support in the first 2-5 years, when duration of untreated psychosis and outcome are most modifiable.
key_points: Duration of untreated psychosis predicts long term outcome.
EPPIC combines low dose antipsychotic + psychosocial + family + vocational.
Delivered via headspace Early Psychosis and state services.
explanation.pearls: Each additional month of untreated psychosis is associated with worse symptomatic and functional outcomes, driving the emphasis on same-week specialist assessment in the Australian early psychosis pathway.

options.rationale: Six weeks of persistent delusions and daily auditory hallucinations meet the threshold for first episode psychosis, not transient adolescent perceptual experiences; watchful waiting worsens duration of untreated psychosis (Source: Orygen EPPIC Model).

First episode psychosis is typically initiated on lower doses of atypical antipsychotic (e.g. risperidone 1-2 mg, aripiprazole 5-10 mg) within a specialist early psychosis pathway; olanzapine 10 mg started in primary care alone misses the multidisciplinary components (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG).
Delay of 8-12 weeks worsens the duration of untreated psychosis, which is a strong predictor of poor long term outcome; urgent early psychosis referral is required (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG).

First episode psychosis in a young person warrants referral to a youth focused early psychosis program (EPPIC model, delivered in Australia through headspace Early Psychosis and state services), which combines low dose atypical antipsychotic, family involvement, psychosocial intervention and vocational support with better long term outcomes than adult community services (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG; Orygen EPPIC Model).

He is cooperative, has no aggression, no self-harm risk, and has agreed to treatment; involuntary admission is not justified when he accepts assessment and treatment via community early psychosis services (Source: NSW Mental Health Act 2007).

explanation.summary: The social and emotional wellbeing (SEWB) framework, articulated in the National Strategic Framework for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples' Mental Health and Social and Emotional Wellbeing, situates mental health within connection to body, mind and emotions, family and kinship, community, culture, Country, and spirituality. Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Services and SEWB workers provide culturally safe care. Mainstream services are offered alongside rather than as substitutes.
key_points: SEWB extends beyond individual mood to family, culture and Country.
ACCHS and SEWB workers are the primary door to care.
Cultural safety is a clinical safety issue, not an add-on.
explanation.pearls: The Kessler K10 has been adapted for use in Aboriginal populations as the K5 and aK10 with revised cut offs in some communities; local ACCHS teams can guide interpretation and follow up in that context.

sources.label: National Strategic Framework for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples' Mental Health and Social and Emotional Wellbeing
RACGP National Guide to a preventive health assessment for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people
