He is engaged, agrees the medication helps and is participating in planning, so a voluntary arrangement should be offered first. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline

options.rationale: A depot preparation removes the daily decision that he identifies as the point of failure, maintains plasma levels for weeks and makes disengagement visible to the team immediately rather than after symptoms return. Australian guidance recommends offering a long-acting injectable early in the course of illness, particularly after relapse attributable to non-adherence, rather than reserving it for repeated failure. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline

explanation.summary: Long term opioid therapy for chronic non cancer pain produces modest analgesic benefit that attenuates over time, while harms accumulate with dose, and Australian guidance recommends keeping doses below 50 mg oral morphine equivalent daily and reviewing carefully above that. Real time prescription monitoring is now operating across Australian jurisdictions and reveals multiple prescriber use that was previously invisible, which is best raised openly with the patient rather than treated as an accusation. Early requests, multiple sources, declining function and loss of analgesic effect together indicate that the treatment is failing and may signal an emerging opioid use disorder, which is assessed on the criteria of impaired control, social impairment, risky use and pharmacological features. Tapering is the intervention, undertaken slowly at around ten per cent of the dose every two to four weeks with faster reduction early and slower reduction at low doses, alongside active non opioid pain management and treatment of sleep and mood. Where a taper repeatedly fails or a use disorder is diagnosed, transfer to buprenorphine or methadone through an opioid treatment program is the appropriate step rather than continued escalation.
key_points: Benefit attenuates over time while dose related harm continues to accumulate
Real time prescription monitoring reveals multiple sourcing and should be raised openly
Abrupt cessation increases overdose death and suicide and drives illicit sourcing
Taper at about ten per cent every two to four weeks with non opioid pain management
A failed taper or a diagnosed use disorder warrants transfer to buprenorphine
explanation.pearls: Prescribe take home naloxone at the same consultation: anyone on more than 50 mg oral morphine equivalent daily is in the higher risk group for overdose, and it is available without prescription in Australian pharmacies under the take home naloxone program, so the barrier is the conversation rather than the cost.

sources.label: RACGP: Prescribing drugs of dependence in general practice

options.rationale: Abrupt cessation after six years of continuous use precipitates withdrawal, drives people to obtain opioids elsewhere, and is associated with increased overdose death and suicide in cohort studies. Naltrexone requires a completed withdrawal before it can be started safely at all. (Source: RACGP: Prescribing drugs of dependence in general practice)
source_refs: RACGP: Prescribing drugs of dependence in general practice

options.rationale: Pregabalin is used for confirmed neuropathic pain, which is argued against here by a negative straight leg raise with normal power, reflexes and sensation. Combining a gabapentinoid with an opioid also substantially increases the risk of respiratory depression and overdose death. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Analgesic)

Consolidating prescribing to one practitioner and one pharmacy stops the multiple sourcing that the monitoring system has identified, and a slow reduction of the order of ten per cent every two to four weeks is tolerable and avoids precipitating withdrawal. Reduction is indicated because the opioid has lost effect, function is deteriorating and the behaviour signals loss of control, and it is combined with active non opioid pain management. (Source: RACGP: Prescribing drugs of dependence in general practice)
source_refs: RACGP: Prescribing drugs of dependence in general practice

options.rationale: Rotating to a more potent lipophilic opioid at a time of escalating use and declining function raises the total opioid load and the overdose risk, and conversion errors between oxycodone and fentanyl are a recognised cause of death. Steadier blood levels do not address tolerance or the loss of control. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Opioid analgesics)

Epidural corticosteroid has a limited role in radicular pain with clear nerve root compression and provides short lived benefit at best, and he has no radicular signs. Deferring the prescribing problem behind a procedural referral leaves multiple sourcing and escalating use running for months. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Analgesic)

explanation.summary: Wernicke encephalopathy results from thiamine deficiency and classically presents with confusion, ophthalmoplegia and ataxia, although the full triad appears in only a minority and many cases are recognised only at autopsy. Untreated or inadequately treated episodes progress to Korsakoff syndrome, a chronic amnestic state characterised by dense anterograde amnesia, variable retrograde amnesia and confabulation, with attention, language and executive function relatively preserved. The dissociation between severely impaired delayed recall and intact attention is the key bedside finding, and it is what separates this from delirium, where attention is disturbed, and from Alzheimer disease, where other cognitive domains decline alongside memory. Australian guidance is to give parenteral thiamine to anyone with hazardous alcohol use who is admitted, because oral absorption is saturable and reduced by alcohol, and to give it before any glucose containing fluid, since a carbohydrate load consumes remaining thiamine and can precipitate the encephalopathy. Recovery in Korsakoff syndrome occurs in roughly a quarter and improves in many more over three to twelve months of abstinence and replacement, so definitive decisions about accommodation, capacity and prognosis are deferred until that trajectory is clear.
key_points: The classic triad is present in a minority and the diagnosis is frequently missed
Dense amnesia with preserved attention and language is the bedside signature
Confabulation is a memory gap filled in, not a delusion, and is not treated with antipsychotics
Oral thiamine absorption is saturable and inadequate in people who drink heavily
Cognition improves over three to twelve months, so placement decisions are deferred
explanation.pearls: Give parenteral thiamine before any glucose containing fluid in anyone with hazardous alcohol use: a carbohydrate load consumes the last of the remaining thiamine as a cofactor and can convert a subclinical deficiency into an irreversible amnestic syndrome within hours.

sources.label: NHMRC: Australian guidelines for the treatment of alcohol problems
RANZCP: Assessment and management of cognitive impairment

options.rationale: Dense anterograde amnesia with confabulation and preserved attention, fluency and executive function is the amnestic syndrome that follows inadequately treated thiamine deficiency, and three days of oral tablets is far short of what is required because oral absorption is saturable and impaired in people who drink heavily. Cognition continues to recover over three to twelve months with abstinence and adequate replacement, so placement, capacity and prognosis decisions made this week will be based on a floor he has not yet reached. (Source: NHMRC: Australian guidelines for the treatment of alcohol problems)
source_refs: NHMRC: Australian guidelines for the treatment of alcohol problems

options.rationale: Cholinesterase inhibition is appropriate for Alzheimer disease, which presents with gradually progressive memory loss accompanied by word finding difficulty, visuospatial decline and functional deterioration over years. His deficit appeared abruptly in the context of repeated withdrawals, spares language and executive function, and has a treatable nutritional cause. (Source: RANZCP: Assessment and management of cognitive impairment)
source_refs: RANZCP: Assessment and management of cognitive impairment

options.rationale: Community follow up is an essential part of his care and should certainly be arranged. Discharging a man who cannot form new memories to live alone means he cannot reliably take medication, keep appointments, manage a stove or recall safety advice, and the amnesia itself will prevent him reporting that he is struggling. (Source: NHMRC: Australian guidelines for the treatment of alcohol problems)
source_refs: NHMRC: Australian guidelines for the treatment of alcohol problems

options.rationale: A guardianship application may ultimately be needed if the impairment proves permanent and he cannot make accommodation decisions. Capacity is assessed at the point a decision must be made and can improve substantially over months here, so applying now risks imposing a durable legal order on the basis of a recoverable state. (Source: RANZCP: Assessment and management of cognitive impairment)
source_refs: RANZCP: Assessment and management of cognitive impairment

options.rationale: Antipsychotic treatment targets delusions, which are fixed beliefs held with conviction and defended against evidence. Confabulation is the unintentional filling of a memory gap with plausible material, is not defended when challenged and varies from telling to telling, so it does not respond to dopamine blockade. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Zolpidem acts selectively at the alpha 1 subunit of the gamma aminobutyric acid type A receptor and can produce complex sleep behaviours in which a person carries out purposeful activity while not fully awake and has no memory of it afterwards. Reported behaviours include eating, cooking, making phone calls, having sex, leaving the house and driving, and Australian regulatory advice carries a specific warning about these events, including serious injuries and deaths. Risk rises with higher doses, with concurrent alcohol or other central nervous system depressants, and in women, who clear the drug more slowly. Because episodes occur at the lowest available dose, the response to any such event is permanent discontinuation rather than dose reduction, and switching to a benzodiazepine does not solve the problem since the mechanism is shared. Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia, covering stimulus control, sleep restriction, cognitive work and sleep hygiene, is the first line treatment for chronic insomnia in Australian guidance and maintains benefit after treatment ends, whereas hypnotics lose effect and are recommended only for short intermittent use.
key_points: Purposeful activity with no recall afterwards defines a complex sleep behaviour
Australian regulatory advice specifically warns about these events with this drug
Episodes occur at the lowest dose, so the drug is ceased rather than reduced
Benzodiazepines share the mechanism, so switching within the class does not help
Cognitive behavioural therapy is first line for chronic insomnia and outlasts hypnotics
explanation.pearls: Ask the bed partner rather than the patient when a hypnotic is being reviewed: the defining feature of these episodes is that the person has no memory of them, so a patient taking zolpidem will truthfully report no adverse effects while their partner has been watching them cook at three in the morning for months.

sources.label: Australian Medicines Handbook: Hypnotics and sedatives
RANZCP: Eating disorders clinical practice guideline

options.rationale: Complex sleep behaviours are more frequent at higher doses, which makes dose reduction an intuitive response, and lower doses are recommended for women because of slower clearance. The reaction occurs at the lowest available dose as well, so continuing the drug at any dose leaves her at risk of an episode involving cooking, driving or leaving the house. (Source: TGA: Zolpidem safety advisory)

Binge eating disorder involves recurrent consumption of large amounts of food with loss of control, distress, and preoccupation with weight and shape, and responds to psychological therapy and fluoxetine. It occurs in wakefulness with full awareness and recall, whereas she is unresponsive during the episodes, has no memory of them and eats substances no one would choose while awake. (Source: RANZCP: Eating disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Eating disorders clinical practice guideline

options.rationale: A sleep study is used when nocturnal seizures are suspected or when the history is genuinely ambiguous, and it may be needed later if behaviours continue after the drug is withdrawn. The history here is characteristic and a study takes weeks to arrange, during which she remains exposed to a recognised and reversible cause. (Source: TGA: Zolpidem safety advisory)

Temazepam acts on the same gamma aminobutyric acid receptor complex and also causes parasomnias, amnesia and next day impairment, so moving within the sedative hypnotic class does not remove the mechanism. Australian guidance limits all hypnotics in this class to short intermittent courses rather than nightly use for months. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Hypnotics and sedatives)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook: Hypnotics and sedatives

options.rationale: Eating, texting, walking or driving while not fully awake with no recollection afterwards is a complex sleep behaviour, a recognised adverse effect of this drug class that carries a regulatory warning in Australia, and the drug is stopped rather than reduced because episodes have occurred at all doses. Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia is the first line treatment for chronic insomnia in any case, outperforms hypnotics beyond the first few weeks and carries none of this risk. (Source: TGA: Zolpidem safety advisory)

explanation.summary: Primary polydipsia occurs in up to a fifth of people with long standing schizophrenia and produces hyponatraemia when water intake exceeds the kidney's maximal excretion capacity of roughly 800 to 1000 mL per hour. The biochemical signature is a low serum osmolality with a maximally dilute urine below about 100 mOsm/kg, which separates it definitively from the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis, where the urine is inappropriately concentrated, and from hypovolaemia, where urine sodium is low but urine osmolality is high. Diurnal weight gain of several kilograms across the day is a practical bedside marker used in inpatient units to detect water loading before it becomes dangerous. Severe symptomatic hyponatraemia with seizures or coma is treated with hypertonic saline regardless of cause, because cerebral oedema is the immediate threat, and the total correction is then limited to 8 to 10 mmol/L over 24 hours to avoid osmotic demyelination. That limit demands particular care in water intoxication, since sodium can rise spontaneously by more than 10 mmol/L in a few hours once drinking stops and the kidney excretes the retained water.
key_points: Urine osmolality below 100 mOsm/kg indicates water intake exceeding excretion capacity
Inappropriate antidiuresis instead produces inappropriately concentrated urine
A seizure means hypertonic saline regardless of the underlying cause
Correction is limited to 8 to 10 mmol/L in 24 hours to prevent osmotic demyelination
Diurnal weight gain is a practical bedside marker of water loading
explanation.pearls: Watch for overcorrection rather than undercorrection once the drinking stops: in water intoxication the kidney excretes the retained free water at up to a litre an hour, sodium can climb past the 10 mmol/L daily limit without any further treatment, and desmopressin is then given deliberately to hold the rise and prevent osmotic demyelination.

sources.label: RANZCP: Physical health of people with severe mental illness

options.rationale: Strict fluid restriction with supervision is the definitive treatment for excessive water intake and will be needed as soon as he is stable, and the sodium then rises on its own as the free water is excreted. It acts far too slowly for a man who has already seized, where the cerebral oedema requires immediate reversal. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

A seizure marks severe symptomatic hyponatraemia with cerebral oedema, and the treatment in that situation is a bolus of 3 per cent sodium chloride to raise the sodium by about 4 to 6 mmol/L quickly, irrespective of the underlying cause. The correction is then capped at no more than 8 to 10 mmol/L in the first 24 hours, which matters especially here because a water loading picture corrects rapidly by itself once drinking stops. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Isotonic saline is the right fluid for hypovolaemic hyponatraemia, where volume repletion switches off antidiuretic hormone. With maximally dilute urine at 78 mOsm/kg the kidney is already excreting free water at full capacity, so isotonic fluid raises the sodium far too slowly for a seizing patient and can worsen it once the salt is excreted and the water retained. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Vasopressin receptor antagonists are used in the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis, where the urine is inappropriately concentrated because antidiuretic hormone is being secreted. A urine osmolality of 78 mOsm/kg shows antidiuretic hormone is already fully suppressed, leaving no receptor activity for the drug to block. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Antipsychotics and antidepressants can cause hyponatraemia through inappropriate antidiuresis, which would show a concentrated urine and typically appears within weeks of starting or changing the drug. He has taken the same agent for six years and his urine is maximally dilute, and stopping it abruptly risks psychotic relapse for no benefit. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antipsychotics)

explanation.summary: Lithium induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus affects up to around a fifth of people on long term treatment and occurs at therapeutic levels, so a normal lithium concentration does not exclude it. Lithium enters principal cells of the collecting duct through the epithelial sodium channel and downregulates aquaporin 2 expression, leaving the tubule unable to respond to circulating vasopressin. The diagnosis is confirmed by polyuria with a dilute urine that fails to concentrate after desmopressin, which separates it from central diabetes insipidus, and by the absence of the diurnal weight gain and suppressed sodium seen in primary polydipsia. Amiloride blocks the channel through which lithium enters and is the specific treatment, with thiazides an alternative that requires lithium dose reduction and close level monitoring because they reduce lithium clearance. Free access to water is essential, since these patients decompensate rapidly into hypernatraemia when intake is interrupted by surgery, illness or a confusional state. Early changes may reverse on stopping lithium, but prolonged exposure produces irreversible tubulointerstitial change, and the decision to continue balances that risk against the drug's efficacy and its evidence for reducing suicide.
key_points: It occurs at therapeutic lithium levels, so a normal level does not exclude it
Failure to concentrate urine after desmopressin localises the defect to the tubule
Amiloride blocks lithium entry into principal cells and is the specific treatment
Thiazides work but reduce lithium clearance and demand dose reduction
Free water access is essential and interruption causes rapid hypernatraemia
explanation.pearls: Flag the polyuria in her perioperative and sick day planning as well as treating it: a fasting patient with obligatory losses above five litres a day becomes profoundly hypernatraemic within hours of being made nil by mouth, which is how lithium related concentrating defects most often cause harm.

sources.label: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.rationale: Thiazides paradoxically reduce urine volume in this condition by inducing mild volume contraction, and they are used as treatment, but they also reduce lithium clearance and raise the serum level into the toxic range if lithium is continued. Stopping lithium abruptly after twelve years of stability carries a high risk of rebound mania, so neither half of this option is safe as written. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Lithium)

Desmopressin replaces antidiuretic hormone and works when the deficiency is central, in the pituitary. The urine osmolality here did not change after desmopressin, which localises the defect to the collecting duct where the hormone is present but the receptor response is impaired. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Fluid restriction is the correct approach when polyuria is driven by excessive drinking, where the kidney is normal and restriction simply removes the load. Here the kidney cannot concentrate urine, so restricting intake while obligatory losses continue at over five litres a day would produce dangerous hypernatraemia, and her sodium is already 147 mmol/L. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Lithium enters the principal cells of the collecting duct through the epithelial sodium channel and desensitises the vasopressin receptor, so blocking that channel with amiloride reduces lithium entry and improves concentrating ability while allowing lithium to continue. The parallel decision about whether to keep lithium is a genuine trade off, since nine years of stability on a drug with unmatched antisuicidal evidence has to be weighed against a renal effect that becomes irreversible with prolonged exposure. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Lithium)

Dose escalation would be considered if she were having breakthrough affective symptoms on a subtherapeutic level, and her level sits at 0.72 mmol/L with nine years of euthymia. Raising the dose worsens the tubular injury that is generating the polyuria in the first place. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Lithium)

explanation.summary: Tardive dyskinesia develops in around a quarter of people on long term first generation antipsychotics and at lower but still significant rates with second generation agents, with older age, female sex, diabetes, cumulative exposure and earlier acute movement effects among the risk factors. It is thought to reflect dopamine receptor supersensitivity, which explains the two characteristic behaviours that confirm the diagnosis at the bedside: the movements worsen when the dose is reduced and are masked when it is increased. The picture is orofacial choreoathetosis with lip smacking, chewing and tongue movements, often with limb and trunk involvement, and it is distinguished from drug induced parkinsonism by the absence of rigidity, bradykinesia and resting tremor, and from akathisia by the absence of subjective restlessness. Management begins with reviewing the need for antipsychotic treatment, then switching to an agent with lower liability, and clozapine has the strongest evidence for improvement. Vesicular monoamine transporter 2 inhibitors such as valbenazine and deutetrabenazine are effective and registered overseas but are not subsidised in Australia, so tetrabenazine is the agent generally used, and anticholinergics must be stopped because they aggravate the movements.
key_points: Worsening on dose reduction and masking on dose increase confirm the mechanism
Absence of rigidity and bradykinesia separates it from drug induced parkinsonism
Anticholinergics aggravate tardive dyskinesia and should be withdrawn
Switching to a lower liability agent is the first step, with clozapine best supported
Tetrabenazine is the pharmacological option generally available in Australia
explanation.pearls: Rate the movements on the Abnormal Involuntary Movement Scale at every change of antipsychotic rather than relying on impression: a transient worsening in the weeks after switching is expected as receptor blockade falls, and without a documented baseline score that predictable rebound gets misread as failure of the switch.

sources.label: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline

options.rationale: Raising the dose does mask the movements for weeks to months, because stronger receptor blockade suppresses the expression of the underlying supersensitivity, and the worsening after his reduction is the same phenomenon in reverse. It deepens the underlying process and makes the movements harder to treat later, so it is avoided in tardive dyskinesia. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline

options.rationale: Anticholinergic agents relieve acute dystonia and drug induced parkinsonism, where the problem is relative cholinergic excess, and they are effective and appropriate there. In tardive dyskinesia they worsen the movements and impair cognition, which is the opposite relationship and a common prescribing error. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Persistent orofacial choreoathetosis that emerged on long term treatment with a high potency first generation agent and worsened on dose reduction is tardive dyskinesia, and the first management step is to move to an agent with lower dopamine receptor affinity, with clozapine having the best evidence and quetiapine a reasonable alternative. The switch is made gradually because abrupt withdrawal transiently worsens the movements, and his five years of stability means psychotic relapse risk must be managed through the change. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline

options.rationale: Beta blockade is used for akathisia, the subjective inner restlessness with an urge to move that typically appears within weeks of starting or increasing an antipsychotic. His movements are involuntary and he is not distressed by an urge to move, which places them in a different category. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Complete withdrawal is occasionally appropriate where the original indication is doubtful, and the movements may remit in a minority of people over months to years. Abrupt cessation transiently worsens dyskinesia and, in a man with schizophrenia stable for five years, carries a high risk of relapse. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline

explanation.summary: Dementia with Lewy bodies accounts for a substantial share of dementia in Australia yet is frequently misdiagnosed as Alzheimer disease or late onset psychosis, and the consequences of that error are serious because standard treatment for either can be dangerous. The core clinical features are fluctuating cognition with pronounced variation in attention and alertness, recurrent well formed visual hallucinations, rapid eye movement sleep behaviour disorder, and spontaneous parkinsonism, with the timing rule that cognitive symptoms precede or accompany motor symptoms within a year. Delusional misidentification, in which a familiar person is believed to have been replaced by an impostor, is far more characteristic of Lewy body disease than of Alzheimer disease and is a common trigger for an antipsychotic request. Severe neuroleptic sensitivity occurs in up to half of these patients and can be fatal, so management starts with review of contributing medications, non-pharmacological strategies and carer safety planning, then a cholinesterase inhibitor, for which the evidence in this condition is stronger than in any other dementia. Where an antipsychotic is unavoidable, quetiapine or clozapine at the lowest effective dose is used with full documentation of the risk, and the dream enactment is treated separately with melatonin or low dose clonazepam.
key_points: Dream enactment often precedes cognitive change by years and is a strong pointer
Fluctuating attention with formed visual hallucinations distinguishes it from Alzheimer disease
Impostor delusions about a spouse are characteristic of Lewy body disease
Severe neuroleptic sensitivity occurs in up to half and carries excess mortality
Cholinesterase inhibitors have their strongest dementia evidence in this condition
explanation.pearls: Ask the partner whether he has acted out dreams during sleep, and how long that has been happening: dream enactment commonly predates the cognitive decline by five to ten years, it is the single most specific pointer to Lewy body disease, and eliciting it is what stops a request for risperidone becoming a fatal sensitivity reaction.

sources.label: RANZCP: Assessment and management of people with behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia
Dementia Australia: Dementia with Lewy bodies

options.rationale: Dream enactment predating cognitive change, fluctuating attention, formed visual hallucinations, visuospatial impairment out of proportion to memory and parkinsonism emerging after the cognitive symptoms together indicate Lewy body disease, in which up to half of patients have a severe sensitivity reaction to dopamine blockade with rigidity, confusion, autonomic instability and a two to threefold increase in mortality. Cholinesterase inhibition is the treatment with the best evidence for the hallucinations and delusions in this condition and improves attention as well. (Source: RANZCP: Assessment and management of people with behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Assessment and management of people with behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia

options.rationale: Risperidone is the only antipsychotic registered in Australia for behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia and would be defensible in Alzheimer disease with persisting aggression after non-pharmacological measures. It is a potent dopamine blocker, and in Lewy body disease that is precisely the exposure that precipitates the severe sensitivity reaction, so monitoring does not make it safe. (Source: RANZCP: Assessment and management of people with behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Assessment and management of people with behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia

options.rationale: Quetiapine has the lowest striatal dopamine receptor occupancy of the available agents and is the one usually chosen when antipsychotic treatment is genuinely unavoidable in this condition. Its randomised evidence for efficacy in Lewy body disease is weak, severe sensitivity reactions have still been reported with it, and it adds orthostatic hypotension and sedation to a man who already has a postural blood pressure drop and two recent falls. (Source: RANZCP: Assessment and management of people with behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Assessment and management of people with behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia

options.rationale: Levodopa is used cautiously for disabling motor symptoms in this condition, starting low and increasing slowly, once the neuropsychiatric picture is stable. Introducing dopaminergic treatment while florid hallucinations and a persecutory misidentification are present predictably aggravates them, and the motor symptoms here are mild. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Clonazepam or melatonin is used for the dream enactment component of this illness and would address one symptom, and melatonin is generally preferred given its better safety profile. Benzodiazepines worsen confusion and falls in a man with fluctuating attention and postural hypotension, and they do nothing for the delusion that is driving his wife out of the house. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Grief is a normal response to loss and most bereaved people adapt without professional intervention, so the clinical task is identifying the minority whose grief becomes persistent and disabling. Prolonged grief disorder is now a formal diagnosis requiring symptoms at least twelve months after the death in adults, with intense yearning or preoccupation plus features such as disbelief, avoidance of reminders, emotional numbness, identity disruption and an inability to re engage with life. It is distinguished from a depressive episode, in which low mood is pervasive rather than focused on the deceased, self worth is reduced and anhedonia is global, although the two frequently coexist. Treatment is psychological and specifically grief focused, with medication reserved for a comorbid depressive or anxiety disorder rather than for the grief itself.
key_points: Diagnosis requires symptoms persisting at least twelve months after the death
Yearning and preoccupation focus on the deceased rather than on global low mood
Preserved self worth and selective enjoyment argue against a depressive episode
Grief focused psychotherapy outperforms generic support and antidepressants
Medication is reserved for comorbid depressive or anxiety disorder
explanation.pearls: Bereavement by suicide, homicide or sudden unexpected death, and the loss of a child, carry the highest risk of prolonged grief disorder, so those groups warrant proactive follow up at around six to twelve months rather than waiting for presentation.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.rationale: Antidepressants are indicated where a depressive episode coexists, which is identified by pervasive anhedonia, worthlessness, guilt unrelated to the death and diurnal variation. Her enjoyment of her grandchildren and preserved self worth argue against that, and trials of antidepressants for grief specific symptoms have been disappointing. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Sedatives blunt the emotional processing that grief work depends on and carry dependence and falls risk in an older adult. Their use in early bereavement is associated with worse rather than better outcomes at follow up. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Normalising grief is the right approach in the first months and for most bereaved people throughout. Symptoms this intense and this disabling more than a year after the death fall outside the expected trajectory, and further watchful waiting has not helped her over the past year. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Intense yearning and preoccupation with avoidance, disbelief and identity disruption persisting beyond twelve months with functional impairment describes prolonged grief disorder, which affects roughly one in ten bereaved people and does not resolve with time alone. Grief focused psychotherapy, which combines exposure to the reality of the loss with restoration of life goals, outperforms both generic supportive counselling and antidepressants for these symptoms. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Peer support groups help many bereaved people and are a reasonable adjunct that she may value. Randomised evidence shows generic support does not reduce prolonged grief symptoms in those who meet criteria, who need a targeted therapy instead. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Nicotine vaping among Australian adolescents rose steeply before regulatory tightening, and many users are dependent without ever having smoked a cigarette, which reverses the historical assumption that vaping is a downstream problem of smoking. Dependence is assessed as it is for tobacco, with time to first use after waking, daily frequency and withdrawal symptoms being the most informative questions. Nicotine replacement therapy is used in dependent adolescents despite being formally studied mainly in adults, because the risks of continued nicotine exposure during brain development outweigh the risks of short term replacement. Varenicline and bupropion are not recommended under 18 years, and behavioural support, whether delivered in the consultation or through quit services, roughly doubles the chance of success when combined with pharmacotherapy.
key_points: Many adolescent users are nicotine dependent without prior cigarette smoking
Time to first use after waking is a key marker of dependence severity
Combination nicotine replacement outperforms a single form
Varenicline and bupropion are not recommended under 18 years
Behavioural support combined with pharmacotherapy doubles quit rates
explanation.pearls: Nicotine withdrawal peaks within the first three days and largely settles by two to four weeks, so scheduling review inside that window rather than at one month is what catches the relapse most attempts fail at.

sources.label: RACGP: Supporting smoking and vaping cessation

options.rationale: Setting a quit date is part of any cessation plan and is worth doing, but advice alone is what has already failed on three occasions. Dependence of this severity predicts withdrawal that undermines unassisted attempts. (Source: RACGP: Supporting smoking and vaping cessation)
source_refs: RACGP: Supporting smoking and vaping cessation

options.rationale: Varenicline is an effective first line agent for nicotine dependence in adults and would be a reasonable choice were he older. It is not approved for use under 18 years and safety and efficacy data in adolescents are lacking. (Source: RACGP: Supporting smoking and vaping cessation)
source_refs: RACGP: Supporting smoking and vaping cessation

options.rationale: Waking use within fifteen minutes, hourly use and withdrawal symptoms on abstinence indicate significant nicotine dependence, for which behavioural support combined with nicotine replacement is the recommended approach in an adolescent who has failed unassisted attempts. Combination replacement, using a patch for background craving with a short-acting form for breakthrough, is more effective than either alone, and structured follow up in the first weeks is when relapse is most likely. (Source: RACGP: Supporting smoking and vaping cessation)
source_refs: RACGP: Supporting smoking and vaping cessation

options.rationale: Tapering the concentration appears logical but users compensate by inhaling more deeply and more often, so actual nicotine intake changes little. It also keeps the behavioural ritual of the device intact, which is a major driver of relapse. (Source: RACGP: Supporting smoking and vaping cessation)
source_refs: RACGP: Supporting smoking and vaping cessation

options.rationale: Specialist referral is warranted for polysubstance use, significant comorbid mental illness or repeated failure of primary care management, none of which apply to a motivated adolescent at his first assisted attempt. Deferring treatment risks losing a window in which he is ready to act. (Source: RACGP: Supporting smoking and vaping cessation)
source_refs: RACGP: Supporting smoking and vaping cessation

explanation.summary: Narcolepsy type 1 results from loss of hypocretin producing neurons in the lateral hypothalamus and typically begins in adolescence or early adulthood, with a diagnostic delay often measured in years because sleepiness is attributed to lifestyle. The defining feature is cataplexy, a brief emotionally triggered loss of muscle tone with fully retained awareness, which represents intrusion of rapid eye movement sleep atonia into wakefulness and is what separates the condition from other causes of hypersomnolence. Other rapid eye movement intrusion phenomena, namely sleep paralysis and hallucinations at sleep onset or waking, support the diagnosis but are not specific and occur in the general population. Diagnosis requires overnight polysomnography followed by a multiple sleep latency test, and because stimulants and antidepressants alter both studies they must be withheld beforehand. Management combines scheduled naps, a wake promoting agent for sleepiness, an agent suppressing rapid eye movement sleep for cataplexy, and mandatory discussion of driving and occupational safety.
key_points: Cataplexy is emotionally triggered atonia with fully retained awareness
Short naps that refresh distinguish it from most other causes of sleepiness
Diagnosis requires polysomnography followed by a multiple sleep latency test
Stimulants and antidepressants must be withheld before testing
Driving and occupational safety must be addressed at diagnosis
explanation.pearls: Antidepressants suppress rapid eye movement sleep and can abolish the early rapid eye movement periods that the multiple sleep latency test depends on, so they are withdrawn for at least two weeks before testing or the study will be falsely negative.

options.rationale: Atonic seizures cause abrupt loss of tone with impaired awareness and frequently with injury and postictal confusion. His episodes are emotionally triggered, awareness is fully retained throughout and there is no postictal phase, which is not the pattern of a seizure. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy)

Insufficient sleep syndrome is the commonest cause of daytime sleepiness in young adults and does respond to scheduling, so this is a reasonable starting point in most presentations. It does not explain emotionally triggered loss of muscle tone, which has a narrow differential. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy)

Wake promoting agents are a mainstay of treatment once the diagnosis is confirmed, so the drug itself is appropriate to the condition. Starting it before objective testing removes the ability to perform a valid multiple sleep latency test later and leaves the diagnosis unconfirmed for life. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy)

Functional collapse attacks are worth considering when episodes are prolonged, variable and inconsistent with any physiological pattern. Stereotyped brief emotionally triggered atonia with retained awareness, alongside sleep paralysis and hallucinations at sleep onset, forms a recognised physiological cluster. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy)

Excessive daytime sleepiness with refreshing short naps, sleep paralysis, hypnagogic hallucinations and emotionally triggered loss of tone with retained awareness is narcolepsy with cataplexy, which is confirmed by overnight polysomnography followed by a multiple sleep latency test the next day. The overnight study is required both to exclude another cause of sleep disruption and to validate the nap test, which looks for a short mean sleep latency with early entry into rapid eye movement sleep. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy)

explanation.summary: Restless legs syndrome is a clinical diagnosis resting on an urge to move the legs with unpleasant sensations, worsening at rest, relief by movement and a circadian pattern peaking in the evening and night, with other causes excluded. Periodic limb movements in sleep accompany it in most affected people and are often what the bed partner reports. Assessment focuses on reversible contributors, principally iron deficiency, renal impairment, pregnancy and drugs including antihistamines, dopamine antagonists and most antidepressants. The threshold for iron replacement is set far higher than the threshold for diagnosing anaemia, because brain iron can be deficient when peripheral stores look acceptable. When drug treatment is needed, alpha 2 delta ligands have displaced dopamine agonists as first line because of augmentation, which is a paradoxical worsening that is difficult to reverse once established.
key_points: Diagnosis is clinical, requiring rest worsening, movement relief and a circadian pattern
Iron replacement is indicated at ferritin 75 micrograms/L or below
Anaemia is not required for iron deficiency to be driving symptoms
Alpha 2 delta ligands are preferred over dopamine agonists when drugs are needed
Antihistamines, dopamine antagonists and most antidepressants aggravate it
explanation.pearls: Augmentation from a dopamine agonist announces itself as symptoms starting earlier in the day, becoming more intense, or spreading to the arms, and the correct response is to withdraw the agonist rather than to increase the dose.

sources.label: Australasian Sleep Association: Restless legs syndrome

options.rationale: Dopamine agonists relieve symptoms quickly and were first line for many years, which is why they remain a tempting choice. Long term use causes augmentation, in which symptoms become earlier, more intense and spread to the arms, and this is now considered severe enough that these agents are no longer recommended first. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Brain iron deficiency underlies the dopaminergic dysfunction of this condition, and iron replacement is recommended when ferritin is at or below 75 micrograms/L or transferrin saturation is under 20 percent, both of which apply here despite the absence of anaemia. Correcting stores improves or resolves symptoms in a substantial proportion and avoids committing her to a drug with long term complications. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Alpha 2 delta ligands such as gabapentin or pregabalin are the preferred pharmacological agents when drug treatment is needed, particularly with coexisting pain or insomnia. They are reserved until reversible contributors have been corrected, because treating over an uncorrected iron deficiency commits the patient to indefinite therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Hypnotics may mask the sleep disturbance but do nothing for the sensory urge to move, which is the core symptom. They also carry tolerance, dependence and falls risk with indefinite use in middle and later life. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Neurophysiology is indicated where a peripheral neuropathy is suspected from sensory loss, absent reflexes or a length dependent distribution, none of which are present. The circadian pattern and relief by movement are not features of neuropathy and do not require electrophysiology. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Autism is substantially under recognised in women and girls, who are diagnosed later and less often than males with comparable needs, in large part because diagnostic constructs were derived from male presentations. Camouflaging, meaning the conscious or learned masking of autistic traits through rehearsed conversation, imitation and forced eye contact, is more common in women and is effortful enough to be a driver of exhaustion, anxiety and depression. Special interests in autistic women are often socially acceptable in content, such as animals, literature or a historical subject, which means they are not recognised as unusual in intensity. The typical history is of serial psychiatric diagnoses with partial treatment response, and formal diagnosis frequently reframes a lifetime of self blame while opening access to supports and workplace adjustments.
key_points: Autistic women are diagnosed later and less often than men with similar needs
Camouflaging can produce apparently normal eye contact and social performance
Interests may be socially typical in content but atypical in intensity
Serial psychiatric labels with partial response is a characteristic history
Diagnosis requires specialist assessment including a developmental history
explanation.pearls: Autistic burnout, a period of profound exhaustion, loss of skills and reduced tolerance to stimulus after prolonged camouflaging, is frequently misdiagnosed and treated as a depressive episode, and it responds to reduced demands and sensory recovery rather than to antidepressant escalation.

sources.label: Autism CRC: National guideline for the assessment and diagnosis of autism in Australia

options.rationale: Dose escalation is appropriate for a partially treated depressive or anxiety disorder that is otherwise well characterised. Fifteen years of partial and short lived response to treatments for two different diagnoses is itself a reason to revisit the formulation rather than to intensify treatment of it. (Source: RACGP: Autism in adults)

Employment, friendship and eye contact are frequently cited to exclude autism in adult women and none of them do so. She has explicitly described learned eye contact, and camouflaging of this kind is a major reason women are identified late or not at all. (Source: RACGP: Autism in adults)

Lifelong social effort and camouflaging, sensory overload requiring recovery, insistence on sameness and circumscribed intense interests, combined with a long history of psychiatric labels that responded only partially, is a characteristic presentation of an undiagnosed autistic adult woman. Diagnosis in Australia requires a specialist multidisciplinary or specialist clinician assessment that includes a developmental history from childhood, since it cannot be made from current presentation alone. (Source: RACGP: Autism in adults)

Screening questionnaires are useful for deciding whether to refer and she would almost certainly score above threshold. They are not diagnostic, cannot capture the childhood history that diagnosis requires, and a score alone will not give her access to supports. (Source: RACGP: Autism in adults)

Personality disorder is a genuine differential and autistic women are commonly given that label, particularly borderline personality disorder, because of emotional dysregulation and unstable relationships. Her difficulties are consistent since early childhood, are driven by sensory and social processing rather than by fear of abandonment or identity disturbance, and do not fluctuate with interpersonal events. (Source: RACGP: Autism in adults)

explanation.summary: Depersonalisation is the experience of detachment from one's own body, thoughts or actions, and derealisation the sense that surroundings are unreal, dreamlike or visually flattened, and brief episodes occur in up to half the general population under stress, fatigue or intoxication. The disorder is diagnosed when the experience is persistent or recurrent, causes distress or impairment, and occurs with fully preserved reality testing, which is the feature that separates it from psychosis and is the single most useful question to ask. It commonly follows acute anxiety, cannabis or hallucinogen use, or severe stress, and a self reinforcing cycle develops in which the fear of going mad amplifies the detachment. Assessment excludes temporal lobe epilepsy, migraine aura, substance effects and the dissociation of post-traumatic stress disorder, and management is psychoeducation plus psychological therapy, since no medication has established efficacy.
key_points: Reality testing is intact, which distinguishes it from psychosis
Cannabis, acute anxiety and severe stress are common precipitants
Fear of going mad maintains and amplifies the symptom
Exclude temporal lobe epilepsy, migraine aura and substance effects
Psychoeducation and psychological therapy have the best evidence
explanation.pearls: Asking directly whether the person believes things really have changed, or only feels as though they have, separates this disorder from psychosis in a single question, and the answer is diagnostic in a way that no investigation is.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for anxiety disorders

options.rationale: Antipsychotics treat psychosis, which requires loss of reality testing through hallucinations or delusions. He knows the experience is not real, which is the defining distinction, and antipsychotics have not been shown to help these symptoms. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Short term anxiolysis may seem attractive given how frightening the symptom is, and anxiety genuinely amplifies it. Regular benzodiazepine use promotes dependence and, on withdrawal, characteristically intensifies these experiences, so the net effect over months is harmful. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Imaging is indicated where the experience is accompanied by focal neurological signs, an altered level of consciousness, olfactory or gustatory phenomena or stereotyped brief episodes suggesting temporal lobe seizures. A continuous seven month experience with a normal neurological examination and intact cognition does not fit that pattern. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Many episodes triggered by intoxication or acute stress do settle within days to weeks, so watchful waiting is reasonable early on. Seven months of continuous daily symptoms with significant distress has already declared itself as persistent rather than transient. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Persistent detachment from oneself or from surroundings with fully intact reality testing, in the absence of another disorder or substance effect, is depersonalisation derealisation disorder, and cannabis is one of its commonest precipitants. Explanation that the experience is a recognised and non psychotic phenomenon substantially reduces the catastrophic fear that maintains it, and psychological therapy targeting symptom monitoring, catastrophic appraisal and avoidance is the treatment with the best evidence. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Akathisia is a movement disorder combining a subjective sense of inner restlessness, usually referred to the legs, with an objective inability to remain still, and it typically emerges within days to weeks of starting or increasing a dopamine antagonist. It is the extrapyramidal syndrome most often missed, because pacing and sleeplessness in a psychotic patient are easily attributed to the illness, and the resulting dose increase produces a cycle of worsening. The distinguishing features from psychotic agitation are that the patient can describe a physical sensation relieved by movement, and that other psychotic symptoms are stable or improving. Akathisia matters beyond discomfort because it is associated with treatment non-adherence and with suicidal ideation and completed suicide, and management centres on reducing or switching the causative agent, with propranolol the best supported adjunct and a benzodiazepine sometimes used short term.
key_points: Subjective inner restlessness plus objective inability to sit still defines it
Onset follows starting or increasing a dopamine antagonist within days to weeks
Improving psychotic symptoms argue against agitation from the illness
Anticholinergics help dystonia and parkinsonism, not akathisia
It carries a recognised association with suicidal ideation and suicide
explanation.pearls: Asking whether the restlessness is felt in the body and eased by moving, rather than felt in the mind, separates akathisia from psychotic agitation at the bedside, and a patient who paces but reports no inner urge usually has something else.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia

options.rationale: Subjective inner restlessness with an objective inability to remain still, appearing days after a dose increase and without rigidity, tremor or fever, is akathisia, and the psychotic symptoms are improving rather than worsening. Management is to reduce the offending dose or switch agent, with propranolol as the best supported pharmacological adjunct, and close observation is essential because akathisia carries a recognised association with suicidal thoughts of exactly the kind he has voiced. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Escalation is the intuitive response to a pacing, sleepless patient on a psychiatric ward, because akathisia is readily misread as psychotic agitation. Increasing the dose worsens the very mechanism causing his distress, and his delusions and hallucinations are in fact receding. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Anticholinergic agents are effective for acute dystonia and for drug induced parkinsonism, which present with sustained abnormal postures or with tremor and cogwheel rigidity. Their benefit in akathisia is poor, and they add cognitive impairment and constipation without addressing the problem. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Abrupt cessation with supportive management is the response to neuroleptic malignant syndrome, which requires fever, rigidity, autonomic instability, altered consciousness and a raised creatine kinase. He is afebrile with a normal creatine kinase, normal cognition and no rigidity, and stopping treatment outright risks relapse of a psychosis that is responding. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Post psychotic depression is a real phenomenon and his statement about being better off dead makes mood a legitimate concern to assess. His distress is explicitly tied to a physical sensation relieved by walking rather than to pervasive low mood, and some antidepressants can themselves induce or worsen akathisia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors are among the commonest drug causes of the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis, with risk concentrated in the first weeks of treatment and in older people, low body weight, female sex and concurrent diuretic use. The presentation is easily mistaken for either a worsening of the depression being treated or for an emerging dementia, because it produces lethargy, confusion, unsteadiness and falls rather than anything that points to sodium. Diagnosis requires a clinically euvolaemic patient with low serum osmolality, urine osmolality inappropriately high for that, urine sodium above 30 mmol/L, and exclusion of hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency and diuretic effect. Correction is deliberately slow, since raising the sodium faster than about 8 to 10 mmol/L per day risks osmotic demyelination, a devastating and irreversible complication.
key_points: Risk is highest in the first weeks and in older patients on a diuretic
Confusion and falls, not thirst or oedema, are the usual presentation
Euvolaemia with low serum and high urine osmolality defines the syndrome
Thyroid and adrenal function must be normal before the diagnosis is made
Correction is limited to about 8 to 10 mmol/L in 24 hours
explanation.pearls: Checking sodium two to four weeks after starting a serotonergic antidepressant in anyone over 65, particularly those on a thiazide, detects this while it is still asymptomatic and is the single most useful monitoring step in that group.

options.rationale: Antipsychotics are used for distressing hyperactive delirium once reversible causes are being treated, so they have a place but not as the first action. Adding one here leaves the cause uncorrected and risks further falls and sedation in an older woman who is already unsteady. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Isotonic saline is the treatment for hypovolaemic hyponatraemia, identified by dry mucous membranes, postural hypotension, a raised urea and a low urine sodium. With euvolaemia and a urine sodium of 52 mmol/L, saline is often excreted with the sodium retained in the urine and the plasma sodium can paradoxically fall further. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Dose reduction may be adequate for mild asymptomatic hyponatraemia detected on routine monitoring. A sodium of 118 mmol/L with confusion and unsteadiness is symptomatic and carries seizure risk, so partial measures and a week of waiting are unsafe. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

A euvolaemic patient with a low serum osmolality, inappropriately concentrated urine and a urine sodium above 30 mmol/L, with normal thyroid and adrenal function, has the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis, and the serotonergic antidepressant started three weeks ago is the precipitant in an older woman already taking a thiazide. Treatment is to withdraw the causative drug and restrict fluid with monitored correction, which needs inpatient care at this sodium level because correcting faster than roughly 8 to 10 mmol/L in 24 hours risks osmotic demyelination. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Neuroimaging is warranted for confusion with focal neurological signs, a history of head injury or anticoagulation, none of which are present. It would be reasonable later if confusion persisted after the sodium was corrected, but it does not address a metabolic cause that is already identified. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: The perimenopause carries a genuinely increased risk of depressive symptoms and of a first depressive episode, with the risk concentrated in the years of most erratic hormonal fluctuation rather than after periods cease. Diagnostic error runs in both directions: attributing a major depressive episode to hormones and treating only with hormone therapy, or dismissing the hormonal context entirely and missing vasomotor symptoms that are themselves disrupting sleep and mood. Oestrogen therapy has evidence for depressive symptoms arising in perimenopause, particularly where vasomotor symptoms are prominent, but it is not established treatment for a major depressive episode, which is managed as it would be at any other time of life. Untreated depression in midlife carries the same risks of chronicity, relapse and suicide as at any other age, and women in this group are under treated relative to their symptom burden.
key_points: Depressive risk peaks during erratic hormonal fluctuation, not after menopause
Perimenopause is diagnosed clinically from cycle change and vasomotor symptoms
Gonadotrophins fluctuate and do not guide treatment in a woman over 45
A major depressive episode is treated on its own terms in this context
Hormone therapy addresses vasomotor symptoms and may assist mood alongside
explanation.pearls: Vasomotor symptoms that wake a woman several times a night are themselves a treatable driver of daytime mood and concentration, so treating them improves depression outcomes even when an antidepressant is the primary treatment.

sources.label: Australasian Menopause Society: Mood and menopause
RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.rationale: Oestrogen therapy has reasonable evidence for depressive symptoms arising in perimenopause, and it will help her vasomotor symptoms, so it is a legitimate part of her care. It has not been shown to treat a major depressive episode of this severity, and relying on it alone leaves a functionally impairing illness untreated for three months. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society: Mood and menopause)
source_refs: Australasian Menopause Society: Mood and menopause

options.rationale: Gonadotrophin measurement is useful for diagnosing premature ovarian insufficiency under 40 years, and for women without a uterus or on hormonal contraception where cycles cannot be tracked. In a woman of 49 with irregular cycles and vasomotor symptoms the perimenopausal diagnosis is clinical, and fluctuating levels do not guide treatment. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society: Mood and menopause)
source_refs: Australasian Menopause Society: Mood and menopause

options.rationale: Daily anhedonia for three months with early morning waking, 5 kg of unintentional weight loss, psychomotor retardation, worthlessness and functional decline at work meets criteria for a moderate to severe depressive episode, which is treated on its own terms regardless of the hormonal context. The perimenopausal diagnosis is not in doubt and hormone therapy remains appropriate for her vasomotor symptoms and may assist mood, so it is discussed alongside rather than instead of the antidepressant and therapy. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society: Mood and menopause)
source_refs: Australasian Menopause Society: Mood and menopause

options.rationale: Psychological therapy alone is appropriate for mild to moderate depression and for patients who prefer it, and it should form part of her treatment. Marked biological features with functional impairment at work place this episode in a range where combined treatment gives better and faster outcomes. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Lifestyle measures improve both vasomotor symptoms and mood and are recommended alongside any treatment, so they belong in the plan. As sole management of a moderate to severe episode with weight loss and impaired work performance they are inadequate and delay effective treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Volatile substance use, involving solvents, aerosols, glues, fuels and butane, is concentrated in young adolescents because the products are cheap, legal and universally available, and prevalence is markedly higher in communities experiencing disadvantage. The acute effect is a brief euphoric disinhibited state with a risk of sudden sniffing death from catecholamine sensitisation of the myocardium, which can occur on a first exposure and is precipitated by sudden exertion or fright. Chronic exposure to toluene containing products produces cerebellar and white matter damage with ataxia, tremor and cognitive decline, along with renal tubular acidosis and hearing loss, and these are dose related and only partly reversible. Management is a health and social response built on engagement, harm reduction, addressing schooling, housing and family circumstances, and neurological assessment where signs have emerged, since no pharmacotherapy exists.
key_points: Products are cheap, legal and universally available, so use starts young
Sudden sniffing death can occur on a first exposure with exertion or fright
A perioral rash is a useful physical clue to recent repeated use
Chronic toluene exposure causes cerebellar and white matter damage
Management is psychosocial and harm reduction based with no pharmacotherapy
explanation.pearls: Sudden sniffing death is precipitated by a surge of catecholamines during or just after inhalation, which is why anyone approaching an intoxicated young person should stay calm and avoid startling or chasing them.

options.rationale: Medically assisted withdrawal is the standard approach for alcohol and benzodiazepine dependence, where an abstinence syndrome is dangerous. Volatile substance withdrawal is mild and largely behavioural, and there is no established pharmacotherapy, so a benzodiazepine adds sedation without benefit. (Source: NSW Health: Volatile substance use)

Volatile substance use in a young person is managed through engagement, harm reduction and addressing the social context rather than through pharmacotherapy, because it is strongly associated with disadvantage, disengagement from school and unmet need rather than with dependence in the classical sense. The new cerebellar signs are the urgent element, since chronic solvent exposure causes a dose related and potentially irreversible leukoencephalopathy, and they require neurological assessment and imaging alongside the psychosocial work. (Source: NSW Health: Volatile substance use)

Isolated experimentation without features of harm can reasonably be managed with education and review, and most adolescents who try a solvent do not continue. Repeated use over two months with new neurological signs has already crossed from experimentation into harm. (Source: NSW Health: Volatile substance use)

Supply restriction at the retail level is a genuine population level strategy and some jurisdictions restrict sales of certain products. A criminal justice response to an individual adolescent damages engagement, and volatile substance use itself is managed as a health issue in Australian policy. (Source: NSW Health: Volatile substance use)

Electroencephalography would be appropriate if the episodes of altered awareness were unexplained, stereotyped and not temporally tied to an exposure. Each episode here begins with inhalation and lasts about twenty minutes, which is the expected pharmacological course rather than a seizure. (Source: NSW Health: Volatile substance use)

explanation.summary: Gender dysphoria describes clinically significant distress arising from incongruence between experienced gender and sex assigned at birth, and in adolescence it commonly intensifies with the physical changes of puberty. Trans and gender diverse young people have markedly elevated rates of self-harm, suicidal ideation and depression compared with their peers, and the evidence consistently identifies family acceptance, use of chosen name and pronouns, and access to care as protective. Australian care operates through specialist multidisciplinary services that combine mental health, paediatric and endocrine expertise, with decisions about pubertal suppression or hormone treatment made within that framework rather than in primary care. The general practitioner's role is nonetheless central, providing continuity, safety planning, practical harm reduction such as binding advice, and management of coexisting mental illness during waits that are frequently measured in many months.
key_points: Distress typically escalates with the physical changes of puberty
Self-harm and suicidality are markedly elevated in this group
Family acceptance and affirmed name use are strongly protective
Assessment and affirming treatment occur within specialist services
Deferring assessment is not neutral because puberty continues meanwhile
explanation.pearls: Daily chest binding with restrictive materials causes skin breakdown, back and chest pain and rib changes, so asking directly about binding practice and advising on a properly fitted binder worn for limited hours is a concrete harm reduction step available at the first consultation.

sources.label: RCH: Australian standards of care for trans and gender diverse children and adolescents
RACGP: Trans and gender diverse health

options.rationale: Gender affirming hormone treatment is an appropriate consideration for some adolescents and it is prescribed in Australia within specialist services after multidisciplinary assessment. Initiating it from general practice at a first consultation bypasses the assessment, consent and endocrine processes that Australian standards require. (Source: RCH: Australian standards of care for trans and gender diverse children and adolescents)
source_refs: RCH: Australian standards of care for trans and gender diverse children and adolescents

options.rationale: Psychological support for self-harm is unquestionably needed and is part of the plan. Separating it from the gender related distress that the young person identifies as its driver addresses the behaviour while leaving its cause unaddressed, and adolescents commonly disengage when that happens. (Source: RCH: Australian standards of care for trans and gender diverse children and adolescents)
source_refs: RCH: Australian standards of care for trans and gender diverse children and adolescents

options.rationale: Delaying assessment until adulthood is sometimes framed as a cautious neutral position, but it is not neutral, because irreversible pubertal development continues during the wait. Australian standards support assessment and support during adolescence rather than deferral. (Source: RCH: Australian standards of care for trans and gender diverse children and adolescents)
source_refs: RCH: Australian standards of care for trans and gender diverse children and adolescents

options.rationale: Family work is valuable where a young person faces rejection or conflict at home, and family support is one of the strongest protective factors in this group. This mother is already supportive and actively seeking help, so directing the intervention at her misplaces the need. (Source: RCH: Australian standards of care for trans and gender diverse children and adolescents)
source_refs: RCH: Australian standards of care for trans and gender diverse children and adolescents

options.rationale: A persistent, consistent and insistent cross gender identity since childhood with escalating distress at pubertal development warrants referral to a specialist multidisciplinary gender service, which is where assessment and any decisions about affirming treatment are made in Australia. The general practitioner's concurrent role is substantial and immediate, covering safety planning for the self-harm, advice on safe chest binding to prevent skin and rib injury, use of the young person's name and pronouns, and being the continuing point of contact during what are often long waits. (Source: RCH: Australian standards of care for trans and gender diverse children and adolescents)
source_refs: RCH: Australian standards of care for trans and gender diverse children and adolescents

explanation.summary: Adjustment disorder is an emotional or behavioural response to an identifiable stressor beginning within three months of it, causing distress out of proportion to what would be expected or significant functional impairment, and not meeting criteria for another disorder. The distinction from a major depressive episode rests on the biological features and on pervasiveness, since preserved reactivity of mood, normal appetite and weight and absence of early morning waking all argue against a depressive episode. This distinction matters because treatment differs: psychological therapy and practical problem solving have evidence in adjustment disorder while antidepressants do not, and prescribing them conveys risk without expected benefit. Suicide risk is nonetheless substantial in adjustment disorder and is not proportional to the diagnostic label, so safety planning and scheduled review are required whenever thoughts of death are disclosed.
key_points: Onset is within three months of an identifiable stressor
Preserved enjoyment, appetite and sleep pattern argue against a depressive episode
Psychological therapy and problem solving are the evidence-based treatment
Antidepressants lack evidence for adjustment disorder specifically
Suicide risk is real and requires safety planning regardless of the label
explanation.pearls: Adjustment disorder is over represented among people who die by suicide relative to how mild the diagnosis sounds, with the act often occurring impulsively and close to the stressor, which is why means restriction and a written safety plan belong in the first consultation.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.rationale: Symptoms proportionate to an identifiable stressor within three months, with preserved enjoyment, intact appetite and weight and no early morning waking, describe an adjustment disorder rather than a major depressive episode, and psychological therapy with practical problem solving is the evidence-based treatment. Passive thoughts of being a burden still require an explicit safety plan and early review, because adjustment disorder carries a real suicide risk despite not meeting depressive criteria. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Acceding to a clear patient request has value and antidepressants would be appropriate if he met criteria for a depressive episode. Evidence does not support antidepressants for adjustment disorder, and prescribing here exposes him to adverse effects, discontinuation problems and a diagnostic label that may affect insurance, without expected benefit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Urgent assessment is indicated for active suicidal intent, a formed plan, access to means with expressed intent, or psychotic depression. Fleeting ego dystonic thoughts that frighten him, with strong protective factors and no plan or intent, do not meet that threshold and an emergency response may deter future disclosure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

His sleep onset difficulty is real and hypnotics would shorten it in the short term. They do not address the worry driving the insomnia, carry dependence risk, and are specifically discouraged where suicidal thoughts are present because of overdose potential. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Normalising his reaction is a reasonable and important part of the conversation, since distress after redundancy is expected. Symptoms that have persisted seven weeks with impairment and passive suicidal thoughts warrant active treatment and scheduled follow up rather than open ended watchful waiting. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Difficulty discarding possessions became a separate diagnosis because it differs from obsessive compulsive disorder in phenomenology, treatment response and course. The accumulation is driven by beliefs about usefulness, waste and emotional attachment rather than by intrusive thoughts that the person is trying to neutralise, and distress arises at the prospect of discarding rather than from the clutter itself. Insight is characteristically poor, which is why referral usually comes from family, neighbours or council rather than the person. Prevalence rises with age and the associated risks are substantial, including falls, fire, structural damage, infestation and eviction. Treatment is a specifically adapted cognitive behavioural program, often combined with practical in home support, and medication addresses comorbid depression or anxiety rather than the behaviour itself.
key_points: Distress arises at discarding, not from the clutter or from intrusive thoughts
Clutter must prevent rooms being used for their intended purpose
Insight is typically poor and referral usually comes from others
Adapted cognitive behavioural therapy is the primary treatment
Late onset accumulation with personality change suggests a frontal process
explanation.pearls: Forced clearance without concurrent psychological treatment is followed by re-accumulation to the previous level in the majority of cases within two years, so a skip bin arranged without therapy is a temporary fix that also destroys the working relationship needed for the real one.

sources.label: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.rationale: High dose serotonergic medication is the pharmacological approach to obsessive compulsive disorder, but response rates in hoarding disorder are considerably lower. Medication is added when depression or anxiety coexists rather than as the primary treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Persistent difficulty parting with possessions, distress at the thought of discarding, and clutter that prevents rooms from being used as intended defines a condition in its own right, and the treatment with the best evidence is a structured cognitive behavioural program covering motivation, sorting skills and graded discarding. It outperforms generic therapy and is delivered over months. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.rationale: Involuntary clearance reliably produces rapid re-accumulation and a rupture in the therapeutic relationship, and it is reserved for imminent and otherwise unmanageable danger. Even then it is coordinated with treatment rather than used instead of it. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders
