options.rationale: Accumulation that begins abruptly in later life, especially with disinhibition, apathy or personality change, does warrant assessment for a frontotemporal process. His cognition screens normally and he continues to manage complex daily tasks. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Hoarding disorder)

Residential placement addresses functional decline from cognitive or physical impairment, neither of which he has, and it does not treat the behaviour that produced the clutter. He manages his medications and finances independently. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

explanation.summary: Recurrent hair pulling typically begins around puberty, affects girls more often than boys in clinical samples, and is frequently concealed for years by hairstyle changes. The diagnosis rests on the behavioural account rather than on the appearance of the scalp, though hairs of varying length within an irregular patch with normal underlying skin is the characteristic finding and separates it from autoimmune and infective causes. It sits with skin picking among the body focused repetitive behaviours, which differ from obsessive compulsive disorder in that the behaviour is preceded by tension or an urge rather than by an intrusive thought, and it responds to behavioural rather than serotonergic treatment. Swallowing the pulled hair occurs in a minority and carries a real risk of a gastric hair mass, so it must be asked about directly.
key_points: An urge with tension before and relief after defines the behaviour
Hairs of varying length within the patch indicate mechanical pulling
Normal scalp skin excludes fungal and autoimmune causes
Habit reversal training is first line and outperforms medication
Ask directly about swallowing hair because of gastric mass risk
explanation.pearls: Around a fifth of people who pull also swallow the hair, and the resulting gastric mass can extend into the small bowel as a tail, so persistent abdominal pain with unexplained iron deficiency in a puller is a surgical presentation rather than a psychiatric one.

sources.label: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.rationale: Serotonergic antidepressants have repeatedly failed to outperform placebo for pulling behaviours, unlike in obsessive compulsive disorder where they are central. They are reserved for coexisting depression or anxiety, neither of which she has. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Topical corticosteroid treats an autoimmune patch of hair loss, which produces a smooth bald area with exclamation mark hairs at the margin rather than hairs of differing lengths within it. Her varying hair lengths indicate mechanical removal at different times. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Alopecia)

Fungal scalp infection also produces patchy loss in a young person, but with scaling, broken hairs close to the skin and often occipital lymphadenopathy. Her scalp skin is entirely normal. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Surgical referral is warranted when hair is swallowed, which produces abdominal pain, vomiting, a palpable mass or iron deficiency. She denies eating hair, her abdomen is normal and her iron studies are unremarkable. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Trichotillomania)

Repetitive pulling with rising tension beforehand and relief afterwards, plus repeated failed attempts to stop, identifies a body focused repetitive behaviour, and habit reversal training combining awareness training with a competing response has the strongest evidence of any intervention. It is first line ahead of any medication in adolescents. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

explanation.summary: The circadian clock runs later during adolescence for biological reasons, and in a minority the shift is severe enough that sleep onset cannot be achieved before the early hours despite adequate opportunity. The diagnostic signature is a normal duration and quality of sleep whenever the timing is unconstrained, contrasted with severe difficulty on school days, which is why holidays and weekends are the most informative part of the history. The pattern is regularly misread as depression, school refusal or laziness, and it does frequently produce secondary low mood, so the direction of causation must be teased out. Treatment combines evening melatonin at a low dose given well before current sleep onset, bright light exposure on waking, avoidance of evening screens and light, and gradual advancement of the schedule, with weekend consistency the hardest and most important element.
key_points: Normal sleep when timing is unconstrained separates this from insomnia
Holidays and weekends are the most informative part of the history
Melatonin works by shifting phase, so timing matters more than dose
Morning bright light consolidates the advance in phase
Secondary low mood is common and resolves as the schedule corrects
explanation.pearls: Melatonin advances the body clock when taken about five hours before habitual sleep onset, so in an adolescent falling asleep at three in the morning the first dose belongs around ten at night, and giving it at the current bedtime wastes the phase shifting effect entirely.

sources.label: RANZCP: Sleep disorders in young people
Australasian Sleep Association: Delayed sleep wake phase disorder

options.rationale: A stable eight hour sleep period that is simply shifted later, with normal quality and refreshed waking when the timing is unconstrained, is a circadian phase problem rather than an inability to sleep. Small doses of melatonin given in the early evening shift the body clock earlier, and timed bright light after waking consolidates the shift. (Source: RANZCP: Sleep disorders in young people)
source_refs: RANZCP: Sleep disorders in young people

options.rationale: Antidepressant treatment addresses a depressive episode, which would show low mood and loss of interest across weekends and holidays as well as school days. His mood and enjoyment are intact whenever the timing constraint is removed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

A hypnotic forces sleep onset without moving the underlying clock, so the pattern returns as soon as it is stopped, and benzodiazepines are not recommended for adolescents. His problem is the timing of the sleep period rather than an inability to sleep at all. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Melatonin shifts the clock through its timing rather than its sedative effect, so a large dose given at the current late bedtime acts as a hypnotic and can even delay the phase further. The drug is appropriate; the dose and timing are not. (Source: RANZCP: Sleep disorders in young people)
source_refs: RANZCP: Sleep disorders in young people

options.rationale: A sleep study answers questions about breathing, limb movements or unusual events during sleep, none of which are suggested here. His diary already demonstrates normal sleep duration and consolidation once the timing is free. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Delayed sleep wake phase disorder)
source_refs: Australasian Sleep Association: Delayed sleep wake phase disorder

explanation.summary: Chronic insomnia is defined by difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep on at least three nights a week for three months with daytime consequences, and it is maintained by behaviours that develop in response to poor sleep rather than by whatever started it. Excessive time in bed, daytime napping and clock watching are the usual culprits, and they are precisely what behavioural therapy targets through stimulus control and sleep restriction. Australian guidance is unambiguous that psychological treatment is first line at all ages and that hypnotics are limited to short courses, because tolerance develops within weeks while the harms of falls, fracture, cognitive impairment and daytime sedation accumulate. Digital and telephone delivered programs have made the therapy accessible outside metropolitan areas, which removes the commonest practical excuse for a repeat script.
key_points: Behavioural therapy is first line for chronic insomnia at any age
Benefits of therapy persist after treatment ends, unlike hypnotics
Hypnotics are limited to two to four weeks because of tolerance
Eleven hours in bed with an afternoon nap dilutes sleep pressure
Benzodiazepines roughly double fall and fracture risk in older people
explanation.pearls: Sleep restriction that sets the time in bed to match actual sleep time, in her case about six hours with a fixed rise time, is the single most effective component of the therapy, and it usually worsens daytime sleepiness in the first fortnight before the improvement appears.

sources.label: RACGP: Prescribing drugs of dependence, benzodiazepines

options.rationale: Benzodiazepine hypnotics are recommended for no more than two to four weeks, and continued use in an older person roughly doubles the risk of falls and hip fracture while the hypnotic effect fades. She has already reached the recommended limit. (Source: RACGP: Prescribing drugs of dependence, benzodiazepines)
source_refs: RACGP: Prescribing drugs of dependence, benzodiazepines

options.rationale: Structured behavioural therapy including stimulus control, sleep restriction and cognitive work is first line for persistent insomnia at every age and produces benefits that persist after treatment ends, unlike hypnotics. Her rising dose requirement after two weeks is tolerance, which is the signal to plan withdrawal rather than to repeat the script. (Source: RACGP: Prescribing drugs of dependence, benzodiazepines)
source_refs: RACGP: Prescribing drugs of dependence, benzodiazepines

options.rationale: Sedating antihistamines carry a substantial anticholinergic burden that contributes to confusion, urinary retention and falls in older people, and tolerance to the sedation develops within days. Substituting one hypnotic for a worse one does not address the maintaining factors. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Sedating antidepressants have a role when insomnia accompanies a depressive episode, but they are not indicated for insomnia without depression. Her depression screen is negative and she remains engaged and active. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

A sleep study is indicated when obstructive breathing, limb movements or parasomnia is suspected, signalled by snoring, witnessed apnoea, a large neck or unrefreshing sleep despite adequate duration. Her partner reports none of these and her neck circumference is small. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Insomnia)

explanation.summary: Australian guidance places trauma-focused psychological therapy ahead of medication for posttraumatic stress disorder, and most people who complete an adequate course improve substantially. Residual symptoms are common and it is worth identifying which domain persists, because the answer differs for daytime intrusions, avoidance, mood and sleep. Trauma related nightmares are among the most persistent symptoms and respond poorly to antidepressants alone, which is why an adjunctive noradrenergic blocker occupies a specific niche and imagery rehearsal therapy is offered where it is available. The evidence for prazosin is mixed, with a large negative trial in stable veterans alongside several positive studies, so it is used as a trial with a clear review point rather than as an open ended prescription, and blood pressure is monitored during titration.
key_points: Trauma-focused psychological therapy is first line, ahead of medication
Identify which symptom domain persists before adding anything
Nightmares respond poorly to antidepressant monotherapy
Benzodiazepines worsen outcomes and are specifically discouraged
Dream enactment with movement suggests a parasomnia, not nightmares
explanation.pearls: Prazosin is started at 1 mg at night because of first dose hypotension, and the postural blood pressure should be rechecked at each increase, with most responders settling between 3 mg and 10 mg nightly over several weeks of titration.

sources.label: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for posttraumatic mental health

options.rationale: Low dose antipsychotics are widely prescribed for sleep in this population but Australian guidance does not support them as adjuncts, and they bring weight gain, metabolic change and sedation. They are considered only for treatment resistant illness under specialist supervision. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for posttraumatic mental health)
source_refs: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for posttraumatic mental health

options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are specifically discouraged in this condition because they suppress the emotional processing that psychological treatment depends on, worsen outcomes in several trials and carry dependence risk in a group with high comorbid substance use. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for posttraumatic mental health)
source_refs: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for posttraumatic mental health

options.rationale: A further course is reasonable when the daytime symptoms have failed to respond, whereas his avoidance and hypervigilance have largely resolved and only the nocturnal symptom persists. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for posttraumatic mental health)
source_refs: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for posttraumatic mental health

options.rationale: Persisting trauma related nightmares after an adequate course of trauma-focused psychological therapy are the recognised indication for adjunctive prazosin, which reduces noradrenergic activity during sleep and is titrated upward from a small night time dose. Postural blood pressure is checked as the dose rises. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for posttraumatic mental health)
source_refs: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for posttraumatic mental health

options.rationale: A sleep study is indicated when the person physically enacts dreams, leaves the bed or injures a partner, which raises a parasomnia of later life. His partner reports shouting only, with no motor enactment. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Parasomnias)

explanation.summary: Gambling disorder is classified with the substance use disorders because it shares tolerance, loss of control, preoccupation, concealment and continuation despite harm, and Australians lose more per adult to gambling than any other population. Chasing losses is the most specific feature and distinguishes problem gambling from recreational betting more reliably than the amount wagered. Screening matters because affected people rarely raise it themselves and present instead with depression, anxiety, relationship breakdown, workplace theft or suicidal thinking, and suicide risk in this group is several times the background rate. Treatment centres on cognitive behavioural therapy addressing beliefs about luck, skill and near misses, combined with practical measures including self exclusion, account blocking and financial counselling, with family involvement where the person agrees.
key_points: Chasing losses is the most specific feature of disordered gambling
Screen for it when depression, debt or relationship crisis presents
Suicide risk is several times higher than in the general population
Cognitive behavioural therapy for gambling is the primary treatment
Financial counselling and self exclusion are adjuncts, not substitutes
explanation.pearls: Continuous forms such as in play sports betting and electronic gaming machines cause disproportionate harm compared with weekly lottery products, because the short interval between stake and outcome allows chasing within a single sitting.

options.rationale: Opioid antagonists have modest evidence in this condition and are considered when psychological therapy has failed or when there is a strong family history of alcohol use disorder. Medication is not the first intervention when structured therapy has not yet been tried. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Excessive gambling occurring only during periods of elevated mood, reduced sleep and other disinhibited spending would point to a mood disorder, which can also cause financial harm. His gambling has been continuous for three years with no elevated episodes. (Source: RANZCP: Gambling disorder)

Tolerance to stake size, chasing losses, concealment and repeated failed attempts to stop define a behavioural addiction, and structured cognitive behavioural therapy targeting gambling related cognitions has the strongest evidence, delivered alongside financial counselling because unresolved debt is a powerful driver of relapse. Both are available free through Australian gambling help services. (Source: RANZCP: Gambling disorder)

Inpatient withdrawal exists to manage the physiological consequences of stopping a substance, and there is no physical withdrawal syndrome from gambling. Removing him from home for a fortnight does not address the cognitions or the debt that will greet him on return. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction)

Self exclusion and blocking software are useful harm reduction measures and should be part of the plan, but used alone they leave the underlying cognitions untreated and online accounts are easily reopened. It is an adjunct rather than a treatment. (Source: RANZCP: Gambling disorder)

explanation.summary: Relapse prevention pharmacotherapy is offered to everyone with moderate to severe alcohol use disorder alongside psychosocial treatment, yet it remains substantially underprescribed in Australian practice. The two first line agents work differently, with acamprosate stabilising glutamatergic transmission to support ongoing abstinence and naltrexone blunting the rewarding effect of alcohol to reduce heavy drinking. The choice between them turns on organ function and on concurrent medication, since acamprosate is renally cleared and contraindicated in severe renal impairment, while naltrexone is hepatically metabolised and is also incompatible with any opioid analgesia. Disulfiram remains an option for motivated people with supervision and normal liver function, and in all cases the medication is a support for counselling rather than a replacement for it.
key_points: Acamprosate is renally cleared and suits significant liver disease
Naltrexone is hepatically metabolised and blocked by opioid use
Disulfiram risks hepatotoxicity and needs supervised administration
Start relapse prevention as soon as withdrawal has resolved
Medication supplements rather than replaces psychosocial treatment
explanation.pearls: Acamprosate is contraindicated once the estimated glomerular filtration rate falls below 30 mL per minute per 1.73 square metres, so the practical rule is that the kidney decides for acamprosate and the liver decides for naltrexone.

options.rationale: Naltrexone is at least as effective for reducing heavy drinking days but undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism and is avoided in significant liver disease, whereas acamprosate is renally cleared and both are otherwise first line. Liver function must also be monitored if it is ever used. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Disulfiram carries a risk of severe hepatotoxicity and depends on a supervised aversive reaction, making it unsuitable in established cirrhosis. It is reserved for highly motivated people with normal liver function and a supervising partner. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction)

Baclofen is renally cleared and is sometimes used in advanced liver disease, but the evidence base is weaker and the Australian position places it as a second line option after the established agents. It also carries sedation and a withdrawal syndrome of its own. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction)

Benzodiazepines treat the withdrawal syndrome and are stopped once it has resolved, which happened 48 hours ago, and continuing them creates dependence while raising encephalopathy risk in cirrhosis. They have no relapse prevention role. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction)

Acamprosate is not metabolised by the liver and is cleared renally, so preserved synthetic function with normal creatinine makes it the appropriate choice in cirrhosis, and it is started immediately after withdrawal is complete. It reduces the risk of returning to any drinking. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction)

explanation.summary: Lamotrigine is effective for maintenance in bipolar disorder, particularly for preventing depressive episodes, and its main hazard is a serious cutaneous reaction that occurs in roughly one in a thousand adults. That risk is driven by how fast the dose is escalated, which is why the initial schedule takes several weeks and why the rate is halved again when the drug is combined with valproate, since valproate roughly doubles lamotrigine concentrations. Enzyme inducers including carbamazepine and oestrogen containing contraception have the opposite effect and require higher doses, so starting or stopping the pill changes the level substantially. After any interruption of about five days or more the person is treated as new to the drug and the full titration is repeated, and every patient should be told to stop the drug and seek review immediately if a rash appears.
key_points: The cutaneous risk tracks the rate of escalation, not the cumulative exposure
An interruption of five days or more resets the titration requirement
Valproate doubles lamotrigine levels and halves the starting dose
Oestrogen containing contraception lowers lamotrigine levels
Any rash means stopping the drug and seeking review the same day
explanation.pearls: Starting a combined oral contraceptive can halve the lamotrigine concentration and precipitate relapse, while stopping it can double the level and cause toxicity, so the contraceptive decision and the mood stabiliser dose must be made in the same consultation.

sources.label: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.rationale: Resuming the full dose after a gap of this length is the specific prescribing error associated with severe cutaneous reactions, since the risk relates to the rate of dose escalation rather than to cumulative past exposure. Three years of tolerance offers no protection once the drug has washed out. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Halving the dose still starts far above the recommended initial step and compresses the escalation into a week, which is the pattern the slow schedule exists to prevent. After this gap, re-titration begins at the original starting dose and follows the original rate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Tolerance to the rash risk is lost after an interruption of about five days or more, so a gap of eleven days means the escalation must begin again from the initial dose with the same slow steps used at first prescription. Previous tolerance of the maintenance dose does not carry over. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Valproate is a recognised mood stabiliser but carries substantial teratogenic risk in a woman of childbearing potential and is subject to pregnancy prevention requirements. Changing agents to avoid a four to six week titration is a disproportionate trade. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

There is no evidence that corticosteroid cover prevents the cutaneous reaction, and premedicating implies that a fast restart is otherwise acceptable. It also risks masking early rash while the reaction progresses. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Carbamazepine causes hyponatraemia in a substantial minority of users through a direct antidiuretic effect, and the incidence rises with age, with higher doses and with concurrent diuretics or antidepressants. The biochemical picture is that of inappropriate antidiuresis, with a low serum osmolality, a urine osmolality that is inappropriately high and a urine sodium above 30 to 40 mmol/L in a clinically euvolaemic patient with normal thyroid and adrenal function. Symptoms are non-specific and in older people are commonly attributed to dementia or to the psychiatric illness itself, so a sodium level belongs in the work up of any confusion or fall in someone taking the drug. Management removes or reduces the cause, restricts fluid, and above all corrects slowly, because raising the sodium faster than 8 to 10 mmol/L in 24 hours risks osmotic demyelination.
key_points: Carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine are common drug causes of low sodium
Euvolaemia with concentrated urine and urine sodium above 40 defines the syndrome
Exclude thyroid and adrenal insufficiency before accepting the diagnosis
Hypertonic saline is only for seizures, coma or severe neurological signs
Correction faster than 8 to 10 mmol/L per day risks osmotic demyelination
explanation.pearls: Check the sodium two to four weeks after starting or increasing carbamazepine in anyone over 65, because the fall is usually asymptomatic at first and is the single most common reason the drug has to be abandoned in older patients.

options.rationale: Withdrawing the agent and restricting fluid is the correct direction, but stopping an anticonvulsant mood stabiliser abruptly in a woman whose illness has been stable for years risks both seizure and relapse, so the dose is reduced with a planned substitution rather than ceased outright. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

A concentrated urine with urine sodium above 40 mmol/L in a euvolaemic patient with normal thyroid and adrenal function defines inappropriate antidiuresis, and carbamazepine is among the commonest drug causes with the risk rising after a dose increase and with age. Reducing the dose with fluid restriction corrects it while avoiding abrupt withdrawal, and daily sodium prevents overcorrection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Isotonic saline is the treatment for hypovolaemic hyponatraemia, which shows dry mucous membranes, a postural drop, a raised urea and a urine sodium below 20 mmol/L. Given in this setting it is excreted while the free water is retained, and the sodium can fall further. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Hypertonic saline is reserved for seizures, coma or other severe neurological manifestations, and she is oriented to place with no focal deficit. Used without that indication it risks correcting the sodium faster than the 8 to 10 mmol/L daily ceiling. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

A vasopressin receptor antagonist is a specialist option for persistent inappropriate antidiuresis where the cause cannot be removed, and it requires close monitoring because of rapid correction. Leaving the responsible drug unchanged treats the consequence while the cause continues. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Long term lithium requires structured monitoring precisely because its important complications develop slowly and silently. Renal function, thyroid function and calcium are checked every six to twelve months, alongside the lithium level itself, and each one detects a different problem. The calcium abnormality arises because lithium shifts the calcium sensing receptor set point upward, so the parathyroid glands behave as though the calcium is lower than it is, and prevalence rises with duration of treatment to affect a meaningful minority of long term users. Symptoms overlap with both depression and lithium side effects, so fatigue, constipation and low mood in a long term user should prompt a calcium rather than a dose change. Management ranges from observation with monitoring in mild asymptomatic cases through to parathyroid surgery when there is stone disease, bone loss or a substantially elevated calcium, and lithium can often be continued if it remains the only effective treatment.
key_points: Lithium raises the parathyroid set point so the hormone stays unsuppressed
Prevalence increases with duration of treatment over years
Malignant and vitamin D related hypercalcaemia suppress the hormone
Symptoms mimic both depression and lithium side effects
Stone disease or bone loss shifts management towards parathyroid surgery
explanation.pearls: Thiazide diuretics also raise calcium and reduce lithium clearance simultaneously, so adding one to a long term lithium user can produce hypercalcaemia and lithium toxicity in the same fortnight, and the combination needs level and calcium checks within a week of starting.

options.rationale: Lithium raises the set point at which calcium suppresses parathyroid hormone, so the hormone remains inappropriately unsuppressed in the face of a high calcium, and the effect accumulates over years of treatment. The low phosphate and the renal stone fit the same mechanism. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Toxicity presents with a raised level alongside coarse tremor, vomiting, ataxia and confusion, and her level is squarely within range with none of those signs. Lithium associated hyperparathyroidism, unlike toxicity, is not concentration dependent and occurs with levels in range. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Tumour related hypercalcaemia suppresses parathyroid hormone to the bottom of the range because the peptide acts on the same receptor. An unsuppressed hormone excludes that mechanism, and she has no weight loss or other features of malignancy. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Hypercalcaemia)

Vitamin D excess raises calcium and phosphate together while suppressing parathyroid hormone, and her phosphate is low with the hormone raised. She also takes no supplement and her vitamin D level is unremarkable. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

The familial condition gives lifelong mild hypercalcaemia with a characteristically low urinary calcium excretion and rarely causes stones. Her hypercalcaemia is new against previously normal results and it has already produced a stone. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Hypercalcaemia)

explanation.summary: Involuntary orofacial movements emerging after prolonged dopamine blockade affect a meaningful proportion of long term antipsychotic users, with risk rising with age, duration of exposure, female sex, diabetes and the use of first generation high potency agents. The movements are choreoathetoid, typically begin in the tongue, lips and jaw, are absent in sleep and often suppress during speech or voluntary tongue protrusion, and they are frequently more distressing to family than to the patient. They must be separated from drug induced parkinsonism, which is rigid and bradykinetic and improves with anticholinergics, and from the restlessness syndrome, which carries a subjective urge to move and responds to beta blockade or dose reduction. Management withdraws anticholinergics, reduces or switches the antipsychotic where psychiatric stability allows, and considers a vesicular monoamine transporter inhibitor where one is available, with regular standardised rating to track change.
key_points: Anticholinergics aggravate these movements and are withdrawn first
Absence of any urge to move separates this from the restlessness syndrome
Increasing the antipsychotic masks the movements and worsens the disorder
Clozapine carries the lowest liability of the available antipsychotics
Standardised rating at each review documents change objectively
explanation.pearls: Standardised rating with the Abnormal Involuntary Movement Scale every six months is recommended for anyone on long term antipsychotic treatment, because the movements are often unnoticed by the patient and a documented baseline is what allows a later change to be attributed correctly.

options.rationale: Raising the anticholinergic dose is the treatment for drug induced parkinsonism and acute dystonia, but it measurably aggravates tardive movements. His examination shows no rigidity or bradykinesia to treat. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

A dose increase suppresses the movements briefly by further blocking the same receptors and then worsens the underlying disorder, which is why it is described as masking. His psychosis has been in remission for six years, so there is nothing to treat. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia clinical practice guideline)

Beta blockade is the treatment for the subjective inner restlessness with an urge to move that can accompany antipsychotic treatment, a condition he explicitly does not have. His movements are unaccompanied by any urge and stop during speech. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Anticholinergics worsen this movement disorder rather than helping it, unlike drug induced parkinsonism where they are used, so withdrawing benzatropine is the first step and costs nothing. Switching from a high potency first generation agent to one with lower liability, most evidence favouring clozapine, is the next consideration. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia clinical practice guideline)

Abrupt cessation frequently unmasks or transiently worsens the movements and carries a high risk of psychotic relapse after 22 years of treatment. Any change to the antipsychotic is made gradually and with a plan for maintaining remission. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia clinical practice guideline)

explanation.summary: Severe premenstrual mood symptoms are distinguished from ordinary premenstrual discomfort by the degree of functional impairment and from an underlying mood or anxiety disorder by the symptom-free interval in the follicular phase. Diagnosis requires prospective daily ratings over at least two cycles rather than retrospective recall, because retrospective report agrees poorly with charted symptoms and a substantial proportion of women who describe this pattern turn out to have premenstrual worsening of a continuous disorder instead. That distinction matters because premenstrual exacerbation of an existing depressive or anxiety disorder is treated by optimising treatment of that disorder rather than by intermittent dosing. Serotonergic antidepressants are first line and uniquely act within days in this condition, which allows luteal phase only dosing, and non-pharmacological measures including exercise and cognitive behavioural therapy have supporting evidence.
key_points: Two cycles of prospective daily ratings are required for the diagnosis
A symptom-free follicular phase separates it from a continuous disorder
Serotonergic response occurs within days rather than over weeks
Luteal phase dosing is as effective as continuous dosing here
Progesterone supplementation does not outperform placebo
explanation.pearls: If the charted ratings show symptoms that improve but never fully remit after menstruation, the diagnosis is premenstrual exacerbation of an underlying disorder, and intermittent dosing will fail because the baseline condition needs continuous treatment.

sources.label: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.rationale: Prospectively confirmed symptoms confined to the luteal phase with complete resolution after menstruation respond to serotonergic treatment within a day or two rather than over weeks, which is why dosing restricted to the second half of the cycle works as well as continuous dosing. It also limits total exposure and side effects. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.rationale: Continuous dosing is equally effective and is preferred when symptoms spill beyond the luteal phase or when cycles are irregular. Her charted symptoms are strictly confined to the luteal phase, which makes intermittent dosing the more economical choice. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.rationale: Suppressing ovulation helps some women and is a reasonable option for those who also want contraception, but the evidence is weaker than for serotonergic treatment and she is not seeking a hormonal method. It is generally second line for the mood symptoms themselves. (Source: RANZCOG: Premenstrual disorders)

Progesterone supplementation has repeatedly failed to outperform placebo for these symptoms and can aggravate them in sensitive women. It persists in practice despite the evidence, which is why it appears here. (Source: RANZCOG: Premenstrual disorders)

Medical suppression of the ovarian cycle is highly effective but is reserved for severe symptoms that have failed serotonergic and hormonal treatment, because of bone loss and menopausal symptoms. It is a specialist step, not a starting point. (Source: RANZCOG: Premenstrual disorders)

explanation.summary: Body dysmorphic disorder affects around two per cent of the population and is markedly overrepresented in cosmetic surgery and dermatology clinics, where it is rarely recognised because the presenting request looks ordinary. The diagnosis requires preoccupation with a perceived defect that is not observable or appears slight to others, repetitive behaviours such as mirror checking, grooming, skin picking or reassurance seeking, and clinically significant distress or impairment. Insight is frequently absent, and delusional conviction is now treated as a specifier rather than as a separate psychotic disorder, which keeps the treatment pathway the same. Cosmetic procedures almost never help, with most patients reporting the same or worse concern afterwards and many transferring the preoccupation to a new feature. Rates of suicidal ideation and attempts are very high, so risk assessment is part of every consultation.
key_points: The perceived defect is not observable or appears slight to others
Repetitive checking, grooming or reassurance seeking is required
Delusional conviction is a specifier, not a separate psychotic disorder
Cosmetic procedures rarely help and often shift the preoccupation
Suicidal ideation and attempts are substantially more common than average
explanation.pearls: Asking how many hours a day the person spends thinking about the feature separates this from ordinary appearance concern, since an hour or more daily is the working threshold, and most people presenting for repeat cosmetic procedures with this disorder report three hours or more.

sources.label: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders
BMJ Best Practice: Body dysmorphic disorder

options.rationale: Adding therapy alongside a fourth procedure still endorses the belief that the nose is the problem and repeats a cycle that has already failed three times. The therapy and risk assessment are appropriate, but providing the referral is not. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.rationale: Absolute conviction occurs in about a third of people with this disorder and is graded as poor insight rather than reclassified as a psychotic illness, so serotonergic treatment and therapy remain the approach. Antipsychotics are used only as augmentation when response is inadequate. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.rationale: Reassurance functions in the same way as his mirror checking, giving momentary relief and reinforcing the preoccupation, and it is one of the behaviours the therapy explicitly targets. It also leaves the suicide risk unassessed for a month. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Body dysmorphic disorder)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Body dysmorphic disorder

options.rationale: Appearance preoccupation in an eating disorder centres on weight and body shape and is accompanied by dietary restriction, compensatory behaviours or binge eating. His concern is confined to a single facial feature with no disordered eating described. (Source: RANZCP: Eating disorders)

Preoccupation with a flaw not observable to others, repetitive checking, avoidance and marked functional loss identifies the disorder, and further surgery predictably fails to relieve it while the risk of suicide in this group is among the highest in psychiatry. Tailored cognitive behavioural therapy with exposure and response prevention is the primary treatment. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

explanation.summary: Excessive daytime sleepiness in a young adult is most often caused by insufficient or irregular sleep, and a sleep diary with actigraphy is what separates that from a primary hypersomnia. Narcolepsy type 1 results from loss of hypocretin producing neurons in the hypothalamus and is defined clinically by sleepiness with cataplexy, a sudden partial or complete loss of muscle tone triggered by strong emotion, most often laughter, during which the person remains fully conscious. Sleep paralysis, hypnagogic hallucinations and disrupted nocturnal sleep complete the tetrad but are individually non-specific, and cataplexy is the feature that carries real diagnostic weight. Diagnosis in Australia requires overnight polysomnography followed by a multiple sleep latency test performed off stimulants and antidepressants, which is why treatment is not started first.
key_points: Cataplexy with preserved awareness is the most specific clinical feature
Refreshing short naps distinguish this from depressive hypersomnia
A sleep diary excludes insufficient sleep as the explanation
The multiple sleep latency test must be performed off stimulants
Diagnosis precedes treatment because access and driving advice both depend on it
explanation.pearls: Cataplexy is frequently misread as syncope or as a seizure, and what separates them at the bedside is that consciousness is fully retained throughout the attack, so a patient who can recount what was said while they were slumped on the floor has had cataplexy rather than a faint.

sources.label: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy diagnosis and management
RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.rationale: Hypersomnia does occur in depression, but he screens negative, describes his mood as good and wakes refreshed from naps, whereas depressive hypersomnia is typically unrefreshing. Serotonergic agents are used in this condition for cataplexy rather than as an initial empirical trial. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.rationale: Starting a wake promoting agent before the sleep study contaminates the multiple sleep latency test, which must be performed off stimulants, and in Australia subsidised access depends on a confirmed diagnosis. Treating first also leaves the driving and workplace safety assessment without a diagnosis to rest on. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy diagnosis and management)
source_refs: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy diagnosis and management

options.rationale: These are reasonable screening tests for fatigue, but they have already been done and are normal, and neither explains sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by emotion. Repeating normal investigations delays the study that establishes the diagnosis. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy diagnosis and management)
source_refs: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy diagnosis and management

options.rationale: Sudden emotionally triggered loss of muscle tone with preserved awareness, refreshing naps, sleep paralysis and severe daytime sleepiness despite adequate nocturnal sleep is the pattern of narcolepsy with cataplexy, and the diagnosis requires overnight polysomnography to exclude other causes followed by a multiple sleep latency test. A mean sleep latency of 8 minutes or less with two or more sleep onset rapid eye movement periods confirms it. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy diagnosis and management)
source_refs: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy diagnosis and management

options.rationale: Sleep hygiene advice addresses insufficient or irregular sleep, which the diary and actigraphy have already excluded by documenting eight consistent hours nightly. Insufficient sleep syndrome is far commoner in this age group but does not produce cataplexy. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy diagnosis and management)
source_refs: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy diagnosis and management

explanation.summary: A seasonal pattern is a specifier applied to recurrent major depressive episodes rather than a separate diagnosis, and it requires episodes that begin and remit at characteristic times of year across at least two consecutive years with no non seasonal episodes in between. The symptom profile is characteristically atypical, with hypersomnia, increased appetite with carbohydrate craving, weight gain and leaden heaviness, in contrast to the insomnia and weight loss of melancholic depression. Prevalence rises with latitude, so the pattern is far more common in Tasmania than in northern Queensland, and a recent move south is a genuinely relevant piece of history. Bright light therapy, cognitive behavioural therapy adapted for the seasonal pattern, and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors all have evidence, and treatment can be started prophylactically in early autumn once the pattern is established.
key_points: The seasonal specifier requires at least two consecutive years of the same pattern
Hypersomnia with carbohydrate craving and weight gain is the typical profile
Absence of any elevated mood episode argues against a bipolar diathesis
Bright light of about 10000 lux for 30 minutes after waking is the usual regimen
Prophylactic treatment can be started before the season in later years
explanation.pearls: Bright light therapy should be given within an hour of waking rather than in the evening, because evening exposure delays the circadian phase and can worsen the hypersomnia the treatment is meant to relieve.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders
BMJ Best Practice: Seasonal affective disorder

options.rationale: Lithium is used where there is a bipolar diathesis, and she has never had an episode of elevated mood, reduced need for sleep or increased goal directed activity. A seasonal pattern alone does not make a depressive illness bipolar. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.rationale: Her vitamin D level is only marginally below the target and supplementation has not been shown to treat depressive episodes, seasonal or otherwise. Correcting the level is reasonable for bone health but is not a treatment for the presenting problem. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.rationale: Electroconvulsive therapy is reserved for severe, treatment resistant, psychotic or life threatening depression, and she is working, eating and not suicidal with a moderate symptom score. Offering it at this stage is disproportionate to the severity. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.rationale: Exercise and daylight exposure are worth encouraging but a three month review takes her to the end of winter, by which time the episode would have remitted regardless of what was done. Morning outdoor light is genuinely useful, but as an adjunct rather than as the whole plan. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.rationale: Depressive episodes with a seasonal pattern and the atypical features of hypersomnia, carbohydrate craving and weight gain respond to bright light of about 10000 lux for 30 minutes soon after waking, with benefit usually apparent within one to two weeks. It is recommended first for moderate seasonal episodes because it works quickly, is well tolerated, and can be started before the winter in subsequent years to prevent recurrence. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

explanation.summary: Burnout is an occupational phenomenon characterised by emotional exhaustion, cynicism or depersonalisation, and reduced professional efficacy, and it is classified as a factor influencing health status rather than as a mental disorder. The clinical task is to separate it from a major depressive episode, because the treatments differ, and context dependence separates them most reliably, since burnout remits away from the workplace while a depressive episode follows the person everywhere. The two overlap and burnout is a risk factor for depression, so a doctor presenting this way needs ongoing review rather than a single assessment. Doctors seeking care for their own mental health face a specific additional barrier in the fear of mandatory notification, and Australian guidance is explicit that treating practitioners notify only where there is substantial risk of harm to the public from impairment, not merely because a colleague is unwell.
key_points: Burnout remits away from work whereas a depressive episode does not
Preserved enjoyment, sleep and appetite argue against major depression
Effective intervention targets workload and role, not only the individual
Mandatory notification requires substantial risk of harm from impairment
Burnout is a risk factor for depression, so continuing review is required
explanation.pearls: Every practitioner should have their own general practitioner and should not self prescribe or be treated by a colleague informally, because self treatment is associated with delayed presentation and with the under recognition of deterioration that turns burnout into a depressive episode.

sources.label: AHPRA: Guidelines for mandatory notifications about registered health practitioners
RACGP: Keeping the doctor alive, a self care guidebook for medical practitioners
RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.rationale: Her symptoms are work bound, remit fully on leave and are accompanied by preserved enjoyment, sleep and appetite elsewhere, which describes occupational burnout rather than a major depressive episode, and the intervention that works is directed at workload, recovery and role rather than at the person alone. The mandatory notification threshold requires that a practitioner is placing the public at substantial risk of harm through an impairment, and a registrar who is functioning safely, has insight and is engaging in treatment does not meet it. (Source: AHPRA: Guidelines for mandatory notifications about registered health practitioners)
source_refs: AHPRA: Guidelines for mandatory notifications about registered health practitioners

options.rationale: Mandatory notification is triggered by impairment, intoxication, significant departure from accepted standards or sexual misconduct placing the public at substantial risk, none of which is present in a practitioner who is working safely and seeking help. Notifying in these circumstances deters doctors from disclosing distress, which is the harm the threshold is set to avoid. (Source: AHPRA: Guidelines for mandatory notifications about registered health practitioners)
source_refs: AHPRA: Guidelines for mandatory notifications about registered health practitioners

options.rationale: Antidepressant treatment is directed at a depressive episode, and her symptoms remit completely on leave with preserved anhedonia free enjoyment, sleep and appetite, which is not that illness. Medicating a workload problem leaves the cause untouched and can delay the changes that would help. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.rationale: Prolonged certified absence without a formal diagnosis or a plan to change the work conditions usually leads to the same symptoms recurring on return, as her own two week experience demonstrates. Time away helps only when it is paired with a change in the demands she returns to. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.rationale: An employee assistance program is a useful adjunct but a single referral without continuing review leaves no one tracking whether she deteriorates into a depressive episode. Adequate care requires ongoing review by her own general practitioner alongside any referral. (Source: RACGP: Keeping the doctor alive, a self care guidebook for medical practitioners)
source_refs: RACGP: Keeping the doctor alive, a self care guidebook for medical practitioners

explanation.summary: Avoidant restrictive food intake disorder is defined by a persistent failure to meet nutritional or energy needs leading to weight loss, nutritional deficiency, dependence on supplements or marked psychosocial interference, in the absence of body image disturbance or a drive for thinness. Three patterns are described, namely sensory sensitivity to the appearance, smell or texture of food, lack of interest in eating, and fear of an aversive consequence such as choking or vomiting, and children commonly show more than one, as this boy does. It is distinguished from ordinary selective eating by the presence of that nutritional or functional impact, and from anorexia nervosa by the absence of weight and shape concerns, which is why the specific questions about fear of weight gain and body checking matter. Medical instability is assessed exactly as it would be in any restrictive eating disorder, since bradycardia, hypotension and electrolyte disturbance carry the same significance whatever the motivation for the restriction.
key_points: The disorder is defined by nutritional impact without weight or shape concern
Sensory, low appetite and aversive consequence patterns often coexist
Bradycardia in an underweight child signals medical instability regardless of diagnosis
Family based treatment for anorexia nervosa is not the correct model here
Treatment combines graded texture exposure with nutritional restoration
explanation.pearls: A resting heart rate below 50 beats per minute, a postural blood pressure drop of more than 20 mmHg, or a temperature below 35.5 degrees Celsius in a child with restrictive eating are indications for medical admission regardless of which eating disorder is causing the restriction.

sources.label: ANZAED: Australia and New Zealand Academy for Eating Disorders practice standards
BMJ Best Practice: Avoidant restrictive food intake disorder

options.rationale: Ordinary selective eating does not cause a fall across centiles, weight loss and bradycardia, and this presentation meets the threshold for a feeding and eating disorder. A year of observation would allow further growth failure and pubertal delay. (Source: ANZAED: Australia and New Zealand Academy for Eating Disorders practice standards)
source_refs: ANZAED: Australia and New Zealand Academy for Eating Disorders practice standards

options.rationale: Family based treatment is the evidence-based approach for anorexia nervosa, which requires a fear of weight gain or behaviour that interferes with it, and he wants to gain weight and has no body image disturbance. Applying a treatment built around challenging a drive for thinness to a sensory and choking based avoidance misses the mechanism. (Source: ANZAED: Australia and New Zealand Academy for Eating Disorders practice standards)
source_refs: ANZAED: Australia and New Zealand Academy for Eating Disorders practice standards

options.rationale: Restriction driven by sensory characteristics of food and by fear of choking, without body image disturbance or fear of weight gain, and producing weight loss with nutritional deficiency, is avoidant restrictive food intake disorder, which is managed by a multidisciplinary eating disorder service with dietetic and psychological input. Treatment uses graded exposure to new textures alongside nutritional restoration rather than the approaches designed for weight and shape concerns. (Source: ANZAED: Australia and New Zealand Academy for Eating Disorders practice standards)
source_refs: ANZAED: Australia and New Zealand Academy for Eating Disorders practice standards

options.rationale: Endoscopy is indicated where there is dysphagia, food impaction, reflux symptoms or suspicion of eosinophilic disease, and his symptoms are texture aversion from toddlerhood rather than difficulty with swallowing itself. Coeliac serology and inflammatory markers are already normal. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Avoidant restrictive food intake disorder)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Avoidant restrictive food intake disorder

options.rationale: No medication has an established role as primary treatment for this disorder, and antidepressants in underweight children carry particular monitoring requirements without addressing the avoidance. Fluoxetine does have a role in bulimia nervosa in adults, which is a different disorder entirely. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Selective mutism is an anxiety disorder in which a child who speaks normally in some settings consistently fails to speak in specific social situations where speech is expected, most often school, for at least one month beyond the first month of attendance. It is frequently misread as oppositional behaviour, as shyness or as a language or hearing problem, and the demonstration that the child speaks fluently somewhere is what settles those questions. Comorbid social anxiety disorder is present in the majority, and a minority have a coexisting language or communication difficulty, so assessment includes both. Treatment is behavioural, using graded exposure, stimulus fading and shaping delivered largely in the setting where the child is mute, with the adults around the child coached not to pressure or to speak for them, and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors reserved for cases that do not respond.
key_points: Fluent speech in one setting excludes hearing loss and language disorder
The diagnostic threshold is one month beyond the first month of school
Comorbid social anxiety disorder is present in most affected children
Treatment is delivered in the setting where the child does not speak
Pressuring the child to speak reliably worsens the avoidance
explanation.pearls: Stimulus fading is the core technique, in which the child first speaks to a trusted person in the empty classroom and a peer or teacher is then gradually introduced into the room, because the aim is to transfer existing speech into the feared setting rather than to teach speech the child already has.

sources.label: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders

options.rationale: Hearing loss is a reasonable consideration for a child who does not speak, but she has passed screening and, more decisively, speaks fluently and sings at home, which requires intact hearing. Repeating the hearing assessment delays the referral that addresses the anxiety. (Source: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders

options.rationale: A developmental language disorder affects language in every setting, whereas her vocabulary and sentence structure are age appropriate at home on the video her parents have brought. Speech pathology may join the team later, but the primary problem is situational anxiety rather than language competence. (Source: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders

options.rationale: Eight months of complete absence of speech in a whole setting is well beyond situational shyness and beyond the one month threshold that defines the disorder. Untreated, the pattern becomes entrenched and predicts later social anxiety disorder and academic underachievement. (Source: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders

options.rationale: Consistent failure to speak in a specific setting for more than a month, with fluent speech elsewhere, is selective mutism, an anxiety disorder for which behavioural treatment using graded exposure and stimulus fading delivered in the school environment is first line. Involving the teacher matters because progress depends on changing how adults in the setting respond, and pressuring the child to speak reliably makes it worse. (Source: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders

options.rationale: Medication is considered when a structured behavioural program has been tried and has not produced progress, or where impairment is severe, and it is an adjunct rather than a first step in a 6-year-old. Fluoxetine does have evidence in selective mutism, but after behavioural treatment rather than instead of it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Restless legs syndrome is diagnosed clinically on five features, namely an urge to move the legs usually with uncomfortable sensations, worsening at rest, relief with movement, a circadian pattern worst in the evening or at night, and the absence of a better explanation such as cramp or positional discomfort. It is commonly confused with akathisia in psychiatric patients, and the distinguishing features are that akathisia is generalised rather than confined to the legs, lacks the evening predominance, is not relieved by brief walking, and is temporally linked to starting or increasing a dopamine blocking drug. Periodic limb movements of sleep, described by a bed partner as repeated leg jerks, accompany the syndrome in most patients and support the diagnosis. Iron deficiency, chronic kidney disease, pregnancy and dopamine blocking or serotonergic drugs are the secondary causes to look for, and iron status should be checked in every patient because replacement can abolish symptoms entirely.
key_points: The five clinical criteria include a circadian pattern and relief with movement
Akathisia is generalised and follows a dose change, unlike this pattern
Periodic limb movements reported by a partner support the diagnosis
Replacement is indicated at a ferritin below about 75 micrograms per litre
Reversible causes are corrected before starting symptomatic drug therapy
explanation.pearls: The ferritin threshold for iron replacement in restless legs syndrome is around 75 micrograms per litre, which is well above the level at which iron deficiency anaemia is diagnosed, so a normal haemoglobin with a ferritin in the 20s is still an indication to treat.

sources.label: Australasian Sleep Association: Restless legs syndrome
BMJ Best Practice: Restless legs syndrome

options.rationale: Akathisia is a subjective restlessness of the whole body that is present throughout the day, is not confined to the legs, is not relieved by brief walking and typically follows a dose increase or a recent start. He has been on an unchanged dose for three years and sits still throughout the interview. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

An urge to move the legs with unpleasant sensations that worsen at rest in the evening, are relieved by movement and are accompanied by periodic limb movements describes restless legs syndrome, and iron deficiency is the commonest reversible cause with replacement indicated when ferritin is below about 75 micrograms per litre. The nosebleeds and restricted diet need their own assessment, since treating the deficiency without finding its source leaves the cause unaddressed. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Restless legs syndrome)
source_refs: Australasian Sleep Association: Restless legs syndrome

options.rationale: Anticholinergic agents treat drug induced parkinsonism and acute dystonia, neither of which is present on examination, and they are ineffective for this circadian urge to move. They also worsen cognition and carry a risk of aggravating tardive movements. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Dopamine agonists do treat the syndrome but are no longer first line because of augmentation, in which symptoms intensify and spread over months of treatment, and they should not be started before reversible causes are corrected. They remain an option once iron is replete and symptoms persist. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Restless legs syndrome)
source_refs: Australasian Sleep Association: Restless legs syndrome

options.rationale: Reducing an effective antipsychotic that has maintained him for three years risks relapse of psychosis, and the symptom pattern here is not the dose related akathisia that a reduction would target. Antipsychotics can aggravate the syndrome, but iron correction is tried before destabilising treatment that is working. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Community treatment orders exist in every Australian state and territory, with differing names and criteria, but all share a requirement that the person has a mental illness requiring treatment, that treatment can be provided in the community, that they are unable or unwilling to consent, and that the order is the least restrictive option available. A documented pattern of relapse following cessation is the evidence base on which such an order is usually justified, and the order authorises treatment rather than detention. Long-acting injectable antipsychotics pair naturally with these orders because non-adherence becomes visible immediately as a missed appointment rather than silently over weeks of untreated illness, and evidence supports their use earlier than has traditionally been the practice. Recovery oriented care still applies under an order, so the plan should include carer involvement, psychosocial supports, regular review and a clear intention to revoke the order when it is no longer needed.
key_points: An order requires that treatment can be safely delivered in the community
Persistent lack of insight is common and does not justify indefinite detention
A pattern of relapse on cessation is the usual evidential basis for an order
Long-acting injectables make non-adherence immediately visible
Treatment resistance and non-adherence are different problems with different answers
explanation.pearls: A community treatment order authorises treatment but not detention, so a person who refuses the injection while on an order is brought in for the medication to be given rather than admitted, and each order carries a statutory review date and a right of appeal to an independent tribunal.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia

options.rationale: This is precisely the plan that has failed on three previous occasions, because supervision does not resolve a stated intention not to take the medication. Repeating an intervention with a documented pattern of failure is not a neutral choice given the harm each relapse causes. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia

options.rationale: Insight often does not return even with full symptomatic remission, so this plan has no endpoint, and continued detention is not the least restrictive option once treatment can be delivered in the community. Mental health legislation across Australia requires the least restrictive setting consistent with safe treatment. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia

options.rationale: Placing the responsibility for enforcing treatment on a family member damages the relationship he depends on and gives her no authority to act when he declines. Carer involvement is valuable as support rather than as a substitute for a treatment framework. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia

options.rationale: Clozapine is indicated for illness that has failed to respond to adequate trials of two antipsychotics, whereas his symptoms respond well whenever he takes medication, so the problem is adherence rather than resistance. Relapse despite taking medication would instead point to treatment resistance. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia

options.rationale: A repeated pattern of relapse on cessation, a stated intention not to continue, and preserved response when treated is the situation community treatment orders exist for, and a long-acting injectable removes the daily decision that adherence otherwise depends on. It is also the least restrictive option that can deliver effective treatment, since the alternative that reliably prevents relapse is continued detention. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia

explanation.summary: Fabricated or induced illness, also described as factitious disorder imposed on another, is a form of child abuse in which a carer exaggerates, fabricates or induces symptoms, resulting in unnecessary investigation and treatment. The recognised warning signs are symptoms witnessed only by one carer, a history that does not fit any recognisable illness, repeatedly normal investigations, symptoms that resolve when the carer is absent, a carer with health care knowledge or unusual familiarity with medical terminology, and a child who remains well between reported events. Harm arises from the investigations and treatments themselves, from school absence and from the child internalising the identity of being ill, so continuing to investigate is not a neutral holding position. Because the diagnosis lives in the pattern across multiple presentations rather than in any one event, the essential step is to assemble the complete record in a multidisciplinary meeting including the treating teams, child protection and often hospital legal advice, before anything is said to the family.
key_points: Symptoms witnessed only by one carer and absent in their absence is the key pattern
Repeatedly normal investigations in a thriving child is a warning sign, not reassurance
Further investigation is itself a source of harm rather than a neutral option
The diagnosis rests on the pattern across the whole record
Confrontation before protective planning risks flight and escalation
explanation.pearls: Covert video surveillance is used in only a small number of Australian centres and never on a clinician's own initiative, because it requires hospital executive approval, legal advice and coordination with police and child protection before any recording begins.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Fabricated or induced illness
RACGP: Abuse and violence, working with our patients in general practice
BMJ Best Practice: Fabricated or induced illness by carers

options.rationale: Two normal studies and normal imaging in a developmentally normal child whose episodes have never been witnessed by a clinician make a third study very unlikely to change anything. Continuing to investigate also escalates the very process that is harming the child. (Source: RCH CPG: Fabricated or induced illness)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Fabricated or induced illness

options.rationale: Treating unwitnessed episodes with normal investigations exposes a well child to the adverse effects of a drug she does not need and appears to validate the reported illness. Empirical treatment in this situation has been shown to prolong the harm rather than resolve the uncertainty. (Source: RCH CPG: Fabricated or induced illness)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Fabricated or induced illness

options.rationale: Episodes occurring only in one person's presence, ceasing entirely in their absence, in a thriving child with repeatedly normal investigations, is the pattern of illness fabricated or induced by a carer, which is a form of child abuse and is notifiable on reasonable suspicion. A multidisciplinary meeting that assembles the whole medical record is essential first, because the diagnosis rests on the pattern across admissions rather than on any single episode, and no single clinician holds that view. (Source: RCH CPG: Fabricated or induced illness)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Fabricated or induced illness

options.rationale: Discharging without addressing the pattern returns the child to the situation generating the episodes and the invasive investigations that follow them. A call plan increases rather than reduces the medical contact that is the mechanism of harm. (Source: RCH CPG: Fabricated or induced illness)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Fabricated or induced illness

options.rationale: Direct confrontation before the protective process is in place risks flight from the hospital, escalation of the behaviour, or a move to another health service where the history begins again. The family is told, but by the protective and medical teams together as part of a planned process rather than by a single clinician on the ward. (Source: RCH CPG: Fabricated or induced illness)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Fabricated or induced illness

explanation.summary: Pregabalin was once regarded as having low misuse potential, but it is now a recognised drug of dependence, particularly among people with a history of opioid or other substance use, in whom it produces euphoria and sedation at supratherapeutic doses. The most serious hazard is the combination with opioids, since both depress respiration and the combination is disproportionately represented in Australian overdose deaths. Real time prescription monitoring is operational across Australian jurisdictions and gives a prescriber an immediate view of all monitored medicines dispensed to a patient, which converts a suspicion of multiple prescribers into documented fact before a conversation takes place. The management principles are to establish the true dose, keep the opioid agonist treatment intact, taper the pregabalin gradually because abrupt cessation causes a withdrawal syndrome including seizures, and treat the underlying pain and sleep problems by other means.
key_points: Pregabalin misuse is concentrated among people with a substance use history
The combination with opioids markedly raises the risk of respiratory depression
Real time prescription monitoring documents supply from multiple prescribers
Abrupt cessation causes a withdrawal syndrome that can include seizures
Opioid agonist treatment is preserved rather than withdrawn as a sanction
explanation.pearls: Pregabalin is renally cleared, so the same dose produces much higher concentrations as kidney function falls, and an older patient or one with chronic kidney disease can develop sedation, ataxia and falls on a dose that was previously well tolerated.

sources.label: RACGP: Prescribing drugs of dependence in general practice

options.rationale: Obtaining supplies from several prescribers is exactly what real time prescription monitoring is designed to reveal, and reviewing it establishes the true total dose before any plan is made. Abrupt cessation of high dose pregabalin risks a withdrawal syndrome with agitation, insomnia and seizures, so the dose is reduced gradually under supervision with the original pain indication reassessed at the same time. (Source: RACGP: Prescribing drugs of dependence in general practice)
source_refs: RACGP: Prescribing drugs of dependence in general practice

options.rationale: Abrupt cessation after months of high dose use can precipitate withdrawal with agitation, sweating, insomnia and seizures, and a four week gap leaves him without support through that period. The drug needs to stop, but by taper rather than by sudden cessation. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Adding a second sedative to a combination of methadone and high dose pregabalin substantially increases the risk of respiratory depression and death. His falls and evening slurring already indicate excessive sedation on the current combination. (Source: RACGP: Prescribing drugs of dependence in general practice)
source_refs: RACGP: Prescribing drugs of dependence in general practice

options.rationale: Prescribing to the level of misuse legitimises a dose that is causing falls and slurred speech and does not address the mechanism, which is the sedative effect rather than uncontrolled neuropathic pain. His straight leg raise is now full and painless, so the original indication has resolved. (Source: RACGP: Prescribing drugs of dependence in general practice)
source_refs: RACGP: Prescribing drugs of dependence in general practice

options.rationale: Removing effective opioid agonist treatment from a man who has been stable on it for two years markedly increases his risk of relapse to injecting and of overdose death. Residential withdrawal has a role for a pregabalin taper that fails in the community, but never at the cost of the opioid treatment that is working. (Source: RACGP: Prescribing drugs of dependence in general practice)
source_refs: RACGP: Prescribing drugs of dependence in general practice

explanation.summary: Intrusive thoughts of accidental or deliberate harm to the infant are reported by most new parents, and they become perinatal obsessive compulsive disorder when they are persistent and distressing enough to drive avoidance, checking, reassurance seeking or other compulsions. The decisive clinical distinction is between egodystonic thoughts, which the mother experiences as unwanted, senseless and contrary to her wishes and which are not associated with an increased risk of harm, and the egosyntonic delusional beliefs of postpartum psychosis, in which the infant may be seen as abnormal, possessed or better off dead and the risk is real and urgent. The two are separated by reality testing, insight, the presence of confusion or perceptual disturbance, and the timing, since psychosis characteristically begins abruptly within the first two weeks. Women very commonly conceal these thoughts for fear that their baby will be removed, so naming the phenomenon, normalising it and explaining that it is treatable is both diagnostic and the first step of treatment.
key_points: Egodystonic intrusive thoughts are not associated with increased risk to the infant
Avoidance and checking are the compulsions that mark the transition to disorder
Preserved insight and reality testing exclude postpartum psychosis
Psychosis usually begins within two weeks with fluctuating confusion
Fear of infant removal is the main barrier to disclosure
explanation.pearls: Sertraline is the usual first choice when a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor is needed in a breastfeeding mother, because it has the lowest relative infant dose of the class and is the best studied, and obsessive compulsive symptoms typically require higher doses and a longer trial of eight to twelve weeks than depressive symptoms do.

sources.label: COPE: Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline
