Sedation is a high risk intervention in its own right, so continuous observation with pulse oximetry, regular vital signs and airway readiness is mandatory afterwards, and the duration of any restraint must be the minimum necessary and fully documented. Every episode requires consideration of the medical differential, since hypoglycaemia, head injury, hypoxia, sepsis, delirium and drug intoxication or withdrawal all present with agitation. A debrief with the patient and with staff afterwards is part of the standard, as is review of whether the legal framework used was appropriate.
key_points: De-escalation and offered oral medication precede parenteral sedation wherever it is safe to attempt them.
Droperidol intramuscularly is the first line parenteral agent in Australian emergency practice.
Continuous monitoring after sedation is mandatory, with over sedation and airway compromise the main risks.
Exclude hypoglycaemia, hypoxia, head injury and sepsis as causes of agitation in every case.
Restraint must be for the shortest necessary period, documented, and followed by a debrief.
explanation.pearls: Check a blood glucose before or immediately alongside sedation in every agitated patient, since hypoglycaemia is the one cause of acute behavioural disturbance that sedation alone will convert from reversible into fatal.

options.rationale: Midazolam works quickly but produces more respiratory depression and more frequent need for airway intervention than droperidol, and an open ended repeat schedule compounds that risk. It is a reasonable adjunct where a single agent has failed rather than a first line choice. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Waiting for a tracing that cannot be obtained in an actively assaultive patient leaves staff at risk and delays treatment indefinitely. Australian emergency data have shown that droperidol at these doses does not produce clinically significant QT related events, which is why a pre-sedation electrocardiogram is not a prerequisite in this setting. (Source: ACEM: Acute Behavioural Disturbance Guideline)

Ketamine is reserved as a rescue agent for severe disturbance that has failed conventional sedation, because it carries higher rates of intubation, laryngospasm and emergence phenomena. Using it before a first line agent has been tried escalates risk without evidence of benefit. (Source: ACEM: Acute Behavioural Disturbance Guideline)

Droperidol given intramuscularly is the agent supported by the largest Australian emergency department trials for acute behavioural disturbance, achieving sedation faster and with fewer additional doses than benzodiazepine monotherapy, and its cardiac safety at these doses has been demonstrated prospectively. Continuous monitoring after administration is part of the intervention rather than an optional extra, because the main risks are over sedation and airway compromise. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Oral medication requires cooperation he has already twice declined, and diazepam has a slow and unpredictable onset by mouth, so this leaves a nurse exposed to imminent assault. Continued de-escalation is correct until the point of physical threat, which has now been crossed. (Source: ACEM: Acute Behavioural Disturbance Guideline)

explanation.summary: Tic disorders affect roughly 1 per cent of school-aged children, with Tourette syndrome requiring multiple motor tics and at least one vocal tic present for more than a year with onset before age 18. The features that distinguish tics from other movement disorders are the premonitory urge, temporary suppressibility with rebound, a waxing and waning course over months, and variation with fatigue, excitement and anxiety. Severity typically peaks in early adolescence and improves substantially through the late teens in the majority, which is an important part of what families are told. Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and obsessive compulsive disorder coexist in a large proportion and frequently cause more functional impairment than the tics themselves, so both are screened for in every case. Treatment is stepped, beginning with education of the family and school and behavioural therapy, with medication reserved for tics causing pain, injury, or genuine impairment reported by the young person rather than by others.
key_points: A premonitory urge relieved by the movement distinguishes a tic from chorea, dystonia or a stereotypy.
Suppression is possible briefly but is effortful and followed by rebound.
Screen every child with tics for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and obsessive compulsive disorder.
Severity usually peaks in early adolescence and improves through the late teens.
Treat the impairment the young person reports, not the disruption reported by others.
explanation.pearls: Habit reversal works by pairing awareness training with a competing response that is physically incompatible with the tic and held for about a minute until the urge subsides, which is why it succeeds where simple instruction to stop reliably fails.

sources.label: RANZCP: Child and Adolescent Psychiatry Guidance

options.rationale: Antipsychotics do reduce tic severity and are used when tics cause pain, injury or substantial impairment, but they bring weight gain, metabolic change and extrapyramidal effects to a boy whose tics bother his school more than they bother him. Tic treatment is guided by the patient's own impairment rather than by an external complaint. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

These agents treat the obsessive compulsive disorder that frequently coexists with tic disorders, but a compulsion is performed to neutralise an obsessional thought whereas his movements follow a physical premonitory urge. He has no obsessions on direct questioning. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Suppression without a substitute response is effortful and followed by a rebound increase, so a reward program built on it sets him up to fail and adds shame to the picture. Habit reversal differs precisely in that it supplies a competing movement to perform when the urge arrives. (Source: RANZCP: Child and Adolescent Psychiatry Guidance)
source_refs: RANZCP: Child and Adolescent Psychiatry Guidance

options.rationale: Investigation is reserved for atypical features such as abrupt onset, a fixed rather than migrating pattern, or abnormal neurological signs, none of which he has after six years of a classical waxing and waning course. A raised streptococcal titre is common in healthy children and would generate uncertainty rather than resolve it. (Source: RANZCP: Child and Adolescent Psychiatry Guidance)
source_refs: RANZCP: Child and Adolescent Psychiatry Guidance

options.rationale: Behavioural therapy built around habit reversal is first line for tic disorders where the tics themselves cause limited impairment, and it teaches a competing response to the premonitory urge rather than attempting suppression. Psychoeducation directed at the school is an essential part of it, because demands to stop the tics increase anxiety and therefore tic frequency. (Source: RANZCP: Child and Adolescent Psychiatry Guidance)
source_refs: RANZCP: Child and Adolescent Psychiatry Guidance

explanation.summary: Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia are common but a sudden change in a resident who has been settled for years should be read as a new symptom with a cause rather than as disease progression. The standard approach examines pain, constipation, urinary retention, infection, drug effects, sensory impairment, and the environmental and interpersonal triggers around care tasks, since resistance confined to showering or toileting almost always signals discomfort or a sense of threat during that activity. Anticholinergic drugs are a frequent and reversible contributor, worsening cognition, precipitating retention, and directly opposing cholinesterase inhibitors prescribed for the dementia itself. Antipsychotics carry an increased risk of cerebrovascular events and death in this population, are restricted under Australian aged care quality standards, require informed consent from the resident or substitute decision maker, and should be reviewed for cessation within twelve weeks when used. Non-pharmacological approaches, including changing who provides care, the time of day and the manner of approach, resolve a large proportion of these presentations.
key_points: A sudden behavioural change in stable dementia is a symptom with a cause until proven otherwise.
Screen for pain, constipation, urinary retention, infection, new drugs and sensory deficits first.
Anticholinergics worsen cognition, cause retention and oppose cholinesterase inhibitors.
Antipsychotics in dementia increase stroke and mortality risk and require consent and time limited review.
Behaviour confined to personal care usually reflects discomfort or perceived threat during that task.
explanation.pearls: A bladder scan at the bedside takes two minutes and a residual volume above 300 mL identifies retention as the cause of agitation in a resident who cannot report it, which is a far higher yield first test than a urine dipstick in this setting.

options.rationale: New behaviour change in established dementia is treated as a symptom with a cause, and the timing after an anticholinergic was started, the dry mouth, the suprapubic fullness and the confinement of distress to toileting and showering all point to retention. Anticholinergics also worsen cognition directly and oppose the cholinesterase inhibitor he is already taking, so reviewing that drug addresses two problems at once. (Source: RACGP: Aged Care Clinical Guide)

Leucocytes without nitrites in an afebrile resident with no dysuria most often represents asymptomatic bacteriuria or sample contamination rather than infection, and treating it drives resistance without improving behaviour. Strong smelling urine is not a diagnostic criterion for urinary tract infection at any age. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Benzodiazepines in older people with dementia increase falls, fractures and confusion and can cause paradoxical disinhibition, and premedicating before care would entrench the problem rather than solve it. Timing sedation to a trigger also concedes that the trigger has not been examined. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Specialist behavioural advice is valuable and the service is a genuine Australian resource, but escalating the cholinesterase inhibitor does not treat acute agitation and the referral pathway takes time he does not need to spend in pain. The immediate task is to look for the reversible cause. (Source: RACGP: Aged Care Clinical Guide)

Antipsychotics in dementia raise the risk of stroke and of death and are indicated only after reversible causes are excluded and non-pharmacological measures have failed, usually where there is severe distress or risk of harm. Prescribing now would treat a behaviour whose trigger is identifiable and whose likely cause is sitting in his medication list. (Source: RACGP: Aged Care Clinical Guide)

explanation.summary: Decisions about admission in eating disorders rest on physiological parameters, the rate of weight loss and psychiatric risk, not on body mass index in isolation, and the group most often missed is those whose starting weight was high and who therefore remain in the population healthy range after losing a dangerous amount. Cardiovascular instability is the dominant acute risk, with bradycardia below 40 beats per minute, postural drops, hypotension, hypothermia and electrolyte disturbance all indicating a need for monitored inpatient care. Refeeding syndrome follows the reintroduction of carbohydrate to a depleted patient, as insulin drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium intracellularly and thiamine stores are consumed, producing arrhythmia, cardiac failure, delirium and seizures. A phosphate already below the reference range before feeding has begun marks a patient at particularly high risk. Australian practice uses supervised refeeding with daily electrolytes in the first week, thiamine before any carbohydrate load, and the recognition that starting too cautiously prolongs malnutrition and carries its own harm.
key_points: Admission decisions rest on physiological instability, not body mass index alone.
Rapid or large weight loss carries risk even when the absolute weight appears normal.
Bradycardia below 40, postural drop over 20 mmHg systolic and hypothermia are admission criteria.
A low phosphate before feeding starts identifies a patient at high risk of refeeding syndrome.
Give thiamine before any carbohydrate load and monitor phosphate, potassium and magnesium daily.
explanation.pearls: Bradycardia in anorexia nervosa is an adaptive energy conserving response, so a pulse that rises while the patient is still losing weight signals infection or another intercurrent illness rather than recovery, and it is a more worrying sign than the bradycardia itself.

sources.label: RANZCP: Eating Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: Fluoxetine has a role in bulimia nervosa and in comorbid depression once weight is restored, but it does not treat restrictive eating and is ineffective in the malnourished state. Starting it now would also delay the medical care that her observations demand. (Source: RANZCP: Eating Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Eating Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: Admission criteria in eating disorders are driven by physiological instability rather than by body mass index, and she has bradycardia below 40, a postural systolic drop over 20 mmHg, hypothermia, hypokalaemia, hypophosphataemia and a prolonged corrected QT interval. The rate and magnitude of weight loss, 16 kg in six months, carries the physiological risk here even though the absolute weight sits in the population healthy range. (Source: ANZAED: Eating Disorder Treatment Principles)
source_refs: RANZCP: Eating Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: Family based treatment is the highest evidence outpatient treatment for adolescents and will be the right framework once she is medically stable, so this is the correct destination reached in the wrong order. Outpatient care assumes physiological stability, which her bradycardia and postural drop exclude. (Source: RANZCP: Eating Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Eating Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: Correcting a single electrolyte while leaving her unmonitored ignores the bradycardia, the prolonged corrected QT interval and the hypophosphataemia, any of which can precipitate an arrhythmia. A week is a long interval for a patient who has already fainted. (Source: ANZAED: Eating Disorder Treatment Principles)

Using body mass index alone as the gate for concern is the specific error this presentation tests, and it is the reasoning that produced the earlier reassurance she now quotes back. A person can be physiologically critical at a normal body weight if the loss has been rapid. (Source: ANZAED: Eating Disorder Treatment Principles)

explanation.summary: Schizoaffective disorder sits between the psychotic and mood disorders and is diagnosed longitudinally rather than cross sectionally, which is why a single interview can never establish it and a documented course is essential. The defining requirement is a period of two weeks or more of delusions or hallucinations without a prominent mood episode, occurring within an illness in which mood episodes are otherwise present for the majority of the time. If psychosis occurs only during mood episodes the diagnosis is a mood disorder with psychotic features, and if mood episodes are brief relative to the psychotic illness the diagnosis is schizophrenia. Substance induced psychosis must be excluded before either, and stimulant related psychosis is a particular problem in Australian practice because methamphetamine use is common, the symptoms are indistinguishable cross sectionally, and a persisting form exists. Diagnostic reasoning therefore rests on the timeline, namely how long the psychosis has outlasted abstinence and what proportion of the illness has been occupied by mood episodes, and the diagnosis is revisited as that picture develops.
key_points: The diagnosis requires two or more weeks of psychosis without a prominent mood episode.
Mood episodes must occupy the majority of the total duration of the illness.
Psychosis confined to mood episodes indicates a mood disorder with psychotic features instead.
Brief mood episodes relative to the psychotic illness indicate schizophrenia instead.
Stimulant induced psychosis usually resolves within a month of abstinence, so a persisting picture needs another explanation.
explanation.pearls: Methamphetamine associated psychosis recurs on re-exposure with far less drug and after a shorter interval than the original episode, a sensitisation effect that makes any return to use the single strongest predictor of relapse and which should shape relapse prevention planning more than adherence to antipsychotic alone.

sources.label: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: This cannot be correct because two discrete episodes of elevated mood with reduced sleep, grandiosity and pressured speech lasting a month each establish mania, which excludes a unipolar diagnosis entirely. Mood incongruent psychosis in unipolar depression does exist but requires that no manic episode has ever occurred. (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: This would be the diagnosis if every psychotic symptom appeared only alongside a mood episode and remitted with it, which was true of his first two years but is not true now. The four months of psychosis with euthymic mood ratings is the finding that breaks this option. (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: The diagnosis requires an uninterrupted period of illness with a major mood episode concurrent with psychotic symptoms, plus delusions or hallucinations for two or more weeks in the absence of a major mood episode, and mood episodes present for the majority of the total illness duration. His four months of psychosis with documented euthymia satisfies the second criterion, while three substantial mood episodes across two years satisfies the third. (Source: RANZCP: Psychosis Clinical Practice Guideline)

Stimulant induced psychosis usually resolves within a month of abstinence and a persisting form is described, which makes this a genuine competing explanation given his history. Fourteen months of supervised negative screens with symptoms continuing at full intensity, alongside three mood episodes, exceeds what the substance can account for. (Source: RANZCP: Psychosis Clinical Practice Guideline)

Schizophrenia is diagnosed when mood episodes are absent or brief relative to the total duration of illness, and his two manic and one depressive episodes occupy a substantial proportion of two years. The distinguishing quantity is the proportion of the illness during which a mood episode is present, which is the single criterion separating these two options. (Source: RANZCP: Psychosis Clinical Practice Guideline)

explanation.summary: Lithium is renally excreted; anything reducing renal function or sodium status raises lithium levels. Common precipitants of chronic toxicity: NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, thiazide diuretics, dehydration, low-salt diet, acute kidney injury. Chronic toxicity typically presents at lower levels than acute (1.2 to 2.5 mmol/L) with neurological features (coarse tremor, hyperreflexia, clonus, ataxia, dysarthria, confusion, drowsiness). Severe toxicity (above 2.5 mmol/L or severe symptoms) causes seizures, coma, arrhythmia. Management: stop lithium and precipitant, intravenous normal saline for volume expansion (aiming for good urine output), monitor lithium 4 to 6 hourly and renal function. Haemodialysis is indicated for level above 4.0 mmol/L, above 2.5 with severe symptoms, or above 2.5 with renal failure. Activated charcoal is ineffective for lithium; whole bowel irrigation is for acute massive sustained-release ingestion.
key_points: Chronic lithium toxicity is precipitated by NSAIDs, ACEi, ARBs, thiazides, dehydration.
Neurological features (tremor, clonus, ataxia, confusion) at levels above 1.2 mmol/L.
Treat with cessation, IV saline; haemodialysis for level above 4.0 or severe symptoms.
explanation.pearls: Chronic lithium toxicity at 1.6 mmol/L with neurological signs after NSAID commencement: stop lithium and ibuprofen, IV saline 200 mL/h and nephrology consult for possible dialysis.

options.rationale: Whole bowel irrigation is considered for acute massive ingestion of sustained-release lithium, not chronic toxicity with NSAID precipitant. (Source: TGA Poisons Information)
Chronic toxicity at 1.6 mmol/L with neurological signs mandates cessation of lithium and admission; outpatient management is unsafe. (Source: TGA Poisons Information)
Charcoal does not bind lithium; it is ineffective. Symptomatic management with saline and dialysis consult is required. (Source: TGA Poisons Information)
Chronic lithium toxicity with neurological features and level >1.5 needs cessation, IV fluid and dialysis consult; NSAID must be stopped as the precipitant. (Source: TGA Poisons Information)
Urinary alkalinisation does not enhance lithium clearance; normal saline volume expansion and dialysis (if severe) is appropriate. (Source: TGA Poisons Information)

explanation.summary: Serotonin syndrome is a clinical diagnosis with the Hunter criteria: serotonergic agent plus one of: spontaneous clonus; inducible clonus with agitation or diaphoresis; ocular clonus with agitation or diaphoresis; tremor and hyperreflexia; or hypertonia, temperature above 38 degC and ocular or inducible clonus. Common precipitants: SSRI plus tramadol, SSRI plus MAOI, SSRI plus linezolid, SSRI plus fentanyl or pethidine, SSRI plus St John wort, MDMA. Onset within hours to days. Distinguishing from NMS: serotonin syndrome features clonus and hyperreflexia predominantly in lower limbs, onset hours after precipitant; NMS features lead-pipe rigidity, onset over days after neuroleptic. Management: stop all serotonergic agents, benzodiazepines (diazepam 5-10 mg IV titrated) for agitation and tremor, active cooling for hyperthermia. Cyproheptadine (5-HT2A antagonist, 12 mg orally then 2 mg every 2 hours) for moderate to severe cases. Muscle relaxation and intubation for severe hyperthermia (above 41 degC).
key_points: Hunter criteria: serotonergic agent plus clonus/hyperreflexia/temperature.
Clonus predominantly lower limbs distinguishes from NMS rigidity.
Treat: stop precipitants, benzodiazepines, cooling, cyproheptadine if severe.
explanation.pearls: SSRI plus tramadol with fever, agitation and lower-limb clonus is serotonin syndrome: stop both agents, give diazepam 5 mg IV titrated, cool actively, add cyproheptadine 12 mg for moderate to severe cases.

options.rationale: Methylene blue itself has serotonergic effects and would worsen the syndrome; it is contraindicated. (Source: TGA Poisons Information)
Bromocriptine and dantrolene are used for NMS not serotonin syndrome; distinguishing features are neuromuscular (clonus vs rigidity) and time course. (Source: TGA Poisons Information)
Continuing serotonergic agents perpetuates the syndrome; haloperidol adds anticholinergic burden without treating cause. (Source: TGA Poisons Information)

Flumazenil is not indicated (no benzodiazepine history); it can precipitate seizures. Serotonin syndrome does not need reversal - it needs cessation of the precipitants. (Source: TGA Poisons Information)

Serotonin syndrome (Hunter criteria met: clonus, hyperthermia, hyperreflexia) after tramadol added to SSRI needs cessation, benzodiazepine, cooling; cyproheptadine for refractory cases. (Source: TGA Poisons Information)

explanation.summary: Clozapine can cause neutropenia and agranulocytosis (1 to 2 percent lifetime risk of agranulocytosis) requiring mandatory haematological monitoring. Australian monitoring (Clopine/Clozaril/Zaponex Patient Monitoring): weekly FBC for the first 18 weeks, then fortnightly to 52 weeks, then 4 weekly indefinitely. Traffic light system in Australia: Green (WCC >=3.5 and ANC >=2.0 x10^9/L) continue at current schedule; Amber (WCC 3.0-3.5 or ANC 1.5-2.0) continue with twice weekly FBC; Red (WCC below 3.0 or ANC below 1.5) stop clozapine and daily FBC (formal cut-offs vary by monitoring service - Clopine Red is WCC below 3.0 x10^9/L or ANC below 1.5 x10^9/L). ANC below 0.5 is severe agranulocytosis requiring reverse isolation and haematology involvement. Benign ethnic neutropenia (common in African, Middle Eastern, some Mediterranean descent) has separate lower thresholds under specialist supervision.
key_points: Clopine Red = WCC <3.0 or ANC <1.5 x10^9/L: stop clozapine, daily FBC.
ANC 1.5-2.0 (amber) = continue clozapine, weekly FBC, screen for infection.
ANC below 0.5 = severe agranulocytosis: haematology, reverse isolation.
explanation.pearls: Clozapine monitoring - ANC 1.7 x10^9/L in a well patient with no infection is in the amber range at RANZCP: continue clozapine, repeat FBC weekly and screen for occult infection - do not stop the drug.

options.rationale: Filgrastim is used in confirmed severe neutropenia (ANC below 0.5) or persistent moderate neutropenia; not indicated in amber range with a well patient. (Source: TGA Clozapine Monitoring Guideline)
Immediate cessation and admission is for ANC below 0.5 x10^9/L (severe neutropenia); ANC 1.7 is amber not red. (Source: TGA Clozapine Monitoring Guideline)
Dose reduction alone is not standard; weekly FBC is required in amber range and dose is unchanged unless further drop. (Source: TGA Clozapine Monitoring Guideline)
ANC 1.5-2.0 x10^9/L is the amber (Watching) range: continue clozapine, repeat FBC weekly, monitor for infection. (Source: TGA Clozapine Monitoring Guideline)
Switching antipsychotic in a stable patient with amber-range neutropenia is not indicated and risks psychotic relapse. (Source: TGA Clozapine Monitoring Guideline)

explanation.summary: Alcohol withdrawal severity is graded on the Alcohol Withdrawal Scale or CIWA-Ar. Mild withdrawal (score below 8): symptomatic care, no benzodiazepine needed. Moderate to severe (score 8 or above): benzodiazepine loading and symptom-triggered dosing. Diazepam 10 to 20 mg orally 2 hourly is first line in patients with normal liver function due to long half-life and active metabolites providing smooth wean. In cirrhosis, hepatic encephalopathy risk and metabolite accumulation make short-acting agents metabolised by glucuronidation (LOT: lorazepam, oxazepam, temazepam) preferred; oxazepam 15 to 30 mg orally 4 hourly is the Australian standard in cirrhosis. Thiamine 300 mg IV daily for 3-5 days before any glucose to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy. Delirium tremens (autonomic instability, hyperthermia, hallucinations) has mortality of 5-15 percent untreated; treat aggressively with high-dose benzodiazepines, IV fluid and monitoring. Phenobarbital is second line for benzodiazepine-refractory delirium tremens.
key_points: Diazepam is first line for alcohol withdrawal in normal liver function.
In cirrhosis, use LOT (lorazepam, oxazepam, temazepam) - glucuronidation not oxidative metabolism.
Thiamine 300 mg IV daily 3-5 days before glucose to prevent Wernicke.
explanation.pearls: Alcohol withdrawal in cirrhosis at NHMRC uses oxazepam 15-30 mg orally 4 hourly (glucuronidated, no active metabolites) instead of diazepam - active nordiazepam metabolite of diazepam accumulates and can precipitate hepatic encephalopathy.

options.rationale: Midazolam is short-acting and unsuitable for withdrawal maintenance; intramuscular route has erratic absorption. (Source: Australian Alcohol Guidelines (NHMRC))
Diazepam has active metabolites (nordiazepam) that accumulate in cirrhosis, risking prolonged sedation and precipitating hepatic encephalopathy. (Source: Australian Alcohol Guidelines (NHMRC))
Oxazepam has no active metabolites and non-hepatic metabolism (glucuronidation), making it safer than diazepam in cirrhosis. (Source: Australian Alcohol Guidelines (NHMRC))
Chlordiazepoxide has active metabolites and hepatic metabolism, so it accumulates in cirrhosis; not preferred here. (Source: Australian Alcohol Guidelines (NHMRC))
Phenobarbital is reserved for benzodiazepine-refractory delirium tremens; it is not first line and requires close monitoring. (Source: Australian Alcohol Guidelines (NHMRC))

explanation.summary: Adolescent major depression (age 12-17) is managed with a stepped approach. Mild MDD: psychoeducation, sleep hygiene, exercise, brief psychological intervention. Moderate to severe MDD or mild MDD failing brief intervention: cognitive behavioural therapy or interpersonal therapy for adolescents as first line for 6 to 8 weeks. If inadequate response or severe presentation, add pharmacotherapy. Fluoxetine 10 to 20 mg daily is the only SSRI with TGA and RANZCP endorsement as first-line pharmacotherapy in adolescents (based on TADS trial data). Sertraline is second line. Venlafaxine and paroxetine are avoided in adolescents due to increased suicidality risk. Weekly clinical review for the first four weeks of any antidepressant in adolescents is mandatory (increased short-term risk of suicidality in the first month). Safety planning should be documented and shared with parents/carers. Combination of CBT and fluoxetine is more effective than either alone (TADS trial).
key_points: Fluoxetine 10-20 mg is first-line adolescent SSRI (TADS trial, TGA and RANZCP endorsed).
Weekly review for 4 weeks after starting antidepressant in adolescents.
Avoid venlafaxine and paroxetine in adolescents (suicidality risk).
explanation.pearls: Adolescent MDD failing CBT: add fluoxetine 10 mg daily and review weekly for 4 weeks - fluoxetine is the only SSRI RANZCP endorses first line in adolescents, not sertraline.

options.rationale: Sertraline is used in adolescent MDD but has weaker adolescent evidence than fluoxetine; fluoxetine is first line in adolescents at RANZCP. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Depression)

Fluoxetine is the only SSRI with TGA and RANZCP recommendation for adolescent MDD after CBT failure; requires weekly review for suicidality first month. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Depression)
Venlafaxine has an FDA black box warning in adolescents with increased suicidality; not first line for adolescent MDD. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Depression)

CBT for 6 weeks without improvement in moderate to severe adolescent MDD is trial failure; RANZCP recommends adding fluoxetine, not continuing psychotherapy alone. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Depression)

Passive SI without plan or intent, with family support and no self-harm history, does not require inpatient admission; outpatient management with fluoxetine and safety planning is appropriate. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Depression)

explanation.summary: First-episode psychosis is a critical intervention window where antipsychotic choice balances efficacy, tolerability, metabolic risk and patient preference to maximise adherence. RANZCP recommends second-generation antipsychotics as first line, matched to patient factors. Aripiprazole has the lowest weight-gain profile (partial dopamine agonist), no prolactin elevation and minimal QTc effect, making it preferred for young men with metabolic risk factors or concern about weight gain. Olanzapine and clozapine carry the highest metabolic burden. Risperidone has dose-related extrapyramidal and prolactin effects. Cannabis use is common in FEP and worsens the psychotic prodrome; concurrent referral to youth AOD services for brief intervention is standard. Depot antipsychotics can be considered early to support adherence. Metabolic monitoring at baseline, 6 weeks, 3 months, then annually is mandated (weight, BP, fasting glucose, lipids).
key_points: Second-generation antipsychotic first line in FEP, matched to patient factors.
Aripiprazole has the lowest weight-gain and prolactin profile; olanzapine the highest.
Refer to youth AOD service concurrently for cannabis brief intervention.
explanation.pearls: FEP in a young man with cannabis use and stated aversion to weight-gaining medications: aripiprazole 10 mg is preferred over olanzapine because aripiprazole has the lowest metabolic burden and best supports adherence.

options.rationale: Olanzapine has the highest weight gain and dyslipidaemia burden of second-generation antipsychotics and directly conflicts with this patient's stated preference and adherence risk. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Schizophrenia)

Aripiprazole has the lowest weight-gain profile among second-generation antipsychotics and is preferred first-line for FEP where metabolic risk and adherence concern medication acceptance. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Schizophrenia)

First-generation antipsychotics are not preferred first line in FEP due to higher extrapyramidal side-effect burden; second-generation agents are preferred. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Schizophrenia)
Risperidone has a dose-related risk of extrapyramidal side effects and prolactin elevation with reduced acceptability in a young man. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Schizophrenia)

Clozapine is reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia (failure of two adequate trials of other antipsychotics); not first line for FEP. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Schizophrenia)

explanation.summary: Emotionally unstable personality disorder (EUPD, ICD-11) or borderline personality disorder is characterised by pervasive instability of affect, interpersonal relationships and self-image, with impulsivity and recurrent self-harm. Repeated brief emergency department presentations after interpersonal stressors are typical. RANZCP evidence-based guideline: psychotherapy (dialectical behaviour therapy, mentalisation based therapy) is first-line treatment. Pharmacotherapy is not routine and should be time-limited if used for a comorbid disorder. Hospital admission does not improve outcomes and can reinforce the pattern of self-harm as help-seeking; brief admission (24 to 72 hours) is reserved for objectively high risk of suicide (specific plan, means, escalation from usual pattern) or acute psychosocial crisis without other supports. In the ED, wound care, brief supportive assessment, validation of distress, safety plan review, and rapid linkage back to the community team is the recommended pathway. Family and case manager should be engaged.
key_points: DBT and MBT are first-line psychotherapies in EUPD; pharmacotherapy not routine.
Admission does not improve outcomes and can reinforce escalation of self-harm.
ED role: wound care, validation, safety plan review, community team linkage.
explanation.pearls: Recurrent superficial self-harm in EUPD at baseline: wound care, safety plan review, discharge to family with case manager next-day contact - admission reinforces the pattern and does not improve outcomes per RANZCP.

sources.label: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder

options.rationale: Repeated superficial self-harm in EUPD without acute high-risk features is best managed in community per RANZCP; ED admission does not improve outcomes and can reinforce escalation. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline BPD)
Involuntary admission is not indicated: she is at baseline, has supports and denies suicidality; inpatient admission worsens outcomes in EUPD. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline BPD)

Pharmacotherapy is not first line for EUPD and quetiapine sedation increases self-harm reinforcement; RANZCP recommends against routine pharmacotherapy. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline BPD)
Intensive care admission is disproportionate and reinforces presentation escalation; DBT plus community support is the evidence-based pathway. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline BPD)
Discharge without case manager liaison or safety plan review misses the opportunity to reinforce structured support and update the crisis plan. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline BPD)

explanation.summary: Refeeding syndrome is the metabolic response to reintroduction of nutrition in a malnourished patient, driven by insulin release causing intracellular shift of phosphate, magnesium and potassium and thiamine consumption. Risk factors: BMI below 16, 15 percent weight loss over 3 months, minimal nutrition intake over 10 days, low pre-refeed electrolytes. Diagnosis is a fall of at least 30 percent in serum phosphate from baseline or an absolute phosphate below 0.6 mmol/L. Australian practice starts refeeding at 20 kcal/kg/day in high-risk anorexia nervosa (previously as low as 10 kcal/kg/day, but current evidence supports 20 kcal/kg/day with intensive electrolyte monitoring and correction). Prevention and management: thiamine 300 mg IV daily for 5 days before or with feed commencement, daily electrolytes for the first week, prompt replacement of phosphate, magnesium and potassium. When refeeding syndrome develops: reduce feed rate to 10 kcal/kg/day, correct electrolytes intravenously if symptomatic or severe, then re-titrate feed upward as electrolytes normalise. Ongoing multidisciplinary eating disorders team involvement is essential.
key_points: Refeeding syndrome: intracellular shift of phosphate, magnesium, potassium with feeding.
Severe hypophosphataemia (below 0.6 mmol/L) or symptomatic: IV replacement, reduce feed.
Thiamine 300 mg IV daily 5 days precedes or accompanies refeeding.
explanation.pearls: Refeeding hypophosphataemia at 48 hours with phosphate 0.42 mmol/L in anorexia nervosa: reduce feed to 10 kcal/kg/day and give IV phosphate 30 mmol plus magnesium and potassium - do not increase or continue full feed rate.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Eating Disorders

options.rationale: Complete feed cessation loses accumulated nutritional gains; graded reduction with correction is preferred; dextrose stimulates insulin and worsens intracellular shift. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Eating Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Eating Disorders

options.rationale: Continued full feed with symptomatic hypophosphataemia risks progression to cardiac and neurological failure; slow feed reduction and IV correction is needed. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Eating Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Eating Disorders

options.rationale: Increasing feed will worsen refeeding syndrome; the pathophysiology is intracellular phosphate shift driven by insulin surge with feeding. (Source: RANZCOG Clinical Practice Guidelines Eating Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Eating Disorders

options.rationale: Symptomatic refeeding syndrome with phosphate 0.42 mmol/L requires calorie reduction plus IV phosphate, magnesium and potassium replacement per RANZCP eating disorders guideline. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Eating Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Eating Disorders

options.rationale: Waiting for phosphate below 0.3 mmol/L or organ failure risks catastrophic outcome; refeeding syndrome is progressive and needs early correction. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Eating Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Eating Disorders

explanation.summary: Second-generation antipsychotics, particularly olanzapine and clozapine, produce most of their metabolic harm in the first year. RANZCP and Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic set 12 week fasting bloods with quarterly repeat through year one, alongside weight and waist at every review. Early weight gain of 8 kg with a rising waist justifies rather than deferring the recommended schedule. Only after the first year does the interval extend to 6 to 12 months if metrics are stable. Skipping fasting glucose in favour of weight alone underdetects the dysglycaemia this drug class produces.
key_points: 12 week fasting glucose and lipids after starting a second-generation antipsychotic
Repeat quarterly during the first year, then 6 to 12 monthly if stable
Weight and waist every visit; blood pressure at each review
explanation.pearls: Olanzapine causes the largest early weight and lipid shift in its class; a rising waist at 12 weeks predicts future dysglycaemia and should trigger active lifestyle input, not a passive wait.

options.rationale: RANZCP and eTG recommend fasting glucose and lipids at 12 weeks after starting a second-generation antipsychotic then quarterly during the first year, with weight and waist at every visit; olanzapine carries the highest metabolic burden and this patient's early weight gain and central adiposity make quarterly checks appropriate (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Metabolic Monitoring Guidance).

Waiting a full year misses the first-year risk window when metabolic derangement on olanzapine is most likely to emerge and be reversible with early switch or lifestyle input (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Metabolic Monitoring Guidance).

OGTT is reserved for equivocal fasting glucose or high-risk patients with normal fasting values; the routine surveillance test is fasting glucose plus HbA1c, not baseline OGTT for every antipsychotic patient (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

Annual only monitoring is inadequate for a high-metabolic-risk antipsychotic in the first year; delegating without a shared plan misses the point of shared care and lets weight and glycaemia drift (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Metabolic Monitoring Guidance).

Weight and blood pressure alone underdetect dyslipidaemia and dysglycaemia on olanzapine; the first-year plan includes fasting glucose or HbA1c plus lipids at 12 weeks and quarterly thereafter (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Metabolic Monitoring Guidance).

explanation.summary: Malignant catatonia is the complication that turns a treatable syndrome into an emergency. It presents as fever, autonomic instability with labile blood pressure and tachycardia, rigidity and a rising creatine kinase, and it overlaps clinically with neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Because it can develop over hours, the monitoring plan for any inpatient with catatonia is frequent vital signs and a regular creatine kinase, alongside daily review of hydration, oral intake and sedation. Early recognition moves the patient to a monitored bed and brings forward electroconvulsive therapy.
key_points: Fever and autonomic instability in catatonia signal malignant progression
A rising creatine kinase supports it and tracks severity
Frequent vital signs matter more than repeated imaging
Malignant catatonia needs a monitored bed and urgent specialist involvement
explanation.pearls: Any new fever in a catatonic patient is malignant catatonia until infection is proven, because the two are managed very differently. In context: catatonia is monitored like a medical illness because its dangerous complications are physiological, not behavioural (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.rationale: Progression to malignant catatonia announces itself as fever, autonomic instability and a rising creatine kinase, so these are the observations that change management (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).
This schedule belongs to nutritional rehabilitation or clozapine haematological monitoring rather than to catatonia (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).
Cardiac monitoring is the answer when a drug that prolongs the QT interval is given or an arrhythmia is suspected (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).
Electroencephalography is the answer when non convulsive status epilepticus is the working differential, not for routine monitoring (Source: ACSQHC Delirium Clinical Care Standard).
Repeat imaging is prompted by a new focal neurological sign; twice weekly observations are too sparse for this risk (Source: ACSQHC Delirium Clinical Care Standard).

explanation.summary: A lapse is a single episode of smoking after the quit date; relapse is a return to regular smoking. Most successful quitters lapse at least once, usually in a social or alcohol-related setting, and the evidence-based response is to normalise it, continue pharmacotherapy for the full course, and use the episode to identify and rehearse the trigger. Stopping the medicine at a lapse converts a recoverable slip into relapse, and the strongest predictors of relapse are alcohol, other smokers in the household and low mood. In context: nicotine dependence is a relapsing condition, so quit attempts are counted rather than graded, and each attempt supported by pharmacotherapy and behavioural support raises the probability of the next one succeeding.
key_points: Lapse is not relapse: continue the pharmacotherapy course
Use the lapse to identify the trigger and rehearse an alternative plan
Alcohol, other household smokers and low mood are the main relapse drivers
Extended pharmacotherapy is a decision for the end of the standard course
explanation.pearls: Framing a lapse as data rather than failure keeps the patient in treatment; the practical script is to ask what was happening in the ten minutes before the first cigarette.

options.rationale: A lapse is not relapse. Continuing the full course while problem-solving the situational trigger with behavioural support gives the best chance of sustained abstinence. (Source: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation)

A fresh course is for someone who has returned to regular smoking and is ready to try again later. Interrupting treatment in a woman abstinent for three days invites full relapse. (Source: AMH: Varenicline)

Adding replacement to varenicline is occasionally used for breakthrough craving despite full dosing, at the cost of more nausea. Her cravings are mild and controlled. (Source: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation)
Bupropion is an alternative when varenicline is contraindicated or not tolerated. Switching an effective, tolerated agent mid-course has no evidence behind it. (Source: AMH: Bupropion)
An extended course is offered at the end of 12 weeks to a patient who has quit and remains at high relapse risk, not decided in week five. (Source: AMH: Varenicline)

explanation.summary: Any drug that reduces renal perfusion or afferent arteriolar prostaglandin activity raises lithium concentration acutely. NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, and thiazide diuretics are the classical precipitants. Here ibuprofen at 400 mg three times daily started 10 days ago aligns with a doubling of creatinine and a lithium level of 2.4 mmol/L in a previously stable patient. Management is cessation of the offending agent, intravenous saline (avoiding hypotonic fluids), continuous cardiac monitoring, and haemodialysis when the level exceeds 4 mmol/L, when neurotoxicity persists, or renal function is severely impaired.
key_points: NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, thiazides raise lithium acutely
Confusion plus level above 2.0 mmol/L is severe toxicity
Dialysis threshold: level above 4 mmol/L or refractory neurotoxicity
explanation.pearls: A level of 2.5 mmol/L with normal renal function may be managed with saline alone; the same level with rising creatinine or refractory neurology needs urgent renal replacement therapy.

options.rationale: Age related eGFR decline is gradual and does not typically produce an acute doubling of creatinine over days; a specific precipitant is required to explain the acute rise (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

NSAIDs reduce afferent arteriolar prostaglandin dependent vasodilation, cutting GFR and lithium clearance; the temporal association with ibuprofen initiation 10 days ago and creatinine doubling identifies this as the primary precipitant (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook (AMH)).
Lithium undergoes essentially no hepatic metabolism and is cleared unchanged by the kidneys; cranberry juice is not the mechanism here (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook (AMH)).

Volume depletion and low salt intake raise lithium levels through proximal tubular sodium and lithium reabsorption, but there is no reported gastrointestinal loss in this scenario; the mechanism described is inaccurate (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

Chronic lithium nephropathy is a slow decline over decades and does not explain an acute doubling of creatinine and a lithium level rise over 10 days; it is a background risk, not the acute precipitant (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Adult ADHD in DSM-5 requires five or more inattentive or hyperactive-impulsive symptoms (rather than six for children), several present before age 12, symptoms in two or more settings, and clear evidence of interference with functioning. Symptoms must not be better explained by another mental disorder or substance effect. This patient has school reports, maternal collateral, cross-setting symptoms (work and home), and unambiguous functional loss. ASRS is a screen, not a diagnosis. Stimulant challenges are not diagnostic and neuropsychology is supportive rather than definitive.
key_points: DSM-5 requires several symptoms before age 12
Symptoms in two or more settings with functional impairment
Screening tools (ASRS) support but do not confirm the diagnosis
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically about primary school reports and third party history; adults commonly reconstruct their childhood as unremarkable, but school reports and parental recall carry more diagnostic weight than adult recall alone.

options.rationale: DSM-5 adult ADHD requires several inattentive or hyperactive-impulsive symptoms present before age 12, in two or more settings, with clear evidence of impairment; this scenario meets all three (Source: DSM-5-TR).
ASRS is a screening tool and mood exclusion does not by itself confirm ADHD; the DSM-5 diagnosis rests on symptoms, cross-situational impairment, and childhood onset (Source: DSM-5-TR).
Stimulant responsiveness is not diagnostic; healthy adults also experience cognitive enhancement, and empirical trials are not used to confirm the disorder (Source: RACGP Adult ADHD Guidance).
DSM-5 requires onset of several symptoms before age 12, not before adolescence; an adolescent onset alone excludes the diagnosis (Source: DSM-5-TR).

Neuropsychological test scores do not confirm or exclude adult ADHD; the disorder is a clinical diagnosis and cognitive testing is complementary rather than definitive (Source: RACGP Adult ADHD Guidance).

explanation.summary: The 2013 NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder places structured evidence-based psychotherapy at the centre of treatment. Dialectical behaviour therapy, mentalisation based therapy, transference focused psychotherapy, and schema therapy have the most consistent evidence for reducing self-harm, emergency presentations, and improving function. Medication has no demonstrated benefit for the core features and should be used only for defined co-occurring conditions and time limited crisis management. Brief admission is reserved for imminent risk; prolonged admission can be iatrogenic. Care coordination, a written safety plan, and consistent multidisciplinary follow up are essential adjuncts.
key_points: Structured psychotherapy (DBT, MBT, TFP, schema) is the primary treatment
Medications have no evidence for core BPD features
Brief admission only for imminent risk
explanation.pearls: A written safety plan (early warning signs, coping strategies, contact numbers, means restriction) reduces subsequent self-harm and is standard of care after any BPD presentation.

options.rationale: NHMRC guidance and Cochrane reviews find no medication with meaningful benefit for the core features of borderline personality disorder; polypharmacy adds harm without benefit (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guideline).

The NHMRC guideline recommends a structured, evidence-based psychotherapy delivered by trained clinicians as the primary treatment for borderline personality disorder; DBT, MBT, transference focused psychotherapy, and schema therapy have the strongest evidence (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guideline).

Prolonged inpatient admission for uncomplicated borderline personality disorder can reinforce dependence and self-harm without changing long term outcome; brief admission is reserved for imminent risk (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guideline).

SSRIs have very limited effect on borderline personality disorder core features and do not reliably reduce self-harm; escalation without a psychological plan is not recommended (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guideline).
Hypnotic regression is not an evidence-based treatment for borderline personality disorder and is not recommended by the NHMRC guideline (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guideline).

explanation.summary: ECT has no absolute contraindications, but recent stroke, raised intracranial pressure, unstable coronary syndrome, aortic aneurysm, retinal detachment, phaeochromocytoma, and severe pulmonary disease are relative contraindications requiring risk assessment and modification. For an ischaemic stroke, RANZCP position statement PS28 recommends deferring ECT for at least 4 to 6 weeks and obtaining neurology and cardiology review with strict perioperative blood pressure control. Anticoagulants such as apixaban are usually continued because the procedure is very low bleeding risk. When severe depression demands ECT sooner, informed decision by treating team and patient (or substitute decision maker) is documented after formal risk balancing.
key_points: No absolute contraindications; recent stroke is relative
Defer at least 4 to 6 weeks after ischaemic stroke
Obtain neurology and cardiology review pre-anaesthesia
explanation.pearls: During ECT, systolic pressure can spike above 200 mmHg for seconds; premedication with a short-acting beta blocker such as esmolol blunts the surge in patients with cardiovascular disease.

options.rationale: There are no absolute contraindications to ECT; recent stroke is a relative one that raises risk. Deferring rather than cancelling is the standard position when depression is severe (Source: RANZCP ECT Position Statement PS28).

Apixaban is generally continued for ECT because the procedure is very low bleeding risk, but this ignores the more pressing recent stroke issue that dominates decision making here (Source: RANZCP ECT Position Statement PS28).

She has failed the antidepressant sequence already and adding olanzapine does not address the severe depression with life threatening malnutrition; alternatives do not match ECT for severity of this magnitude (Source: RANZCP ECT Position Statement PS28).

The recommended interval after a stroke is at least 4 to 6 weeks with cardiovascular and neurology review to define residual deficit and blood pressure control; going ahead the next day without that review is premature (Source: RANZCP ECT Position Statement PS28).

Recent ischaemic stroke is a relative contraindication; RANZCP recommends deferring at least 4 to 6 weeks and obtaining specialist assessment of stroke risk with strict perioperative blood pressure targets before proceeding (Source: RANZCP ECT Position Statement PS28).

explanation.summary: The TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Program (2023) requires that any woman of childbearing potential prescribed valproate has documented understanding of teratogenic risk, effective contraception, an annual review, and a plan for pregnancy that involves an alternative mood stabiliser. Valproate carries a 10 percent risk of major congenital malformation (including neural tube defects) and a 30 to 40 percent risk of neurodevelopmental impairment, well above lamotrigine (2 to 3 percent) or lithium (2 to 3 percent). The immediate step for a woman planning conception within 12 months is urgent specialist review to plan a gradual switch, not folate, dose reduction, or long term LARC on unchanged therapy.
key_points: Valproate MCM risk 10 percent; neurodevelopmental risk 30 to 40 percent
TGA program requires contraception plus annual review
Preconception switch to lamotrigine or lithium with specialist supervision
explanation.pearls: Lamotrigine dose typically needs to be doubled by the third trimester because oestrogen induces UGT glucuronidation; drop back to preconception dose within 3 days postpartum.

options.rationale: Valproate causes major congenital malformation in 10 percent and neurodevelopmental impairment in 30 to 40 percent of exposed pregnancies; TGA guidance mandates a documented pregnancy prevention plan and specialist review for any woman of childbearing potential (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Program).

Folate supplementation does not offset valproate teratogenicity and continuing valproate without discussion of alternatives fails the pregnancy prevention program (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Program).
Abrupt cessation risks acute relapse; switch should be gradual under specialist supervision with careful cross titration and monitoring (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

LARC is essential during ongoing valproate therapy, but she plans to conceive within 12 months so the aim is a preconception switch, not indefinite contraception (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Program).

Teratogenic risk is dose related but even lower doses carry unacceptable risk versus alternatives; the plan is to switch off valproate preconception, not to reduce dose (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Program).

explanation.summary: DSM-5 discriminates short duration psychoses by two axes: symptom duration and functional recovery. Brief psychotic disorder requires 1 day to less than 1 month with full return to premorbid functioning. Schizophreniform disorder covers 1 month to less than 6 months. Schizophrenia requires 6 months of continuous disturbance including 1 month of active phase symptoms. Delusional disorder requires delusions of 1 month or more without prominent hallucinations, mood disturbance, or bizarre behaviour. Substance induced psychotic disorder requires temporal linkage and evidence of substance exposure. In this 12 day episode with full resolution, brief psychotic disorder is the correct provisional diagnosis; recurrence would trigger reclassification.
key_points: Brief psychotic disorder: 1 day to less than 1 month with full recovery
Schizophreniform: 1 to less than 6 months
Schizophrenia: 6 months continuous with 1 month active phase
explanation.pearls: About 50 percent of brief psychotic disorder episodes progress to another psychotic diagnosis over 5 years; longitudinal follow up rather than a definitive label is the safer position early on.

options.rationale: Schizophrenia requires continuous signs for at least 6 months including active phase symptoms of at least 1 month; a 12 day episode does not meet criteria (Source: DSM-5-TR).
Schizophreniform disorder requires symptoms for at least 1 month but less than 6 months; a 12 day episode does not reach the 1 month threshold (Source: DSM-5-TR).

Brief psychotic disorder in DSM-5 requires at least one of delusions, hallucinations or disorganised speech lasting at least 1 day but less than 1 month with eventual full return to premorbid functioning; a 12 day episode meets this criterion exactly (Source: DSM-5-TR).

A substance induced diagnosis requires temporal linkage to intoxication or withdrawal and evidence of substance exposure; UDS was negative and hair testing did not support recent use (Source: DSM-5-TR).

Delusional disorder requires delusions for at least 1 month without prominent hallucinations, mood disturbance, or bizarre behaviour; hallucinations are prominent here and duration is under 1 month (Source: DSM-5-TR).

explanation.summary: Australian rapid tranquillisation guidance (Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; RANZCP position) recommends verbal de-escalation and oral options first; when parenteral therapy is needed, intramuscular olanzapine 10 mg is a first line monotherapy for known psychosis, or intramuscular droperidol 10 mg. Concurrent IM benzodiazepines are avoided due to risk of respiratory depression. Continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring with pulse oximetry for at least 1 hour follows any dose, plus glucose check within 30 minutes. If the initial dose is inadequate, repeat after 30 to 60 minutes rather than stacking multiple agents. Vital signs, glucose, ECG for QT, and search for reversible causes (hypoxia, hypoglycaemia, drug or alcohol intoxication) are essential adjuncts.
key_points: IM olanzapine 10 mg or IM droperidol 10 mg first line monotherapy
Avoid concurrent IM benzodiazepine (respiratory depression risk)
Monitor SpO2, pulse, BP, glucose after every dose
explanation.pearls: Do not repeat IM olanzapine within 2 hours; peak concentrations at 15 to 45 minutes mean early re-dosing risks cumulative sedation and hypotension.

options.rationale: The RANZCP and eTG rapid tranquillisation position places IM olanzapine 10 mg monotherapy as first line for acute behavioural disturbance in known psychosis; avoid concurrent IM benzodiazepine to reduce respiratory depression risk (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

Combined IM droperidol and IM midazolam increases risk of respiratory depression and hypotension and is not the first line combination; same site injection is also poor technique (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

Haloperidol 10 mg carries higher extrapyramidal risk than lower doses; combined with promethazine 50 mg the anticholinergic burden and QT risk make this a second line rather than first choice (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

Ziprasidone is not widely available in Australia, and moving toward propofol induction without a trial of first line IM options is unnecessarily invasive (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

Ketamine dissociative sedation is a prehospital or resistant restraint option; it is not the initial pharmacological choice in the emergency department with staff and safer options available (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: DSM-5 substance induced psychotic disorder is diagnosed when psychotic symptoms arise during or soon after substance intoxication or withdrawal and resolve within a month of cessation. Symptoms lasting beyond this period despite confirmed abstinence should be reclassified as a primary psychotic disorder, most often schizophrenia spectrum, with cannabis acting as an important environmental trigger. Heavy high potency cannabis use in adolescence multiplies the risk of schizophrenia several fold. Ongoing antipsychotic therapy and specialist follow up are appropriate; prolactin elevation on risperidone is dose related and monitored, not diagnostic of a separate condition. Weekly urine cannabis screening is reliable for confirming abstinence over the preceding week in a previously heavy user.
key_points: Substance induced psychosis resolves within 1 month of cessation
Persistence beyond 1 month reclassifies to a primary psychotic disorder
Heavy adolescent cannabis use multiplies schizophrenia risk
explanation.pearls: Cannabis withdrawal alone can produce sleep disturbance and irritability for weeks but does not sustain positive psychotic symptoms; new hallucinations at 6 weeks abstinent point at a primary disorder.

sources.label: RACP Chapter of Addiction Medicine Position

options.rationale: DSM-5 substance induced psychotic disorder should resolve within a month of cessation of the substance; persistence beyond a month suggests reclassification (Source: DSM-5-TR).

Positive symptoms persisting 6 weeks after cannabis cessation exceed the 1 month cut off for substance induced psychosis; DSM-5 and RANZCP guidance treat this as an emerging primary psychotic disorder with cannabis as a precipitant, not the diagnosis (Source: DSM-5-TR).

Elevated prolactin on risperidone is a medication effect (D2 blockade); prolactinoma related psychosis is not a recognised entity and does not explain his symptoms (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

Weekly UDS is highly reliable for detecting cannabis use over the preceding week in an abstinent user; sustained negatives over 6 weeks make continued use very unlikely (Source: RACP Chapter of Addiction Medicine Position).
source_refs: RACP Chapter of Addiction Medicine Position

options.rationale: Persistent perception disorder is visual and follows classical hallucinogen use; auditory hallucinations after cannabis use do not fit this diagnosis (Source: DSM-5-TR).

explanation.summary: Severe anorexia nervosa with BMI below 14, bradycardia below 50, hypokalaemia, or postural hypotension is a medical admission per MARSIPAN Australia and RANZCP eating disorder guidance. Refeeding syndrome (hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, fluid overload, cardiac failure, Wernicke encephalopathy) is prevented by starting calories at 10 to 20 kcal per kg per day for the first 3 days, giving thiamine 200 mg daily orally before feeds begin, and prescribing empirical replacement of phosphate, potassium, and magnesium. Electrolytes are checked twice daily for the first 5 days and calories are escalated as tolerated. Cardiac monitoring is required for QTc above 500 ms or pulse below 40.
key_points: Start at 10 to 20 kcal per kg per day for first 3 days
Thiamine 200 mg daily before feeds; empirical PO4, K+, Mg replacement
Twice daily electrolytes for 5 days; cardiac monitoring for severe bradycardia
explanation.pearls: The MEED Australian tool (medical emergencies in eating disorders) sets specific thresholds for cardiac monitoring: pulse below 40, systolic BP below 90, QTc above 500 ms, or postural drop above 20 mmHg.

sources.label: RANZCP Eating Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: Full calorie loading of a severely malnourished patient rapidly triggers refeeding syndrome; guidelines call for a cautious start with proactive electrolyte replacement (Source: RANZCP Eating Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline).
source_refs: RANZCP Eating Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: MARSIPAN Australia and RANZCP guidance recommend cautious refeeding at 10 to 20 kcal per kg per day for the first 3 days, thiamine 200 mg daily before or with the first meal, and empirical phosphate, potassium, and magnesium supplementation with twice daily electrolyte checks (Source: RANZCP Eating Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline).
source_refs: RANZCP Eating Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: BMI below 14 with bradycardia and hypokalaemia meets criteria for medical admission; community management alone would be unsafe (Source: MARSIPAN Australia Guidance).

Intravenous dextrose without thiamine and electrolyte replacement precipitates Wernicke encephalopathy and severe refeeding hypophosphataemia (Source: RANZCP Eating Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline).
source_refs: RANZCP Eating Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: Rapid nasogastric feeding rates deliver too many calories on the first day of a severely malnourished patient; slow escalation with prophylactic electrolyte replacement is required (Source: MARSIPAN Australia Guidance).

explanation.summary: Structured family intervention (family psychoeducation, communication skills, problem solving, and modification of high expressed emotion) delivered over at least 3 months by trained clinicians reduces relapse in first episode psychosis by about 50 percent at 12 months. High expressed emotion (criticism, hostility, emotional overinvolvement) is the single most robust family predictor of relapse. Interventions include the patient wherever possible and combine group and individual family sessions. Single session psychoeducation, peer support, and separation from family are less effective when used alone. This intervention sits alongside medication adherence work, vocational recovery, and physical health monitoring.
key_points: Structured family intervention over 3 or more months
High expressed emotion is a major relapse predictor
Reduces relapse by around 50 percent at 12 months
explanation.pearls: Reducing criticism and emotional overinvolvement is more effective than raising warmth alone; simple weekly problem solving meetings taught to families can achieve this over 8 to 12 sessions.

sources.label: Orygen Australian Clinical Guidelines for Early Psychosis

options.rationale: Individual parent counselling alone has less evidence than structured family intervention that includes the patient and addresses expressed emotion (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia).
One off sessions are insufficient; sustained multisession psychoeducation across 3 to 6 months is required to reduce relapse (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia).

Meta analyses and RANZCP guidance find structured family intervention lasting 3 months or more, addressing expressed emotion (high criticism, hostility, emotional overinvolvement), problem solving skills, and psychoeducation reduces relapse by around 50 percent at 12 months (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia).

Peer support groups are valuable adjuncts but have less evidence for relapse prevention than structured family intervention delivered by trained clinicians (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia).

Separation is not standard of care and disrupts a supportive attachment; structured family work addresses the specific expressed emotion pattern without separation (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia).

explanation.summary: Adult autism spectrum disorder in women is under recognised because of masking (learned social scripts, mimicking peers, camouflage). Presentation includes lifelong social exhaustion, restricted interests (often narrower topic focus that can be socially acceptable), routines, and sensory sensitivities. DSM-5 requires persistent deficits in social communication and interaction (across multiple settings), restricted or repetitive behaviours (at least two), symptoms present in early childhood (though masked), clinically significant impairment, and no better explanation. Diagnosis rests on structured multidisciplinary assessment including a developmental history from a knowledgeable informant (parent, older sibling, longstanding friend), review of school and childhood records, and use of validated tools (ADOS-2, ADI-R, DISCO). Screening tools like AQ and RAADS-R suggest but do not confirm the diagnosis.
key_points: Masking commonly hides autism in women and girls
DSM-5 requires early onset even if only apparent in retrospect
Diagnosis by structured multidisciplinary assessment with informant
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically about school playground time (spent alone or with a single peer, watching from the edge, playing structured games only); adult recall of primary school playtime is often more diagnostic than academic performance.

sources.label: Amaze Australia Autism in Women and Girls Position

options.rationale: Attributing the presentation to social anxiety without full assessment risks missing autism spectrum disorder; the pattern here (early onset, special interests, sensory, routines) is not social anxiety (Source: NICE CG142 Adult Autism).

Autistic girls and women commonly present as well behaved in school reports because of masking; absence of behavioural concerns in childhood does not exclude the diagnosis (Source: Amaze Australia Autism in Women and Girls Position).
source_refs: Amaze Australia Autism in Women and Girls Position

options.rationale: Genetic testing is offered in children where a specific syndrome is suspected; in adults without intellectual disability it is not the diagnostic step (Source: NICE CG142 Adult Autism).

NICE CG142 and Australian autism diagnostic guidelines recommend structured multidisciplinary assessment including a developmental history from a knowledgeable informant, DSM-5 criteria review, and validated tools such as the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule or interview (Source: NICE CG142 Adult Autism).

A stimulant trial is not a diagnostic test for autism spectrum disorder and would not clarify the presenting picture; formal ADHD assessment is separate and does not substitute (Source: RACGP Adult ADHD Guidance).

explanation.summary: DSM-5 renamed conversion disorder as functional neurological symptom disorder to emphasise that the diagnosis rests on positive clinical signs of internal inconsistency (Hoover sign for functional leg weakness, tremor entrainment, tubular visual fields) rather than an exclusion diagnosis. Management is delivering a clear positive explanation using neutral, non stigmatising language, engaging the patient in physiotherapy with a graded rehabilitation approach, and psychological therapy for common comorbid anxiety or trauma. Repeated imaging and specialist referrals reinforce illness behaviour and worsen outcome. Malingering (intentional falsification for external gain) and factitious disorder (intentional falsification to adopt the sick role) are separate diagnoses; both require intentional deception which is absent in conversion disorder.
key_points: Positive signs (Hoover, entrainment) confirm the diagnosis
Deliver a clear positive explanation early to aid recovery
Physiotherapy plus psychology; avoid repeat imaging
explanation.pearls: Websites like neurosymptoms.org (Jon Stone) are useful patient information adjuncts; sharing the positive diagnostic reasoning with the patient improves prognosis more than months of exclusion investigations.

options.rationale: Malingering requires external incentive (compensation, avoiding duty, obtaining medication) which is absent here; her goal is return to work; symptoms are not consciously produced (Source: DSM-5-TR).

Factitious disorder requires intentional falsification of symptoms motivated by adopting the sick role; there is no evidence of intentional falsification and she is not seeking the sick role (Source: DSM-5-TR).

DSM-5 functional neurological (conversion) disorder requires positive clinical signs of internal inconsistency (Hoover sign, spontaneous movement out of keeping with formal testing); management is delivering a clear positive diagnosis, physiotherapy, and psychological therapy, not repeat imaging (Source: DSM-5-TR).

Somatic symptom disorder focuses on excessive thoughts, feelings, or behaviours about somatic symptoms; conversion disorder is a distinct diagnosis with positive neurological signs of incongruity (Source: DSM-5-TR).
Repeat neuroimaging without new clinical features reinforces illness behaviour and undermines the positive diagnosis; conversion disorder requires positive signs, not exclusion (Source: DSM-5-TR).

explanation.summary: Relapse prevention pharmacotherapy for alcohol use disorder in AU practice centres on acamprosate and naltrexone with disulfiram as an adjunct in highly selected patients. Acamprosate is renally cleared and is preferred when there is significant liver disease; naltrexone is hepatically metabolised and contraindicated in acute hepatitis or advanced liver failure. Disulfiram is contraindicated in significant liver disease. Benzodiazepines have no role beyond acute withdrawal. Gabapentin has limited evidence and is not first-line.
key_points: Acamprosate preferred when significant hepatic impairment coexists with alcohol use disorder
Naltrexone contraindicated in acute hepatitis or advanced liver failure
Disulfiram is not first-line and requires excellent adherence and no hepatic risk
explanation.pearls: The renal versus hepatic clearance profile of acamprosate versus naltrexone decides the choice more often than efficacy; check eGFR and LFTs before either prescription.

sources.label: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners AOD Clinical Guidelines

options.rationale: Acamprosate is renally excreted and preferred over naltrexone when there is significant hepatic impairment; it is safe in liver disease as long as renal function is adequate and reduces relapse to heavy drinking (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction).

Disulfiram is contraindicated in significant liver disease because of the risk of severe hepatotoxicity and requires strict abstinence; it is not first-line and is unsafe with these LFTs (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction).

Gabapentin has limited evidence for alcohol use disorder relapse prevention and is not a first-line agent in AU practice; acamprosate or naltrexone are the recommended options (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction).

Naltrexone is hepatically metabolised and carries a black box warning of hepatotoxicity in advanced liver disease; with AST double the upper reference range and significant fibrosis, acamprosate is safer (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction).
Benzodiazepines have no role in relapse prevention beyond the acute withdrawal window and expose him to cross-dependence and withdrawal reinstatement risk (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction).

explanation.summary: Moderate to severe postnatal depression requires combined pharmacotherapy and psychological treatment. Sertraline is the first-line SSRI in breastfeeding because its relative infant dose is under 2 percent and the safety data is the largest of the class. A prior therapeutic response is a strong indication to use the same drug. Fluoxetine is second-line because of a longer half-life and higher relative infant dose. Inpatient mother-baby unit admission is reserved for active suicidality, infanticidal intent, psychosis, or inability to care for the infant; passive ideation with strong supports is managed in the community with a clear escalation plan.
key_points: Sertraline is the first-line SSRI in breastfeeding; do not interrupt breastfeeding
Combined SSRI plus psychological therapy for moderate to severe postnatal depression
Inpatient care reserved for active suicidality, infanticidal intent, or psychosis
explanation.pearls: EPDS item 10 (self-harm thoughts) is the trigger for direct safety enquiry; any positive answer needs a clear plan even when the total score is not extreme.

options.rationale: Fluoxetine has a longer half-life and higher relative infant dose than sertraline and is not first-line in breastfeeding; stopping breastfeeding is not needed when a compatible SSRI exists (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Guidelines).

Inpatient admission is reserved for women with active suicidal or infanticidal intent, psychosis, or inability to care for the infant; this woman has passive ideation only and strong community supports and can be managed in the community with escalation criteria (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Guidelines).

Sertraline is the first-line SSRI in breastfeeding women because of the lowest relative infant dose and best safety data, and her prior treatment response makes it the appropriate agent; breastfeeding does not need to be interrupted (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Guidelines).
