Moderate to severe postnatal depression (EPDS 21 with passive suicidal ideation) warrants pharmacotherapy with psychological therapy in parallel; therapy alone is inadequate at this severity (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Guidelines).
Benzodiazepines are not first-line for postnatal depression, sedate infants through breastmilk, and do not treat the underlying mood disorder (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Clozapine has a small but persistent risk of neutropenia and agranulocytosis, peaking in the 6 to 18 week window. The Australian clozapine monitoring program requires weekly FBC for the first 18 weeks, fortnightly to 52 weeks, and monthly indefinitely; dispensing is contingent on the FBC. Fever should also trigger an FBC regardless of schedule. Baseline metabolic and cardiac assessment is done before commencement and repeated at 3 to 6 months. The other main monitoring risks are cardiac (myocarditis in the first 3 months) and constipation-related ileus.
key_points: Clozapine monitoring: weekly FBC for 18 weeks, then fortnightly to 52 weeks, then monthly
Fever mandates an unscheduled FBC regardless of last check
Baseline and follow-up ECG, troponin, and metabolic parameters at 3 to 6 months
explanation.pearls: Clozapine dispensing in Australia is program-linked; the pharmacy cannot dispense unless the FBC has been submitted and cleared in the last week.

sources.label: Australian Clozapine Product Information and RANZCP Clozapine Prescribing Guidelines

options.rationale: Daily monitoring is disproportionate to the risk profile and imposes an impractical burden without changing detection of the true onset window of neutropenia which is weeks 6 to 18 (Source: Australian Clozapine Product Information and RANZCP Clozapine Prescribing Guidelines).
source_refs: Australian Clozapine Product Information and RANZCP Clozapine Prescribing Guidelines

options.rationale: Symptom-triggered monitoring alone misses asymptomatic neutropenia and does not meet program requirements; clozapine dispensing requires the FBC to be checked on schedule (Source: Australian Clozapine Product Information and RANZCP Clozapine Prescribing Guidelines).
source_refs: Australian Clozapine Product Information and RANZCP Clozapine Prescribing Guidelines

options.rationale: This underscreens for clozapine-induced neutropenia, which peaks in the 6 to 18 week window; the AU program requires weekly to 18 weeks (Source: Australian Clozapine Product Information and RANZCP Clozapine Prescribing Guidelines).
source_refs: Australian Clozapine Product Information and RANZCP Clozapine Prescribing Guidelines

options.rationale: The Australian clozapine monitoring program requires weekly FBC for the first 18 weeks, then fortnightly to 52 weeks, then monthly indefinitely; this reflects the temporal risk of clozapine-induced neutropenia (Source: Australian Clozapine Product Information and RANZCP Clozapine Prescribing Guidelines).
source_refs: Australian Clozapine Product Information and RANZCP Clozapine Prescribing Guidelines

options.rationale: Fortnightly from the outset misses the highest risk window; weekly for 18 weeks is mandated at the start of therapy (Source: Australian Clozapine Product Information and RANZCP Clozapine Prescribing Guidelines).
source_refs: Australian Clozapine Product Information and RANZCP Clozapine Prescribing Guidelines

explanation.summary: Generalised anxiety disorder in an older adult should be treated with combined SSRI and cognitive behavioural therapy when both are accessible. Escitalopram is first-line with the starting dose halved (5 mg) and a cap of 10 mg in over-65s because of QT prolongation and hyponatraemia risk; sodium is checked at 4 weeks and any symptom of hyponatraemia (headache, confusion, seizure) prompts immediate assessment. Chronic benzodiazepines and tricyclics are on the Beers list. Quetiapine has metabolic and mortality signals in older adults. Pregabalin is second-line.
key_points: SSRI (escitalopram) first-line for GAD across age groups
Older adult escitalopram cap 10 mg per PBS/TGA to reduce QT prolongation
Check sodium at 4 weeks after SSRI initiation in older adults
explanation.pearls: SSRI-induced hyponatraemia typically appears within the first month; older women with low body weight are the highest-risk group and warrant a scheduled sodium recheck.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine Position Statement on Prescribing

options.rationale: Escitalopram is first-line for generalised anxiety disorder in Australia with strong efficacy data; in older adults the starting dose is halved to 5 mg with a cap of 10 mg (QT and hyponatraemia risk), and sodium is checked at 4 weeks because SSRI hyponatraemia risk rises with age (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).
Tricyclic antidepressants are anticholinergic and pro-arrhythmic and are on the Beers list to avoid in older adults; they are not first-line for GAD (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

Pregabalin is second-line for GAD in AU practice with dose adjustment needed in reduced eGFR and a growing recognition of dependence; SSRI is tried first (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

Chronic benzodiazepines in older adults are avoided per the Beers criteria because of falls, cognitive impairment, and dependence; short courses only during SSRI initiation are acceptable but not as maintenance (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

Quetiapine is not first-line for GAD, carries metabolic and QT risks, and is associated with excess mortality in older adults when used for behavioural symptoms (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Families watching a relative who cannot speak or move often assume the worst, and clear information changes how they engage with treatment. Catatonia carries one of the better short term prognoses in psychiatry: most patients improve substantially with benzodiazepines, frequently within hours to days, and electroconvulsive therapy is highly effective for those who do not. The honest message is that the syndrome usually responds quickly, that the underlying illness then needs its own treatment, and that nursing care during immobility prevents the serious complications.
key_points: Most people with catatonia respond well to benzodiazepines within days
Electroconvulsive therapy is effective for those who do not respond
The underlying mood, psychotic or medical illness still needs treatment
Complications of immobility are prevented by active nursing care
explanation.pearls: Telling the family that the patient can usually hear and remember what is said at the bedside changes how the whole team speaks in the room. In context: catatonia is among the more treatable syndromes in psychiatry, and saying so early is both accurate and therapeutic for the family (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.rationale: Benzodiazepines produce substantial improvement in most people with catatonia, often within hours to days, which is honest and supports engagement (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

Electroconvulsive therapy leads when catatonia is malignant or has failed an adequate benzodiazepine trial, not at the outset in a stable patient (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.rationale: This holds only for brief, mild catatonia in someone still eating and drinking; sustained immobility causes thromboembolism, dehydration and pressure injury (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).
Antipsychotics are the mainstay of the psychotic illness that sometimes underlies catatonia, but they can deepen the catatonia itself (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).
A prolonged course is seen in treatment resistant illness; it is not the expected trajectory of newly treated catatonia (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

explanation.summary: TCA overdose kills through sodium-channel blockade producing QRS widening, hypotension, seizures, and ventricular arrhythmia. ECG features that predict toxicity are a QRS of 100 ms or more, R wave in aVR of 3 mm or more, and an R/S ratio in aVR of 0.7 or more. Treatment is sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg IV bolus with a pH target of 7.45 to 7.55, repeated as needed, plus intubation for airway protection, benzodiazepines for seizures, and fluid or vasopressors for hypotension. Class Ia, Ic, and III antiarrhythmics are contraindicated. Intralipid is rescue therapy for refractory cardiotoxicity, not first-line.
key_points: QRS 100 ms or more or R wave in aVR 3 mm or more triggers sodium bicarbonate in TCA overdose
Target pH 7.45 to 7.55 with 1 to 2 mmol/kg IV bicarbonate boluses
Avoid flumazenil and Class Ia/Ic/III antiarrhythmics; use intralipid only as rescue
explanation.pearls: The R wave in aVR is easier to measure than the QRS in an untidy trace; a tall R in aVR alone is a valid trigger to alkalinise.

sources.label: Australian College of Emergency Medicine Toxicology Guidelines

options.rationale: Class Ia and III antiarrhythmics prolong the QT and worsen sodium-channel blockade in TCA toxicity; sodium bicarbonate is the antiarrhythmic in this context, not amiodarone (Source: Australian College of Emergency Medicine Toxicology Guidelines).
source_refs: Australian College of Emergency Medicine Toxicology Guidelines

options.rationale: Activated charcoal at 90 minutes post-ingestion in a drowsy patient without a protected airway risks aspiration and provides little benefit; airway protection is not adequate for a drowsy woman and cardiotoxicity is the immediate threat (Source: Australian College of Emergency Medicine Toxicology Guidelines).
source_refs: Australian College of Emergency Medicine Toxicology Guidelines

options.rationale: Intralipid is a rescue therapy for lipophilic drug cardiotoxicity when standard treatment fails; sodium bicarbonate is first-line for TCA overdose and intralipid is not initial therapy (Source: Australian College of Emergency Medicine Toxicology Guidelines).
source_refs: Australian College of Emergency Medicine Toxicology Guidelines

options.rationale: Flumazenil is contraindicated in TCA overdose because it can precipitate seizures in mixed TCA-benzodiazepine ingestion and does not reverse TCA toxicity (Source: Australian College of Emergency Medicine Toxicology Guidelines).
source_refs: Australian College of Emergency Medicine Toxicology Guidelines

options.rationale: QRS 100 ms or more and R wave in aVR 3 mm or more predict TCA cardiotoxicity; sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg IV bolus with pH target 7.45 to 7.55 reverses sodium-channel blockade and is the first-line treatment for TCA toxicity per AU toxicology guidance (Source: Australian College of Emergency Medicine Toxicology Guidelines).
source_refs: Australian College of Emergency Medicine Toxicology Guidelines

explanation.summary: Sodium valproate has the highest teratogenicity of the AU-available anticonvulsants and mood stabilisers, with a 10 percent major malformation rate (neural tube defects, cardiac, facial) and a 30 to 40 percent rate of impaired neurodevelopmental outcome. TGA mandates a pregnancy prevention program for all women of reproductive potential prescribed valproate. When conception is planned, cross-titration to lithium (with careful monitoring) or lamotrigine (with slow titration) is the standard, with effective contraception maintained until the switch is complete and the woman is stable on the new regimen for at least 3 months.
key_points: Valproate: 10 percent major malformation; 30 to 40 percent neurodevelopmental risk
TGA pregnancy prevention program mandates alternative therapy in women who could conceive
Cross-titrate to lithium or lamotrigine with contraception until switch is complete
explanation.pearls: Lamotrigine dose needs to be increased through pregnancy because glucuronidation clearance rises; lithium dose needs monitoring across trimesters because renal clearance rises then falls postpartum.

sources.label: TGA Sodium Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Program

options.rationale: Sodium valproate carries a 10 percent major congenital malformation rate and 30 to 40 percent risk of neurodevelopmental disorders; RANZCP and TGA-mandated pregnancy prevention programs require withdrawal wherever safe, with a cross-titration to lithium or lamotrigine and continued contraception until the switch is complete (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Guidelines).

Folate supplementation does not offset the intrinsic teratogenic and neurodevelopmental risks of valproate; TGA and RANZCP mandate switching where possible in women who could become pregnant, not continuation with folate (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Guidelines).

Abrupt discontinuation without a replacement mood stabiliser carries a high relapse risk in bipolar I disorder; cross-titration protects mood stability while removing teratogen exposure (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Guidelines).

There is no safe teratogenic dose of valproate; reducing dose reduces but does not eliminate risk and is not an acceptable strategy when a switch is possible (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Guidelines).

Psychological therapy does not neutralise valproate teratogenicity; continuing valproate while trying to conceive is not consistent with the program she is enrolled in (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Guidelines).

explanation.summary: First episode psychosis is managed with an atypical antipsychotic chosen for its side effect profile rather than for a specific mechanism of action because the atypicals have similar efficacy in this setting. Aripiprazole is often chosen for young metabolically clean patients because it has the lowest weight gain and prolactin elevation among the first line agents. Olanzapine has the highest metabolic burden and is avoided when weight or diabetic risk is a concern. Clozapine is reserved for treatment resistant schizophrenia after two adequate trials of other antipsychotics.
key_points: Aripiprazole: lowest weight gain and prolactin among first line atypicals.
Olanzapine has the highest metabolic burden.
Clozapine reserved for treatment resistant schizophrenia after 2 adequate trials.
explanation.pearls: In first episode psychosis the atypicals have equivalent efficacy but very different side effect profiles; matching the drug to the patient's own priorities (metabolic, sedation, sexual side effects) improves adherence and long term outcomes.

options.rationale: Aripiprazole has the lowest metabolic burden among first line atypicals with minimal weight gain and prolactin elevation; the RANZCP schizophrenia guideline lists it among first line agents in first episode psychosis, and it aligns with the patient's expressed priority (Source: RANZCP schizophrenia guideline; TG Psychotropic).

Olanzapine has efficacy in first episode psychosis but has the highest weight gain and metabolic burden of the atypicals and is generally avoided in a metabolically clean young man who has raised the concern (Source: RANZCP schizophrenia guideline; TG Psychotropic).

Typical antipsychotics such as haloperidol are not first line in first episode psychosis because of higher extrapyramidal side effects that increase the risk of medication discontinuation (Source: RANZCP schizophrenia guideline).

Clozapine is reserved for treatment resistant schizophrenia after two adequate trials of other antipsychotics due to its haematological and metabolic risks; it is not a first line choice in a treatment naive patient (Source: RANZCP schizophrenia guideline).

Quetiapine has moderate weight gain and sedation and is not as effective as other atypicals at doses under 400 mg per day; it is not the preferred first line agent for a metabolically conscious young man with first episode psychosis (Source: RANZCP schizophrenia guideline).

explanation.summary: Long term lithium therapy is associated with a progressive decline in glomerular filtration rate; the risk rises with duration, high concentrations, episodes of toxicity and concurrent nephrotoxic drugs. When the estimated glomerular filtration rate falls below 60 mL/min per 1.73 m squared the RANZCP guidance is to reduce the dose to the lowest effective concentration, review co medication such as ACE inhibitors, ARBs, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and thiazide diuretics, and consider nephrology referral. Thyroid dysfunction and hyperparathyroidism are also long term concerns and require targeted testing. Discontinuation is a specialist decision and requires slow tapering over months with alternative mood stabilisation planned.
key_points: eGFR below 60 mL/min per 1.73 m squared triggers dose review and specialist input.
ACE inhibitors, ARBs, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and thiazides increase lithium levels.
Slow taper over months if discontinuation is required.
explanation.pearls: A creatinine rise of even 20 micromol/L in a stable lithium patient warrants review of nephrotoxic co medication because the combination of lithium plus non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug plus ACE inhibitor can accelerate irreversible renal decline within months.

options.rationale: Abrupt lithium discontinuation risks relapse of bipolar illness within weeks and switching without discussion is inappropriate; renal decline is managed by review of contributing drugs and dose reduction with continued monitoring under specialist input (Source: RANZCP mood disorders guideline; TG Psychotropic).

The falling estimated glomerular filtration rate reflects contributions from long term lithium, ibuprofen and perindopril; the guideline recommends dose reduction to the lowest effective concentration, review of nephrotoxic co medication in collaboration with the general practitioner and nephrology referral once the eGFR is below 60 mL/min per 1.73 m squared (Source: RANZCP mood disorders guideline; TG Psychotropic).

Higher lithium concentrations increase the risk of long term nephrotoxicity and thyroid dysfunction; in a euthymic patient the aim is to use the lowest effective concentration rather than the highest tolerated (Source: RANZCP mood disorders guideline).

Thiazide diuretics reduce renal clearance of lithium and precipitate toxicity; they should not be added without careful review of the lithium dose (Source: RANZCP mood disorders guideline; TG Psychotropic).

A drop in eGFR of 20 mL/min per 1.73 m squared over 6 months is significant and requires active management; delayed review of 12 months risks irreversible renal decline (Source: RANZCP mood disorders guideline).

explanation.summary: SSRI discontinuation syndrome typically appears within 1 to 3 days of stopping a short half life SSRI such as paroxetine, includes dizziness, paraesthesia, brain zaps, irritability and flu like symptoms, and resolves within 1 to 3 weeks. It is distinguished from depressive relapse by the timing, absence of core depressive symptoms, and rapid response to restarting the drug. Restarting at the usual dose and tapering over 6 to 8 weeks is the standard approach. Fluoxetine bridging is an option if re exposure to the original drug is not tolerated.
key_points: Onset within days of stopping suggests discontinuation, not relapse.
Paroxetine and venlafaxine have the shortest half lives and cause the most severe discontinuation.
Taper over 6 to 8 weeks after restarting.
explanation.pearls: A PHQ-9 under 5 with dizziness, brain zaps and paraesthesia within a week of stopping paroxetine reads as discontinuation, not relapse; restart the drug and taper over 6 to 8 weeks rather than escalating dose.

options.rationale: Relapse presents with a return of core depressive symptoms over weeks, not with dizziness and brain zaps within days of stopping; the pattern here fits discontinuation syndrome and increasing to a higher dose is not warranted (Source: TG Psychotropic).

Untreated paroxetine discontinuation typically lasts 1 to 3 weeks and can be severe; simply waiting is unpleasant for the patient and misses the opportunity to teach appropriate tapering practice (Source: TG Psychotropic).

Bridging with fluoxetine may be considered when a patient cannot tolerate re exposure to the original drug; it is not the first step when the pragmatic option of restarting the original drug and tapering is available (Source: TG Psychotropic).

The onset within days of stopping short half life SSRI, presence of dizziness and paraesthesia and absence of core depressive symptoms is classical SSRI discontinuation syndrome; restarting at the previous dose and tapering over 6 to 8 weeks resolves symptoms and avoids conflating them with relapse (Source: TG Psychotropic; RANZCP mood disorders guideline).

Discontinuation symptoms are the expected pharmacological response, not a hypersensitivity reaction; hypersensitivity would present with rash, angioedema or serotonin syndrome, none of which is present (Source: TG Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose produces sodium channel blockade with QRS widening, terminal R wave in aVR and risk of cardiovascular collapse and seizures, plus anticholinergic effects. A QRS above 100 ms or a terminal R wave in aVR of at least 3 mm is an indication for a sodium bicarbonate bolus of 1 to 2 mmol/kg, repeated to keep the QRS narrow and to buffer acidosis. Benzodiazepines are used for seizures; phenytoin is contraindicated because it worsens the sodium channel blockade. Activated charcoal is only useful within 1 to 2 hours of ingestion and gastric lavage is not routine due to aspiration risk.
key_points: QRS above 100 ms or aVR terminal R at least 3 mm: give sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg.
Benzodiazepines for seizures; phenytoin is contraindicated.
Charcoal only within 1 to 2 hours; lavage is not routine.
explanation.pearls: A tricyclic overdose with QRS above 160 ms carries a 50 percent risk of ventricular arrhythmia, so give the first sodium bicarbonate bolus at the bedside as soon as the ECG is seen rather than waiting on blood gas results.

options.rationale: Activated charcoal is not routinely given beyond 1 to 2 hours of ingestion because gastric absorption is largely complete; more importantly the ECG changes require immediate sodium bicarbonate rather than delayed decontamination (Source: Australian Poisons Information Centre).

Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines and has no role in tricyclic overdose; it may precipitate seizures in mixed overdoses and unmask sodium channel toxicity (Source: Australian Poisons Information Centre).

Gastric lavage is not standard care beyond the first hour and carries aspiration risk in a drowsy patient; magnesium is for polymorphic ventricular tachycardia and not first line without arrhythmia (Source: Australian Poisons Information Centre).

Phenytoin is contraindicated in tricyclic overdose because it shares sodium channel blockade and worsens cardiotoxicity; benzodiazepines are the anticonvulsant of choice (Source: Australian Poisons Information Centre).

A QRS above 100 ms and terminal R wave in aVR indicate significant sodium channel blockade and predict cardiovascular collapse and seizures in tricyclic overdose; sodium bicarbonate at 1 to 2 mmol/kg (100 mL of 8.4 percent for a 70 kg adult) narrows the QRS and reduces arrhythmia risk (Source: Australian Poisons Information Centre; TG Toxicology).

explanation.summary: Adult ADHD is diagnosed clinically on the presence of childhood onset symptoms of inattention or hyperactivity impulsivity, functional impairment across two or more domains, and exclusion of alternative causes; screening tools such as the Adult ADHD Self Report Scale support but do not replace formal assessment. In Australia the initiation of stimulant medication requires an authority prescription by a psychiatrist or paediatrician. Non stimulant options such as atomoxetine and guanfacine are second line. Fitness to drive is preserved unless there is evidence of significant impairment or repeated at fault crashes.
key_points: Diagnosis is clinical with childhood onset and functional impairment.
Stimulant initiation requires psychiatrist or paediatrician authority in Australia.
Neuropsychological testing is not required for the diagnosis.
explanation.pearls: For a working adult with functional impairment and a positive ASRS Part A, refer directly to a psychiatrist or paediatrician; only they can start stimulant medication under the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme authority rules in Australia.

sources.label: Australian evidence based clinical practice guideline for ADHD

options.rationale: The clinical picture is suggestive of adult ADHD with childhood onset symptoms and functional impairment; Australian practice is a formal assessment by a psychiatrist or paediatrician to confirm diagnosis, exclude co morbidity and initiate stimulant treatment under authority arrangements (Source: RANZCP ADHD guideline; Australian evidence based clinical practice guideline for ADHD).
source_refs: Australian evidence based clinical practice guideline for ADHD

options.rationale: In Australia stimulant medication for ADHD requires an authority from a psychiatrist or paediatrician; the general practitioner cannot initiate it and must refer for formal assessment (Source: RANZCP ADHD guideline; PBS authority conditions).
There are no core anxiety symptoms; treating a presumed anxiety disorder without evidence risks missing the underlying ADHD and delays appropriate care (Source: RANZCP ADHD guideline).

Australian fitness to drive standards do not require driving cessation while awaiting ADHD assessment in a patient with no crashes and no significant impairment behind the wheel (Source: Austroads assessing fitness to drive).

Neuropsychological testing is not required for ADHD diagnosis in most cases; the diagnosis is clinical, based on symptom criteria plus childhood onset and functional impairment (Source: Australian evidence based clinical practice guideline for ADHD).
source_refs: Australian evidence based clinical practice guideline for ADHD

explanation.summary: The Australian clozapine monitoring services use a standard neutrophil alert threshold of 1.5 x10^9/L below which the drug is stopped, however a benign ethnic neutropenia protocol lowers the alert to 1.0 x10^9/L when a registered lower baseline has been documented. In a registered patient with an asymptomatic neutrophil count between 1.0 and 1.5 x10^9/L, clozapine may continue with increased monitoring frequency and clinical review for infective symptoms. Granulocyte colony stimulating factor and lithium are not first line and are reserved for specific circumstances. Dose reduction does not reduce agranulocytosis risk because the toxicity is idiosyncratic rather than dose dependent.
key_points: Standard neutrophil alert threshold on clozapine is 1.5 x10^9/L.
Benign ethnic neutropenia lowers the alert to 1.0 x10^9/L if registered.
Clozapine agranulocytosis is idiosyncratic, not dose dependent.
explanation.pearls: A registered benign ethnic neutropenia protocol on Clopine Connect allows clozapine to continue with a neutrophil count between 1.0 and 1.5 x10^9/L, provided monitoring frequency doubles and any fever or infective symptom triggers immediate cessation and haematology review.

options.rationale: Under the benign ethnic neutropenia framework the alert threshold is a neutrophil count under 1.0 x10^9/L rather than the general 1.5 x10^9/L cut off; a count of 1.3 x10^9/L does not mandate immediate cessation and haematology admission (Source: Clopine Connect monitoring guidance; RANZCP clozapine consensus).

The registered benign ethnic neutropenia protocol allows continued clozapine while the neutrophil count remains at or above 1.0 x10^9/L, with an increased monitoring frequency to at least twice weekly counts and a clinical review for infective symptoms; a count of 1.3 x10^9/L in an asymptomatic patient meets that requirement (Source: Clopine Connect monitoring guidance; RANZCP clozapine consensus).

Lithium is sometimes used to raise neutrophil counts but is not first line and does not replace protocol monitoring; adding lithium in an otherwise stable patient introduces long term risk without an evidence-based indication (Source: RANZCP clozapine consensus).

Granulocyte colony stimulating factor is used for clozapine associated neutropenia below 0.5 x10^9/L or with fever, not for a mild reduction in an asymptomatic patient with benign ethnic neutropenia already registered (Source: RANZCP clozapine consensus).
Clozapine induced agranulocytosis is not dose dependent; halving the dose does not reduce the risk and risks psychiatric relapse (Source: RANZCP clozapine consensus).

explanation.summary: In a woman with bipolar I disorder and prior manic episodes the risk of postpartum psychosis or mania is around 50 percent without prophylactic mood stabilisation, so continuation of lithium in pregnancy is often justified. The absolute risk of Ebstein anomaly with first trimester lithium exposure is around 6 per 1000 births compared with 1 per 1000 in the general population, an increase that is small relative to the relapse risk of stopping the drug. Sodium valproate is contraindicated in pregnancy because of its high risk of major malformations and neurodevelopmental impairment. Continuation of lithium is accompanied by more frequent level monitoring due to increased renal clearance and a fetal cardiac ultrasound at 20 weeks.
key_points: Ebstein risk about 6 per 1000 versus 1 per 1000 baseline with first trimester lithium.
Postpartum relapse risk about 50 percent without a mood stabiliser in bipolar I disorder.
Sodium valproate is contraindicated in pregnancy.
explanation.pearls: In pregnancy the volume of distribution and renal clearance of lithium change, so serum lithium levels are checked monthly until 34 weeks and then weekly, with the dose held on the day of delivery to avoid postpartum toxicity.

options.rationale: Sodium valproate is contraindicated in pregnancy because of a 10 percent risk of major congenital malformation and a further 30 to 40 percent risk of neurodevelopmental impairment; it is never a substitute for lithium in a pregnant woman (Source: RANZCP mood disorders in pregnancy; TG Psychotropic).

Lamotrigine is safer in pregnancy but is less effective at preventing manic episodes; switching from an effective lithium regimen in a woman with prior manic episodes risks relapse and is not first line (Source: RANZCP mood disorders in pregnancy).

In a woman with severe bipolar I disorder and prior manic episodes, the risk of postpartum relapse without a mood stabiliser is around 50 percent and outweighs the small absolute increase in Ebstein anomaly risk with lithium (about 6 per 1000 versus 1 per 1000 baseline); the RANZCP advice is to continue at the lowest effective dose with a fetal cardiac ultrasound at 20 weeks and level monitoring through pregnancy (Source: RANZCP mood disorders in pregnancy; TG Psychotropic).

Discontinuation of lithium during the first trimester exposes the woman to a high risk of relapse and does not eliminate cardiac teratogenicity risk; consistent continuation with monitoring is safer than intermittent stopping (Source: RANZCP mood disorders in pregnancy).

Olanzapine is a reasonable alternative to lithium but replacing an effective lithium regimen introduces its own metabolic risks and gestational diabetes risk without meaningful reduction in overall teratogenicity risk; the risk versus benefit favours continuing lithium in a woman with two prior manic episodes (Source: RANZCP mood disorders in pregnancy).

explanation.summary: Acute behavioural disturbance is managed on a graded ladder: environmental measures and verbal de-escalation first, then offered oral medication, then parenteral sedation, with restraint and seclusion reserved for imminent serious harm and used for the shortest possible time. A patient who is still talking and willing to take a tablet has not exhausted the less restrictive options, and choosing an injection at that point is both clinically unnecessary and hard to justify against the least restrictive principle that underpins New South Wales mental health law. Every episode needs post-sedation observations, documentation, and a debrief with the patient afterwards. In context: schizoaffective disorder combines psychotic and mood symptoms, and agitation during an admission is usually driven by psychosis, mania, fear, substance withdrawal or an unmet need such as pain, so looking for and treating the driver is as important as the sedative chosen.

sources.label: NSW Health: Management of patients with acute severe behavioural disturbance

options.rationale: When de-escalation has failed but the patient accepts medication, the oral route is used before any parenteral one, and a benzodiazepine is first choice for acute behavioural disturbance in an adult already on an antipsychotic.
source_refs: NSW Health: Management of patients with acute severe behavioural disturbance

options.rationale: Parenteral droperidol is used when oral treatment is refused or the disturbance is severe enough that waiting is unsafe. It requires cardiorespiratory monitoring afterwards.
source_refs: NSW Health: Management of patients with acute severe behavioural disturbance

options.rationale: Intramuscular olanzapine is an alternative parenteral option in a patient who refuses oral medication, and it should not be combined with parenteral benzodiazepines because of the risk of respiratory depression.
Seclusion is a last resort when there is an immediate risk of serious harm that less restrictive measures cannot contain, is legally regulated and time limited, and requires documented review.
source_refs: NSW Health: Management of patients with acute severe behavioural disturbance

options.rationale: Restraint is reserved for imminent serious harm, usually to enable urgent parenteral treatment, and carries risks of injury, aspiration and sudden death. It is not used while a patient is accepting oral medication.
source_refs: NSW Health: Management of patients with acute severe behavioural disturbance

explanation.summary: Serotonin syndrome is diagnosed using the Hunter criteria: exposure to a serotonergic drug plus spontaneous clonus, or inducible clonus with agitation or diaphoresis, or ocular clonus with agitation or diaphoresis, or tremor and hyperreflexia, or hypertonia with temperature above 38 degrees Celsius and either ocular or inducible clonus. It develops within 6 to 24 hours of a new serotonergic drug or dose increase, with lower limb predominant clonus and hyperreflexia. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome develops over days to 2 weeks after an antipsychotic dose change and presents with lead-pipe rigidity, bradyreflexia and mental slowing. Treatment of serotonin toxicity involves cessation of the offending drug, benzodiazepines for agitation and clonus, active cooling and cyproheptadine in severe cases.
key_points: Serotonin syndrome: lower limb clonus, hyperreflexia, agitation, mydriasis; rapid onset.
NMS: lead-pipe rigidity, bradyreflexia, mental slowing; onset over days.
Sertraline plus tramadol is a classic serotonin syndrome combination.
explanation.pearls: Any patient on a serotonergic drug who develops lower limb clonus and hyperreflexia within 24 hours of adding tramadol should be treated as serotonin toxicity; withhold serotonergic drugs, give benzodiazepines and add cyproheptadine 12 mg orally then 2 mg every 2 hours if severe.

options.rationale: The rapid onset within 24 hours of adding a second serotonergic drug, lower limb predominant clonus, hyperreflexia, mydriasis, agitation, diaphoresis and hyperthermia fit the Hunter serotonin toxicity criteria; sertraline plus tramadol is a classic combination (Source: Hunter serotonin toxicity criteria; TG Psychotropic).

Neuroleptic malignant syndrome develops over days to 2 weeks after an antipsychotic dose change and presents with lead-pipe rigidity, bradyreflexia and stupor rather than clonus and hyperreflexia; sertraline is not a dopamine antagonist (Source: TG Psychotropic).
Malignant hyperthermia occurs after exposure to volatile anaesthetics or depolarising muscle relaxants such as suxamethonium; there is no such exposure here (Source: TG Toxicology).

Anticholinergic toxidrome presents with dry hot flushed skin, mydriasis, urinary retention and delirium; the diaphoresis and hyperreflexia are inconsistent, and tramadol is primarily a serotonergic and opioid drug rather than anticholinergic (Source: TG Toxicology).

Sodium is 138 mmol/L and there has been no correction of hyponatraemia; the picture is inconsistent with central pontine myelinolysis, which presents with locked in syndrome and dysarthria (Source: TG Nephrology).

explanation.summary: Postnatal depression at 8 weeks with an Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale of 13 or higher and functional impairment warrants active treatment. First line pharmacotherapy in a breastfeeding mother is sertraline because of its lowest relative infant dose among SSRIs (about 0.5 percent) and reassuring longitudinal safety data. Fluoxetine and paroxetine are not first line: fluoxetine because of long half life accumulation in the infant, paroxetine because of discontinuation effects. Psychological therapy (CBT or IPT) is added alongside pharmacotherapy.
key_points: Sertraline is first line SSRI in breastfeeding.
Fluoxetine avoided due to long half life and infant accumulation.
Combine with psychological therapy for best outcomes.
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically about intrusive obsessional thoughts of harming the baby; obsessive compulsive disorder frequently first presents in the postnatal period and may be under recognised because women fear disclosure will trigger child protection involvement.

options.rationale: Fluoxetine has a long half life and higher relative infant dose than sertraline (about 5 to 9 percent); it accumulates in breastfed infants and is not preferred first line in this setting (Source: RANZCP perinatal guideline; AMH).

Sertraline has the lowest relative infant dose (about 0.5 percent) among SSRIs and is the preferred first line antidepressant in breastfeeding mothers; starting low and titrating minimises adverse effects (Source: RANZCP perinatal guideline; AMH).

Paroxetine transfers to breast milk in low quantities but has significant discontinuation and anticholinergic side effects; sertraline is preferred first line in breastfeeding (Source: RANZCP perinatal guideline; AMH).
SNRIs like venlafaxine are second line in perinatal setting; discontinuation symptoms and elevated blood pressure limit their first line use over sertraline (Source: RANZCP perinatal guideline).
Tricyclic antidepressants have overdose lethality and anticholinergic effects that make them non first line; sertraline is safer in this population (Source: RANZCP perinatal guideline; AMH).

explanation.summary: Baseline investigations before commencing lithium target the organs lithium can affect over time: kidney (UEC and eGFR), thyroid, parathyroid (measured via corrected calcium), and cardiac conduction (ECG in patients over 40 or with cardiac risk factors). Beta HCG is done in people who could become pregnant because lithium is associated with Ebstein anomaly at first trimester exposure. A full blood count is baseline for benign leucocytosis. Ongoing monitoring is 6 monthly UEC, TFTs and calcium with lithium levels 12 hours post dose at week 1, week 2, and any dose change.
key_points: Baseline: UEC, TFT, calcium, FBC, beta HCG if applicable, ECG.
Monitoring: 6 monthly UEC, TFT, calcium; lithium level 12 h post dose.
Target therapeutic level 0.6 to 0.8 mmol/L in maintenance; 0.8 to 1.0 in acute mania.
explanation.pearls: Warn the patient about NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors and thiazides, which reduce lithium clearance; dehydration from vomiting, diarrhoea or heat exposure is a common trigger for lithium toxicity and warrants a same day lithium level and hold.

options.rationale: Liver function is not lithium relevant (renally excreted) and echocardiogram is not routine baseline; this bundle overtests without adding lithium safety information (Source: RANZCP mood disorders guideline).

24 hour urine creatinine clearance is not needed baseline; eGFR from serum creatinine is standard and 24 hour collection is reserved for CKD monitoring or when eGFR is discordant with clinical picture (Source: RANZCP mood disorders guideline).

Standard baseline before lithium includes renal function (UEC), thyroid function, calcium (parathyroid effect), FBC, pregnancy testing where relevant, and ECG in patients over 40 or with cardiac risk factors; this covers organs lithium can affect (Source: RANZCP mood disorders guideline; AMH).

Parathyroid hormone, vitamin D and phosphate are not routine baseline; calcium is measured as a proxy for parathyroid effect and PTH is checked only if calcium is high (Source: RANZCP mood disorders guideline).

Chest x ray is not part of lithium baseline; calcium and ECG (in over 40 or with cardiac risk) are the necessary additions to renal and thyroid function testing (Source: RANZCP mood disorders guideline).

explanation.summary: Clozapine agranulocytosis risk is highest in the first 18 weeks of therapy (about 0.8 percent lifetime risk overall). Australian monitoring per AMH and the RANZCP schizophrenia guideline is weekly full blood count for the first 18 weeks, fortnightly to 12 months, then monthly for life. Patient and prescriber must be registered on the manufacturer clozapine patient monitoring service. Additional monitoring includes weekly troponin and CRP for the first 4 weeks for myocarditis, and 3 monthly metabolic monitoring (weight, lipids, HbA1c).
key_points: Weekly FBC for 18 weeks then fortnightly to 12 months then monthly for life.
Weekly troponin and CRP for first 4 weeks to detect myocarditis.
Register both patient and prescriber on the manufacturer monitoring service.
explanation.pearls: Any interruption of clozapine over 48 hours mandates retitration from the starting dose because postural hypotension and sedation return rapidly; check the reset protocol before restart rather than resuming the previous dose.

options.rationale: Monthly monitoring is inadequate for the first 18 weeks when agranulocytosis risk is highest; weekly is mandated (Source: AMH; RANZCP schizophrenia guideline).
Weekly monitoring extends to 18 weeks because agranulocytosis risk is highest in the first 18 weeks; stopping weekly at 4 weeks misses the risk window (Source: AMH).
Weekly rather than fortnightly monitoring is required for the first 18 weeks because agranulocytosis risk is dose independent and time dependent (Source: AMH; RANZCP schizophrenia guideline).

AMH and RANZCP clozapine monitoring requires weekly FBC for the first 18 weeks (highest agranulocytosis risk), fortnightly to 12 months, then monthly for life with registration on the manufacturer monitoring service (Source: AMH; RANZCP schizophrenia guideline).
This schedule does not match the AMH mandated protocol; weekly for 18 weeks then fortnightly to 12 months then monthly is the correct protocol (Source: AMH).

explanation.summary: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome and serotonin syndrome can present with hyperthermia, altered mental state and autonomic instability but are discriminated by the neuromuscular examination. NMS presents with lead-pipe rigidity, hyporeflexia, mutism and bradykinesia within 1 to 2 weeks of starting or increasing a dopamine antagonist. Serotonin syndrome presents with neuromuscular hyperactivity: hyperreflexia, clonus (especially lower limbs), shivering, and myoclonus within 24 hours of a serotonergic agent change. Creatine kinase is typically higher in NMS.
key_points: NMS: lead-pipe rigidity, hyporeflexia, high CK, dopamine antagonist trigger.
Serotonin syndrome: hyperreflexia, clonus, shivering, serotonergic trigger.
Onset: NMS days to weeks; serotonin syndrome hours.
explanation.pearls: Management of NMS is stop the antipsychotic, aggressive cooling, IV fluid resuscitation to protect against rhabdomyolysis induced acute kidney injury, and dantrolene or bromocriptine in refractory cases; ECT is considered for prolonged severe cases.

options.rationale: Serotonin syndrome features neuromuscular hyperactivity with hyperreflexia, clonus (especially lower limbs) and shivering; this patient has hyporeflexia, no clonus and lead-pipe rigidity, which is the NMS pattern (Source: Sternbach; Hunter criteria).

There is a clear temporal association with commencement of haloperidol and a classic NMS syndrome (rigidity, hyperthermia, autonomic instability, elevated creatine kinase); encephalitis would not usually produce lead-pipe rigidity and elevated creatine kinase (Source: RANZCP schizophrenia guideline).
Malignant hyperthermia is triggered by volatile anaesthetics or suxamethonium; there is no anaesthetic exposure in this history so the diagnosis does not fit (Source: RANZCP schizophrenia guideline).

Anticholinergic toxicity produces dry skin (not diffuse sweating), mydriasis, and urinary retention without rigidity or elevated creatine kinase; the sweating and rigidity here argues against it (Source: RANZCP schizophrenia guideline).

NMS presents with lead-pipe rigidity, hyporeflexia (not hyperreflexia), hyperthermia, autonomic instability and elevated creatine kinase within 1 to 2 weeks of starting a dopamine antagonist; his picture fits Levenson and DSM 5 TR criteria (Source: Sternbach; RANZCP schizophrenia guideline).

explanation.summary: Postpartum psychosis typically presents between day 3 and day 14 postpartum with a rapid onset of confusion, mood instability, delusions (often involving the baby), hallucinations, and severe sleep disturbance. Risk factors include personal or family history of bipolar disorder or previous postpartum psychosis. It is a psychiatric emergency: infanticide and suicide rates are elevated. Management is admission (voluntary or involuntary) to a mother and baby unit where possible, with an antipsychotic and mood stabiliser, and consideration of ECT for refractory cases.
key_points: Typical onset day 3 to 14 postpartum with rapid deterioration.
Delusions about the baby plus manic features are hallmarks.
Admit; mother and baby unit preferred; antipsychotic plus mood stabiliser.
explanation.pearls: A first cousin history of postpartum psychosis raises risk, and any first degree relative with bipolar disorder increases postpartum psychosis risk to about 25 to 50 percent; document risk factors antenatally and plan follow up in the first 2 weeks postpartum for high risk women.

options.rationale: Postpartum psychosis with delusions about the baby, infanticidal ideation and refusal of voluntary admission requires involuntary detention for inpatient care; a mother and baby unit is preferred to preserve bonding when safe (Source: RANZCP perinatal guideline).

Postpartum psychosis with active persecutory delusions involving the baby and infanticidal risk is a psychiatric emergency requiring immediate admission; community outpatient care underestimates the risk to mother and baby (Source: RANZCP perinatal guideline).

Her presentation includes overt psychotic features (persecutory delusion, delusion of baby substitution) and manic features (reduced sleep, pressure of speech, agitation), which are the hallmarks of postpartum psychosis, not depression (Source: RANZCP perinatal guideline).

Postpartum psychosis is not managed with a single anxiolytic dose in the community; admission with antipsychotic and mood stabiliser is standard care and delay risks harm to mother or infant (Source: RANZCP perinatal guideline).

A child protection notification may be appropriate but does not replace immediate inpatient psychiatric care; her insight is impaired given the delusions, so outpatient follow up is not safe (Source: RANZCP perinatal guideline).

explanation.summary: Catatonia is a syndrome, so a successful lorazepam response is the start of treatment, not the end. The underlying illness is most often a mood disorder, and the history decides its polarity. A documented hypomanic episode makes this bipolar depression, where Australian guidance favours quetiapine, lithium or lamotrigine rather than antidepressant monotherapy, which risks a switch into hypomania or a mixed state. The benzodiazepine cover continues while the mood treatment takes effect and is tapered slowly afterwards.
key_points: Always identify and treat the illness underlying the catatonia
A past hypomanic episode redefines the depression as bipolar
Antidepressant monotherapy is avoided in bipolar depression
Continue benzodiazepine cover while the mood treatment takes effect
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically about periods of reduced need for sleep with sustained increased activity, since patients rarely volunteer hypomania as a problem. In context: catatonia most often sits on a mood disorder, so the polarity of that disorder drives every decision that follows recovery (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders).

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.rationale: The prior hypomanic episode makes this bipolar depression, where an atypical antipsychotic such as quetiapine is a first line option and antidepressant monotherapy is avoided (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.rationale: Dose escalation is the answer in unipolar depression with a partial response, where there is no history suggesting a bipolar course (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.rationale: Lithium augmentation is a recognised step in treatment resistant unipolar depression; here the antidepressant itself is the problem (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.rationale: Stopping everything is the answer when a drug induced syndrome is suspected, and here it would risk immediate relapse of the catatonia (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).
Switching antidepressant is the answer for intolerance or non response in unipolar illness; any antidepressant alone carries switch risk here (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Lithium associated hyperparathyroidism affects up to 10 per cent of patients on long term therapy and is often missed because calcium is not always on the routine lithium panel. It differs from primary hyperparathyroidism in that the parathyroid glands are frequently diffusely hyperplastic rather than a single adenoma. The abnormality can persist after lithium cessation, so stopping the drug is not a reliable cure and is rarely the first move in a patient who has been well for over a decade. Management is shared between psychiatry and endocrinology and weighs relapse risk against the degree of hypercalcaemia.
key_points: Corrected calcium belongs on the annual lithium panel alongside creatinine, eGFR and thyroid function
Lithium hypercalcaemia is parathyroid hormone dependent, so parathyroid hormone will be normal or high rather than suppressed
Thiazides both raise calcium and reduce lithium clearance and are the wrong agent here
Hypercalcaemia may persist after lithium is stopped because of parathyroid hyperplasia
explanation.pearls: Lithium also causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and reduced eGFR, so an annual panel needs calcium, creatinine, eGFR and thyroid function together; a trough level alone will look reassuring while calcium climbs.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.rationale: Lithium reduces the sensitivity of the parathyroid calcium sensing receptor and causes a parathyroid hormone dependent hypercalcaemia that is inappropriately non suppressed; a paired parathyroid hormone and calcium is the test that separates this from malignancy or vitamin D excess (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook; RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders).

The lithium level is mid range and the calcium abnormality is not dose-dependent toxicity, so dose reduction neither explains nor corrects the hypercalcaemia and risks losing 12 years of mood stability (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

Abrupt lithium cessation carries a rebound mania risk and the hypercalcaemia has not yet been characterised biochemically; any switch decision follows the parathyroid hormone result rather than preceding it (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.rationale: Thiazides raise serum calcium and reduce renal lithium clearance, so this worsens both problems at once; thiazides are used for lithium induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, which is a different complication (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

Antiresorptive therapy treats a consequence rather than establishing the cause, and starting it before the parathyroid hormone is known will confound later interpretation of bone turnover (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

explanation.summary: Non bizarre persecutory beliefs describe situations that could happen, which is exactly what makes them hard. Being followed, being defrauded, having a flat entered and having a partner who is unfaithful all occur in reality, and a diagnosis of delusional disorder requires that the belief be false as well as fixed. Collateral history from family, housing records, workplaces or police is the step that establishes this, and it doubles as the risk assessment by revealing what the patient has already done about the belief.
key_points: A delusion must be false as well as fixed and unshakeable
Non bizarre beliefs describe plausible events, so verification matters
Collateral history establishes the facts and maps the risk at the same time
Treatment decisions follow the diagnosis rather than preceding it
explanation.pearls: Where the belief turns out to be partly true, the question becomes whether the interpretation built on it is out of proportion, which is often where the psychopathology sits. In context: delusional disorder is diagnosed by excluding a factual basis and other psychotic features, not by the strangeness of the story alone (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Management of Schizophrenia and Related Disorders).

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Management of Schizophrenia and Related Disorders

options.rationale: A delusion is a fixed belief that is demonstrably false, so a plausible belief is checked against collateral sources before any psychotic disorder is diagnosed (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Management of Schizophrenia and Related Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Management of Schizophrenia and Related Disorders

options.rationale: Starting treatment is the answer once the belief is established as false and fixed and is causing distress, risk or impairment (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Management of Schizophrenia and Related Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Management of Schizophrenia and Related Disorders

options.rationale: Neuroimaging is the answer when there are neurological signs or cognitive decline, particularly at a first presentation in later life (Source: ACSQHC Delirium Clinical Care Standard).

Psychological therapy is an adjunct once a psychotic disorder has been diagnosed and the patient is engaged (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Management of Schizophrenia and Related Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Management of Schizophrenia and Related Disorders

options.rationale: Direct contradiction is rarely useful and damages engagement; it would only follow once the belief were clearly disproven (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: The distinction between a cannabis induced psychotic disorder and a first episode of a primary psychotic illness is made on the course after abstinence rather than at the index presentation. Symptoms that outlast roughly one month of verified abstinence, and the appearance of negative symptoms such as reduced speech and social withdrawal, point away from a purely substance induced picture. Duration of untreated psychosis is one of the few modifiable predictors of long term outcome, which is why deferring treatment has a real cost. Early psychosis services combine low dose antipsychotic therapy with vocational support, family work and ongoing substance intervention.
key_points: Verified abstinence, not self report, is what makes the substance induced versus primary distinction interpretable
Negative symptoms emerging during abstinence favour a primary psychotic disorder
Baseline weight, waist circumference, fasting glucose, lipids and prolactin precede antipsychotic initiation
Longer duration of untreated psychosis predicts poorer functional recovery
explanation.pearls: Start risperidone at 1 mg daily in first episode psychosis and titrate no faster than weekly; doses above 4 mg daily add extrapyramidal effects and prolactin elevation without improving response rates in this group.

options.rationale: Symptoms attributable to cannabis alone would be expected to settle within about one month of abstinence, so continued watchful waiting delays treatment of an emerging primary disorder (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Schizophrenia).

Substance work remains important but cannot be the only intervention when psychosis has persisted seven weeks beyond verified abstinence and negative symptoms are emerging (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Schizophrenia).
Benzodiazepines treat neither hallucinations nor negative symptoms and carry dependence risk in a young person with a substance use history (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

Depot formulation is an alternative to oral therapy but is reserved for established adherence problems or patient preference after an oral trial has established tolerability (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

Psychosis persisting well beyond one month of verified abstinence, with emerging negative symptoms and functional decline, is treated as first episode psychosis with a low dose second generation antipsychotic and specialist early psychosis care (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Schizophrenia; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Autistic women are diagnosed later and less often than men, largely because camouflaging behaviours mask the social features while the resulting exhaustion presents as anxiety or depression. Repeated antidepressant non response in a person with lifelong sensory sensitivity and need for sameness should prompt a developmental reformulation rather than another pharmacological step. Australian practice requires a multidisciplinary assessment with a structured instrument and a corroborated developmental history rather than a single clinic impression. Diagnosis matters practically because it changes the therapeutic approach, opens funded supports and reduces the risk of iatrogenic harm from repeated medication trials.
key_points: Camouflaging delays autism diagnosis in women and presents as anxiety, exhaustion or depression
Three failed adequate antidepressant trials should prompt diagnostic review, not a fourth escalation
Australian diagnosis needs a structured tool plus corroborated developmental history
Borderline personality disorder is a common misdiagnosis in this group and requires affective instability and identity disturbance to be present
explanation.pearls: Distinguishing autistic sensory intolerance from social anxiety turns on whether distress occurs when alone with the stimulus; social anxiety requires an audience, sensory intolerance does not.

sources.label: National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism in Australia
RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Anxiety Disorders
RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Personality Disorders
Australian Evidence Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.rationale: Augmentation treats the presumed anxiety disorder as the primary problem, yet the lifelong sensory, social and routine features suggest the wrong condition is being treated (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Anxiety Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Anxiety Disorders

options.rationale: Lifelong sensory sensitivity, social camouflaging, insistence on sameness and circumscribed interests warrant formal diagnostic assessment, which in Australia requires a structured tool plus a corroborated developmental history (Source: National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism in Australia).
source_refs: National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism in Australia

options.rationale: There is no affective instability, no identity disturbance, no self-harm and no pattern of unstable relationships, and this misdiagnosis is a documented pathway for autistic women (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Personality Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Personality Disorders

options.rationale: Inattention is not the reported problem and stimulants will not address sensory intolerance or social exhaustion, although the two conditions do co occur and can be screened after diagnosis (Source: Australian Evidence Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD).
source_refs: Australian Evidence Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.rationale: A fourth serotonergic escalation after three adequate trials repeats a failed strategy, and exposure work aimed at social anxiety does not target sensory or routine driven distress (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Anxiety Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Anxiety Disorders

explanation.summary: Repeated emergency presentations with self-harm in borderline personality disorder are best met with brief, structured, respectful crisis intervention rather than admission. Australian guidance is explicit that hospitalisation should be short and purposeful, reserved for acute risk that cannot be managed in the community, because longer stays are associated with regression and escalating self-harm. Structured psychological therapy such as dialectical behaviour therapy, mentalisation based therapy or schema therapy is the definitive treatment and belongs in the community. Medication is adjunctive at most, targeted at comorbid conditions rather than the core disorder.
key_points: Brief crisis intervention and rapid return to the treating team beat prolonged admission
No medication is recommended for the core features of borderline personality disorder
Structured psychological therapy is the definitive treatment and is delivered in the community
A written, collaboratively developed crisis plan is more effective than a generic list of phone numbers
explanation.pearls: Chronic suicidal ideation in borderline personality disorder is a baseline state, not an admission trigger; the change that warrants escalation is a shift in intent, plan or access to means from that individual's documented baseline.

sources.label: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder

options.rationale: Australian guidance favours brief structured crisis intervention, collaborative safety planning and rapid return to the treating team over admission, which in this pattern has been followed by escalation (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder).
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder

options.rationale: Prolonged admission is associated with regression, dependence and escalating self-harm in borderline personality disorder, and her own history shows exactly that sequence (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder).
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder

options.rationale: No medication has a licensed or guideline supported role for the core features of borderline personality disorder, and quetiapine adds metabolic risk without addressing the crisis (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder).
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder

options.rationale: Mood stabilisers are not recommended for the core disorder and valproate carries substantial teratogenic risk in a woman of reproductive age (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder; Australian Medicines Handbook).
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder

options.rationale: Discharge without an individualised plan or any change in follow up timing omits the collaborative safety planning that reduces repetition (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder).
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder

explanation.summary: Refugee and asylum seeker mental health presentations are shaped as much by present circumstances as by past trauma, and visa insecurity, family separation and financial precarity are frequently the dominant drivers of symptom fluctuation. A professional interpreter is a clinical necessity rather than a courtesy, because family members suppress disclosure of torture, sexual violence and suicidality. Australia has a state based network of specialist torture and trauma services that combine psychological therapy with social, legal and settlement support at no cost to the client. Diagnosis and treatment planning should follow, not precede, an interpreted assessment.
key_points: Use a credentialled interpreter, never a family member, for trauma assessment
Symptom exacerbation timed to visa events reflects ongoing stressors rather than treatment failure
State torture and trauma services offer combined psychological and psychosocial care
Benzodiazepines are avoided in trauma related presentations in this group
explanation.pearls: Ask directly about visa status and stage at every review; symptom worsening timed to a visa interview or a refusal letter predicts crisis presentations more reliably than any symptom score in this population.

sources.label: Foundation House Guide to Working with People from Refugee Backgrounds
Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Acute Stress Disorder, PTSD and Complex PTSD

options.rationale: Prescribing before a language competent assessment risks treating symptoms without understanding the formulation, and pharmacotherapy is not first line for trauma related presentations (Source: Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Acute Stress Disorder, PTSD and Complex PTSD).
source_refs: Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Acute Stress Disorder, PTSD and Complex PTSD

options.rationale: Family interpreters distort disclosure of torture, sexual violence and suicidal ideation and cannot be relied on for a trauma assessment, however willing they are (Source: Foundation House Guide to Working with People from Refugee Backgrounds).
source_refs: Foundation House Guide to Working with People from Refugee Backgrounds

options.rationale: A credentialled interpreter is a prerequisite for valid assessment, and the specialist torture and trauma services provide the combined psychological, social and visa related support this presentation needs (Source: Foundation House Guide to Working with People from Refugee Backgrounds; Australian Refugee Health Practice Guide).
source_refs: Foundation House Guide to Working with People from Refugee Backgrounds

options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are advised against in trauma related presentations because they impair emotional processing, and dependence risk is high in this population (Source: Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Acute Stress Disorder, PTSD and Complex PTSD).
source_refs: Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Acute Stress Disorder, PTSD and Complex PTSD

options.rationale: A generic referral without interpreter funding or refugee specific expertise commonly results in non attendance, and it does not address the visa and family separation stressors driving symptoms (Source: Australian Refugee Health Practice Guide).

explanation.summary: Acute severe behavioural disturbance is managed on a graded pathway that starts with environmental measures and verbal de escalation, moves to offered oral medication, and only then to parenteral sedation. Australian emergency practice favours intramuscular droperidol as the first parenteral agent, supported by randomised data showing faster sedation than midazolam with fewer airway events. Once any parenteral sedative is given the patient requires continuous observation with pulse oximetry, regular vital signs and airway readiness, because the commonest serious complication is oversedation rather than treatment failure. Every episode also requires a medical screen for delirium, hypoglycaemia, head injury and intoxication, since these change both the drug choice and the disposition.
key_points: Pathway order is environment, verbal de escalation, offered oral medication, then parenteral sedation
Intramuscular droperidol is the Australian first line parenteral agent for severe disturbance
Avoid combining parenteral olanzapine with parenteral benzodiazepines
Continuous observation with pulse oximetry follows every parenteral sedation
explanation.pearls: Check a capillary glucose before sedating any acutely disturbed patient; hypoglycaemia and delirium both present as agitation and both worsen if treated with an antipsychotic instead of the underlying cause.

sources.label: NSW Health Management of Patients with Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance

options.rationale: Establishing intravenous access in an advancing, physically resistant patient is unsafe for staff and delays sedation, which is why the intramuscular route is the standard in this scenario (Source: NSW Health Management of Patients with Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance).
source_refs: NSW Health Management of Patients with Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance

options.rationale: Intramuscular droperidol is the recommended Australian first line parenteral agent for acute severe behavioural disturbance where oral treatment is refused, with monitoring for oversedation and airway compromise once given (Source: NSW Health Management of Patients with Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).
source_refs: NSW Health Management of Patients with Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance

options.rationale: Combining parenteral olanzapine with a parenteral benzodiazepine is specifically cautioned against because of additive respiratory depression and cardiorespiratory collapse (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

This combination is used in some international settings but carries more dystonia and prolonged sedation than droperidol, which has the stronger Australian emergency evidence base (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

Restraint without timely sedation prolongs struggle and raises the risk of rhabdomyolysis and positional asphyxia, so restraint is a bridge to medication rather than an alternative to it (Source: NSW Health Management of Patients with Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance).
source_refs: NSW Health Management of Patients with Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance

explanation.summary: Australian practice for adults has moved from a psychiatric gatekeeping model to an informed consent model, in which the prescriber confirms capacity, sustained gender incongruence and understanding of effects, then initiates therapy with appropriate monitoring. Mental health assessment remains relevant where a condition might impair capacity or where comorbidity needs treatment in its own right, but it is not a universal prerequisite. Fertility discussion must occur before starting, because testosterone reduces fertility and oocyte cryopreservation is far simpler before treatment begins. Ongoing monitoring focuses on haematocrit, lipids, liver function and blood pressure, with dose adjusted to symptom response and testosterone level.
key_points: Informed consent, not mandatory psychiatric clearance, is the Australian adult standard
Baseline haematocrit, lipids, liver function and blood pressure precede initiation
Fertility preservation is discussed and documented before therapy starts
Erythrocytosis is the commonest dose limiting adverse effect of testosterone therapy
explanation.pearls: Monitor haematocrit at three, six and twelve months then annually on testosterone; a haematocrit above 0.54 requires dose reduction or a switch to a lower peak formulation rather than simple reassurance.

sources.label: Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy

options.rationale: A mandatory extended psychiatric gatekeeping period is not part of current Australian practice and is associated with delayed care and worse mental health outcomes (Source: Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy).
source_refs: Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy

options.rationale: Baseline haematocrit, lipids and liver function are needed before starting, since erythrocytosis is the commonest dose limiting adverse effect and cannot be interpreted without a pretreatment value (Source: Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy).
source_refs: Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy

options.rationale: The distress described is gender dysphoria rather than a depressive disorder, and an antidepressant neither treats it nor is a prerequisite for hormone therapy (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

Referral alone with waiting times often exceeding a year leaves the patient without care and without the baseline investigations that any prescriber will need at the first appointment (Source: Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy).
source_refs: Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy

options.rationale: Australian informed consent practice for an adult with sustained gender incongruence and capacity is baseline biochemistry plus documented discussion of fertility, reversibility and expected effects, after which a general practitioner may initiate or co manage therapy (Source: Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy).
source_refs: Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy

explanation.summary: Tricyclic antidepressant poisoning kills through fast sodium channel blockade producing QRS widening, ventricular arrhythmia and myocardial depression, compounded by alpha blockade and antimuscarinic effects. The electrocardiogram is the main severity tool, with a QRS above 100 ms predicting seizures and above 160 ms predicting ventricular arrhythmia, and a terminal R wave in aVR above 3 mm supporting the diagnosis. Hypertonic sodium bicarbonate works through two mechanisms at once and is titrated against the QRS duration rather than against a fixed dose. Acidosis from seizure or hypoventilation worsens toxicity, so airway control with adequate ventilation is part of the treatment rather than a separate issue.
key_points: QRS above 100 ms predicts seizures; above 160 ms predicts ventricular arrhythmia
Sodium bicarbonate is titrated to QRS narrowing, not to a fixed total dose
Phenytoin, amiodarone and other sodium channel blocking antiarrhythmics are contraindicated
Benzodiazepines are the anticonvulsant of choice in this poisoning
explanation.pearls: Aim for a serum pH of 7.50 to 7.55 during bicarbonate therapy for tricyclic toxicity and recheck the QRS after each 100 mmol bolus; a QRS that stops narrowing despite target pH signals the need for vasopressor support.

options.rationale: Phenytoin is a sodium channel blocker itself and worsens cardiotoxicity in this poisoning; benzodiazepines are the anticonvulsant of choice here (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

Class Ia and Ic and class III antiarrhythmics all worsen sodium channel blockade and are contraindicated, which is the key difference from a primary ventricular tachycardia (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

Vasopressors have a role once sodium loading and alkalinisation have been given, but starting with noradrenaline leaves the sodium channel blockade itself untreated (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

Hypertonic sodium bicarbonate reverses tricyclic sodium channel blockade by both sodium loading and alkalinisation, and is indicated for a QRS above 100 ms, seizures or hypotension in this poisoning (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology; NSW Poisons Information Centre).

Lipid emulsion is a rescue therapy considered only in cardiac arrest or refractory collapse after bicarbonate has failed, not as the first line intervention (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

explanation.summary: New South Wales law lets several people start an involuntary assessment, and the right instrument depends on who is present. A medical practitioner or accredited person who has personally examined the patient within the preceding day completes a mental health certificate, which allows the person to be taken to and detained at a declared mental health facility for assessment by an authorised medical officer; police and ambulance powers exist for situations where no examination has occurred. The threshold is a mentally ill or mentally disordered person for whom no less restrictive care is appropriate and reasonably available, and refusal of food with serious physical consequences meets a risk of serious harm to health. In context: schizoaffective disorder relapses with persecutory beliefs of this kind, and the general practitioner is often the only clinician who sees the patient, so knowing the certificate pathway and the local acute care team contact is practical core knowledge.

sources.label: NSW Health: Management of patients with acute severe behavioural disturbance

options.rationale: A medical practitioner who has examined the person and believes they are a mentally ill person needing care that is not otherwise available may complete the certificate under the Mental Health Act 2007 (NSW), which authorises transport to and detention at a declared mental health facility.
source_refs: NSW Health: Management of patients with acute severe behavioural disturbance
