options.rationale: Persistent depressive disorder requires depressed mood for at least two years, whereas his symptoms lasted eight months and he was well through an earlier abstinent period (Source: American Psychiatric Association Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition Text Revision).
source_refs: American Psychiatric Association Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition Text Revision

options.rationale: Protracted withdrawal would explain persisting symptoms rather than their complete resolution, and he is now entirely asymptomatic at four weeks (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine).

explanation.summary: Refeeding syndrome arises when carbohydrate delivery to a starved patient triggers an insulin surge that drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells, on top of total body stores that are already depleted. Phosphate depletion impairs adenosine triphosphate generation and red cell oxygen delivery, producing the weakness, breathlessness and cardiac dysfunction seen here. The historical response of stopping feeding has been superseded, because starvation itself is what the patient is being treated for, and current practice slows the rate while replacing electrolytes and continuing thiamine. Highest risk features include a body mass index below 14, negligible intake for more than five days, and low baseline electrolytes, all of which mandate cardiac monitoring and at least daily biochemistry during the first week.
key_points: Insulin driven intracellular shift of phosphate, potassium and magnesium is the mechanism
Slow the rate of feeding rather than stopping it and replace the electrolytes
Magnesium must be corrected before hypokalaemia will respond to potassium replacement
Thiamine is given before and throughout refeeding to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy
explanation.pearls: Check phosphate, potassium and magnesium at least daily for the first week of refeeding in anyone with a body mass index under 14, because the nadir typically falls on days two to four rather than on the day feeding starts.

sources.label: ANZAED and RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Eating Disorders

options.rationale: Stopping nutrition in a severely malnourished patient causes further deterioration and prolongs the period of risk, and it is not what current guidance recommends for a correctable biochemical abnormality (Source: ANZAED and RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Eating Disorders).
source_refs: ANZAED and RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Eating Disorders

options.rationale: Escalating the caloric load drives further intracellular shift of phosphate, potassium and magnesium, and a 24 hour interval is far too long once the phosphate has already fallen this low (Source: ANZAED and RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Eating Disorders).
source_refs: ANZAED and RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Eating Disorders

options.rationale: Sodium and volume loading risks precipitating cardiac failure in a myocardium that is atrophied and poorly compliant, and it does nothing about the electrolyte deficits driving her symptoms (Source: ANZAED and RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Eating Disorders).
source_refs: ANZAED and RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Eating Disorders

options.rationale: Refeeding syndrome is managed by slowing rather than ceasing nutrition while aggressively correcting the three electrolytes that shift intracellularly, with continuous cardiac monitoring given the prolonged corrected QT interval (Source: ANZAED and RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Eating Disorders; Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal).
source_refs: ANZAED and RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Eating Disorders

options.rationale: Correcting phosphate while leaving hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia untreated leaves the arrhythmia risk in place, and magnesium repletion is required before potassium will correct at all (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal).

explanation.summary: The absolute teratogenic risk of first trimester lithium has been revised sharply downward from early registry estimates, with the risk of Ebstein anomaly now put at roughly 1 in 1000 against a background population rate of about 1 in 20000. That has to be weighed against relapse rates above 50 per cent when lithium is stopped in pregnancy, rising further with abrupt cessation, and against the consequences of mania in pregnancy for both mother and fetus. By seven weeks the cardiac outflow tract has already formed, so stopping now removes future protection without undoing past exposure. Practical management involves more frequent level monitoring as renal clearance rises through pregnancy, a fetal echocardiogram at around 18 to 20 weeks, and a plan to withhold or reduce the dose around labour when volume shifts make toxicity likely.
key_points: Ebstein anomaly risk with first trimester lithium is about 1 in 1000
Relapse risk after stopping lithium in pregnancy exceeds 50 per cent and rises with abrupt cessation
Cardiac organogenesis is complete by seven weeks, so stopping does not undo exposure
Renal clearance rises through pregnancy so levels need checking more often
explanation.pearls: Lithium clearance falls abruptly at delivery as plasma volume contracts, so withhold the dose at the onset of labour and recheck the level within 24 hours postpartum before restarting the pre-pregnancy dose.

sources.label: COPE Australian Clinical Practice Guideline for Perinatal Mental Health
RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.rationale: The absolute risk of Ebstein anomaly is roughly 1 in 1000 with first trimester lithium, which is far outweighed by a relapse risk above 50 per cent after cessation in a woman with four manic episodes and no alternative that has worked (Source: COPE Australian Clinical Practice Guideline for Perinatal Mental Health; RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders).
source_refs: COPE Australian Clinical Practice Guideline for Perinatal Mental Health
RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.rationale: Abrupt cessation carries the highest relapse risk of any option and has already precipitated one manic episode in her history, and organogenesis is in any case well advanced by seven weeks (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.rationale: Valproate is the most teratogenic of all the mood stabilisers and swapping to it in pregnancy exchanges a small cardiac risk for a much larger malformation and neurodevelopmental risk (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

Lamotrigine protects mainly against depressive relapse and has weak evidence for mania prevention, so it is a poor substitute in an illness that has been consistently manic (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.rationale: A subtherapeutic level leaves her exposed to the drug while removing its prophylactic effect, and the teratogenic association is with exposure rather than being reliably dose avoidable (Source: COPE Australian Clinical Practice Guideline for Perinatal Mental Health).
source_refs: COPE Australian Clinical Practice Guideline for Perinatal Mental Health

explanation.summary: Serotonin toxicity is a clinical diagnosis made on the triad of neuromuscular excitation, autonomic instability and altered mental state, with the Hunter criteria resting heavily on clonus. It is separated from neuroleptic malignant syndrome by tempo and by the character of the motor findings, since serotonin toxicity develops within hours and produces clonus and hyperreflexia that are greater in the legs, while neuroleptic malignant syndrome evolves over days with generalised lead-pipe rigidity and bradykinesia. Monoamine oxidase inhibitors combined with any serotonergic drug produce the most severe form, and fluoxetine's long half life means a washout of about five weeks is required before starting one. Treatment is withdrawal of the offending agents, benzodiazepines for agitation and rigidity, active cooling, and cyproheptadine for moderate to severe cases, with paralysis and intubation if hyperthermia exceeds 39 degrees.
key_points: Clonus, hyperreflexia and lower limb predominant hypertonia define serotonin toxicity
Onset within hours contrasts with the days long evolution of neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Fluoxetine requires about five weeks of washout before a monoamine oxidase inhibitor
Antipyretics do not work because the heat is generated by muscular activity
explanation.pearls: A temperature above 39 degrees in serotonin toxicity is an indication for immediate paralysis, intubation and active cooling rather than escalating drug therapy, because the hyperthermia itself causes rhabdomyolysis and disseminated intravascular coagulation within hours.

options.rationale: These agents treat neuroleptic malignant syndrome, which is excluded by the absence of any antipsychotic exposure and by clonus and hyperreflexia rather than lead-pipe rigidity and bradykinesia (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

Reintroducing a serotonin reuptake inhibitor alongside a monoamine oxidase inhibitor is the interaction that caused this presentation and would make it substantially worse (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

Withdrawal of the serotonergic agents with benzodiazepine sedation is the foundation of treatment, and cyproheptadine is the serotonin antagonist added when features are moderate to severe as they are with hyperthermia and clonus (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology; Austin Health Toxicology Handbook).

Antipsychotics with dopamine blockade do not treat serotonin toxicity, impair heat dissipation and can convert the presentation into a mixed and more dangerous syndrome (Source: Austin Health Toxicology Handbook).

Hyperthermia here is generated by muscular hyperactivity rather than by a raised hypothalamic set point, so antipyretics are ineffective and ward observation underestimates the risk (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

explanation.summary: Clozapine induced myocarditis occurs in roughly 1 to 3 per cent of Australian patients and clusters tightly in the second and third weeks of titration, which is why many local protocols include baseline and weekly troponin and C reactive protein for the first four weeks. It is a hypersensitivity reaction rather than a dose-dependent toxicity, and eosinophilia is a supportive feature. The early symptoms of fatigue, breathlessness, tachycardia and low grade fever are easily attributed to clozapine's known sedation or to an incidental viral illness, and that misattribution is the main cause of death. Neutrophil monitoring, which is mandatory and familiar, gives no protection against this complication at all, so a normal neutrophil count is falsely reassuring.
key_points: Myocarditis clusters between days 14 and 21 of clozapine titration
Baseline and weekly troponin and C reactive protein for the first four weeks are standard in Australia
It is a hypersensitivity reaction and is not dose dependent
A normal neutrophil count offers no reassurance about myocarditis
explanation.pearls: A persistent resting tachycardia above 120 beats per minute in the third week of clozapine titration warrants a troponin and C reactive protein the same day, even when the patient attributes the breathlessness to being unfit.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

options.rationale: Continuing the drug in the face of a rising troponin and C reactive protein risks progression to fulminant myocarditis and death, and a 48 hour delay is not a safe observation interval (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

options.rationale: Myocarditis is a hypersensitivity reaction that is not dose dependent, so halving the dose provides no protection and defers the investigation that decides management (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

options.rationale: A single withheld dose followed by rechallenge exposes him again to the agent causing the reaction, and rechallenge after confirmed myocarditis is undertaken only in highly specialised settings (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

The clear chest radiograph, normal neutrophil count and absence of a septic focus make bacterial infection unlikely, and treating it does not address the cardiac injury (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

Tachycardia, breathlessness and fever with a rising troponin, C reactive protein and eosinophil count between days 14 and 21 of titration is clozapine induced myocarditis until proven otherwise, and immediate cessation with urgent cardiac assessment is the standard response (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia; Australian Medicines Handbook).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

explanation.summary: Chronic insomnia disorder requires difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep at least three nights a week for at least three months, with daytime consequences, in the presence of adequate opportunity to sleep. Assessment excludes contributors such as obstructive sleep apnoea, restless legs, shift work, substances, pain and untreated mood or anxiety disorder. Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia combines stimulus control, sleep restriction, cognitive restructuring and relaxation, and it outperforms hypnotics at follow up because its gains persist after treatment ends. Australian access has broadened through digital programs and psychologists trained in the model, which matters where face to face therapy is limited.
key_points: Diagnosis requires three nights weekly for three months with daytime impairment
Exclude sleep apnoea, restless legs, substances and untreated mood or anxiety disorder
Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia is first line and its gains persist after treatment
Sleep restriction targets low sleep efficiency and is the most active ingredient
Hypnotics are short term adjuncts, not maintenance therapy
explanation.pearls: Sleep restriction sets time in bed to the average total sleep time from the diary, never below five hours, then extends it by fifteen minutes each week once sleep efficiency exceeds 85 per cent.

options.rationale: Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia is first line for chronic insomnia disorder, and the excessive time in bed with poor sleep efficiency is precisely what its sleep restriction component targets (Source: RACGP: Management of Chronic Insomnia; Sleep Health Foundation Australia).

Benzodiazepines are for short term situational insomnia only, and starting one in a nine month problem sets up tolerance and rebound insomnia on withdrawal (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).
Sedating antidepressants are prescribed off label for sleep but have anticholinergic effects and no evidence base as first line in primary insomnia (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).
Modified release melatonin is approved for people aged 55 and over and has modest effects on sleep onset, so it does not displace structured therapy here (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).
Sleep hygiene as a standalone intervention performs poorly in trials and is the weakest component of the therapy package rather than a substitute for it (Source: Sleep Health Foundation Australia).

explanation.summary: Gambling disorder is classified with the substance related and addictive disorders because of shared features of tolerance, withdrawal-like irritability, loss of control and chasing losses. It is strongly associated with depression, anxiety, alcohol use disorder and suicide, with suicide risk several times that of the general population, so risk assessment is part of every consultation. Cognitive behavioural therapy has the strongest evidence, delivered face to face, by telephone or online, alongside financial counselling and practical barriers such as the national self-exclusion register and bank gambling blocks. Comorbid depression is treated in its own right when it does not remit as gambling reduces.
key_points: Classified with addictive disorders and shares tolerance and loss of control features
Suicide risk is markedly elevated and is assessed at every contact
Cognitive behavioural therapy is the best evidenced treatment
Self-exclusion registration, bank blocks and financial counselling are practical adjuncts
Treat comorbid depression separately if it persists as gambling reduces
explanation.pearls: The national self-exclusion register blocks a person from all licensed Australian online and telephone wagering operators for a chosen period of at least three months, and registration is a concrete first session task rather than general advice.

sources.label: Gambling Help Australia and BetStop National Self-Exclusion Register

options.rationale: Antidepressants do not treat the disorder itself and his mood tracks his betting, so treating mood alone leaves the driver of the presentation untouched (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).
Opioid antagonists show benefit in some trials but are an adjunct after psychological therapy has been organised, not the opening intervention (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

Cognitive behavioural therapy is the best evidenced treatment, and it is paired with a suicide risk assessment and practical harm reduction such as national self-exclusion registration and financial safeguards (Source: Gambling Help Australia and BetStop National Self-Exclusion Register; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).
source_refs: Gambling Help Australia and BetStop National Self-Exclusion Register

options.rationale: Disclosure is often part of recovery but is his decision to time, and advice alone provides no treatment for a disorder with a high relapse rate (Source: Gambling Help Australia and BetStop National Self-Exclusion Register).
source_refs: Gambling Help Australia and BetStop National Self-Exclusion Register

options.rationale: There is no physiological withdrawal syndrome requiring admission, and inpatient care is reserved for acute suicide risk or severe comorbidity (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Contemporary Australian standards for adult gender affirming care use an informed consent model in which capacity, understanding of the effects and limits of treatment, and management of relevant medical risks are what matter, rather than psychiatric gatekeeping. Mental health problems are common in trans and gender diverse populations and largely reflect minority stress, family rejection and discrimination, so they are treated alongside affirming care rather than as a precondition for it. Psychiatric input is valuable where diagnostic uncertainty, significant mental illness affecting capacity, or complex comorbidity exists. Cohort data consistently show improvement in depression, anxiety and quality of life after commencing affirming hormone therapy.
key_points: Adult care follows an informed consent model, not compulsory psychiatric approval
Real life experience requirements have been removed from current standards
Coexisting mood and anxiety symptoms are treated alongside affirming care
Minority stress explains much of the psychological distress in this population
Psychiatric input is for capacity concerns, diagnostic uncertainty or complex comorbidity
explanation.pearls: Feminising hormone therapy produces breast development and body fat redistribution over one to two years but does not change voice pitch, which is why speech pathology referral is discussed at the same visit rather than after treatment disappoints.

sources.label: RANZCP Position Statement on Gender Diversity

options.rationale: Requiring full remission before affirming care sets a threshold not applied to other treatments and delays an intervention that itself improves mood (Source: AusPATH Standards of Care; RANZCP Position Statement on Gender Diversity).
source_refs: RANZCP Position Statement on Gender Diversity

options.rationale: Mandatory real life experience requirements have been removed from contemporary standards as a barrier without evidence of benefit (Source: AusPATH Standards of Care).

Medicating distress that arises largely from rejection and misgendering, while postponing the affirming intervention, treats the symptom and not the situation (Source: RANZCP Position Statement on Gender Diversity).
source_refs: RANZCP Position Statement on Gender Diversity

options.rationale: Australian standards support an informed consent model delivered by experienced prescribers, with mental health input available rather than compulsory (Source: AusPATH Standards of Care).

Coexisting mood or anxiety symptoms are not a barrier to affirming care when capacity is intact, and gender affirming hormone therapy is associated with improved psychological outcomes while the mood symptoms are treated concurrently (Source: AusPATH Standards of Care; RANZCP Position Statement on Gender Diversity).
source_refs: RANZCP Position Statement on Gender Diversity

explanation.summary: Relapse prevention in schizophrenia rests on effective antipsychotic treatment that is actually taken, on avoiding substances, and on the psychosocial environment. High expressed emotion in the household, meaning criticism, hostility or emotional over-involvement, is one of the most consistent predictors of relapse and is modifiable. Structured family intervention delivered over at least ten sessions reduces relapse and readmission by roughly half in the year after treatment and also reduces carer burden. Attributing negative symptoms to laziness is a common and correctable misunderstanding that psychoeducation directly targets.
key_points: High expressed emotion in the household predicts relapse and is modifiable
Family intervention needs at least ten sessions to show benefit
It reduces relapse and readmission and lowers carer burden
Negative symptoms misread as laziness drive household criticism
Polypharmacy and dose escalation do not address environmental relapse drivers
explanation.pearls: Family intervention reduces twelve month relapse from around 50 per cent to around 25 per cent in high expressed emotion households, an effect size comparable to that of maintenance antipsychotic treatment itself.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia
Cochrane Review: Family Intervention for Schizophrenia

options.rationale: Dose escalation targets breakthrough symptoms or non-adherence, and he has neither, so it adds adverse effect burden without addressing the pattern (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

options.rationale: Antipsychotic polypharmacy increases adverse effects without consistent efficacy gains and is discouraged outside treatment resistance (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

options.rationale: Moving out may eventually suit him, but separating a young person from his main supports is a large step before the family has been offered treatment (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

options.rationale: Individual therapy helps residual symptoms and distress, but it does not modify the household environment that has preceded both relapses (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

options.rationale: Family intervention including psychoeducation, communication training and problem solving reduces relapse and readmission where household criticism is high, and it is the highest yield addition when medication is already effective and taken (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

explanation.summary: Supported decision making aims to keep the person at the centre of their own care rather than replacing their decisions with someone else's. NSW does this without the statutory machinery Victoria has: there is no advance statement of preferences and no nominated support person. What NSW offers is an advance care directive at common law, which must be made with capacity and must be taken into account even though it cannot override compulsory treatment, and the nomination of up to two designated carers, which is a written appointment on the approved form and lasts twelve months. Guardianship is a separate and larger step, and it does not extend to treatment given under the Mental Health Act 2007.
key_points: NSW has no statutory advance statement and no nominated support person.
An advance care directive is common law: valid, considered, but not binding under the Act.
A designated carer nomination is written, covers up to two people, and lasts twelve months.
Enduring guardianship substitutes decisions and does not reach Mental Health Act treatment.
explanation.pearls: The practical lever in NSW is not a statutory duty to give written reasons, which does not exist here. It is specificity: a directive naming the drug, the reaction and the alternative is the one a registrar at 2 am can actually act on.

NSW Health: designated carers and principal care providers
NSW Mental Health Review Tribunal: community treatment orders

options.rationale: Community treatment orders are compulsory instruments made by the Tribunal or a Magistrate when the criteria are met, and cannot be arranged in advance by a well patient. (Source: NSW Mental Health Review Tribunal: community treatment orders)
source_refs: NSW Mental Health Review Tribunal: community treatment orders

options.rationale: Enduring guardianship under the Guardianship Act 1987 substitutes another person's decisions, is a larger step than she needs, and does not reach treatment given under the Mental Health Act 2007. (Source: NSW Mental Health Rights Manual: advance care directives)
source_refs: NSW Mental Health Rights Manual: advance care directives

options.rationale: These are the two NSW instruments. A directive made now, while she has capacity, records her objection to olanzapine and the reason for it, and must be taken into account even though it cannot override treatment under the Act. A designated carer nomination, valid for twelve months, is what makes her sister rather than her father the person informed and involved. (Source: NSW Mental Health Rights Manual: advance care directives; NSW Health: designated carers and principal care providers)
source_refs: NSW Mental Health Rights Manual: advance care directives
NSW Health: designated carers and principal care providers

options.rationale: Recording intolerance as an allergy misstates an adverse effect, and it does nothing at all about who she wants informed and involved. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)
No document can exclude involuntary treatment in advance where the statutory criteria are met, so promising her this would be misleading. (Source: NSW Mental Health Act 2007)

explanation.summary: Autism is frequently missed in women and girls who camouflage social difficulty by rehearsing interactions and copying peers, which is effortful and leads to exhaustion and anxiety rather than to obvious social difference. The typical adult presentation is treatment resistant anxiety or depression, burnout after a change in role or demands, and long standing sensory sensitivity that has never been asked about. Australian diagnostic practice uses a structured multidisciplinary assessment with a developmental history from childhood, informants where available and standardised instruments. Diagnosis changes management by shifting the focus to environmental accommodations, sensory strategies and adjusted therapy techniques rather than further sequential drug trials.
key_points: Camouflaging conceals autism in women and delays diagnosis into adulthood
Treatment resistant anxiety with lifelong sensory sensitivity is a common presentation
Diagnosis requires a developmental history from childhood, not current presentation alone
Family history of autism raises prior probability substantially
Diagnosis redirects management toward accommodations and adapted therapy
explanation.pearls: Standard cognitive behavioural therapy is adapted for autistic adults with more concrete language, written summaries and longer sessions, and unadapted therapy failing twice is itself a diagnostic clue rather than evidence of treatment resistance.

sources.label: National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism in Australia

options.rationale: A third sequential trial repeats a strategy that has failed twice and does not test the possibility that the formulation itself is wrong (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

Lifelong social camouflaging, sensory sensitivity, need for sameness and enduring narrow interests with a family history point to autism presenting as treatment resistant anxiety, and Australian practice requires a structured assessment with a developmental history for diagnosis in adults (Source: National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism in Australia; RANZCP Position Statement on Autism).
source_refs: National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism in Australia

options.rationale: Social anxiety involves fear of negative evaluation rather than the lifelong sensory and sameness features described here, and exposure alone does not address them (Source: RANZCP Position Statement on Autism).
Avoidant personality disorder is driven by fear of rejection and inadequacy, and it does not account for sensory pain or distress at timetable changes (Source: RANZCP Position Statement on Autism).
Antipsychotics are used in autism only for severe irritability or aggression, and they do not treat sensory sensitivity or anxiety of this kind (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Long term benzodiazepine use in older people roughly doubles the risk of falls and hip fracture and contributes to cognitive impairment and motor vehicle crashes, with hypnotic benefit largely lost to tolerance within weeks. Deprescribing succeeds when it is negotiated rather than imposed, paired with education about how little benefit remains and with behavioural strategies for sleep. Typical tapers reduce the dose by about a quarter every one to two weeks, slowing near the end where withdrawal symptoms cluster, and switching to a longer acting agent such as diazepam can smooth the final stages. Around two thirds of motivated long term users can stop with structured support.
key_points: Long term use doubles falls and hip fracture risk in older people
Hypnotic efficacy is largely lost to tolerance within weeks
Taper by about a quarter of the dose every one to two weeks, slowing at the end
Pair the taper with behavioural sleep strategies rather than another sedative
Zopiclone and zolpidem carry comparable falls risk and are not a safe substitute
explanation.pearls: The final quarter of a benzodiazepine taper is where most attempts fail, so slowing to reductions every four weeks at low doses, rather than holding the earlier pace, is what converts a failed attempt into a completed one.

options.rationale: Long duration of use is not evidence of safety, and the fall itself is the harm that long term use predicts in older people (Source: RACGP: Prescribing Drugs of Dependence).
Abrupt cessation after eleven years risks withdrawal insomnia, agitation and seizures, and the failed past attempts show exactly this pattern (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).
The non-benzodiazepine hypnotics carry a similar falls and fracture risk in older people and simply relabel the problem (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

Gradual dose reduction agreed with the patient, supported by behavioural sleep strategies, achieves cessation in a substantial proportion of long term users while avoiding withdrawal (Source: RACGP: Prescribing Drugs of Dependence; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).
Adding a second sedating agent increases total sedative burden and falls risk without a mood disorder to justify it (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia are approached by first describing the behaviour precisely, then looking for a cause, since most have one. Pain, constipation, urinary retention, infection, sensory impairment, medicine adverse effects and the way care tasks are delivered account for the majority, and behaviour confined to a single task points strongly to that task rather than to disease progression. Non-pharmacological management including analgesia trials, routine modification, environmental change and carer training is first line. Antipsychotics are used only for severe distress, aggression or psychosis after these measures fail, with informed consent about stroke and mortality risk and a defined review point.
key_points: Describe the behaviour and its trigger before treating it
Pain is the commonest reversible driver of care resistant behaviour
Behaviour confined to one care task implicates that task, not disease progression
Non-pharmacological measures and analgesia trials come first
Risperidone is the only approved agent, used with consent and reviewed within twelve weeks
explanation.pearls: A scheduled paracetamol trial of 1 g three times daily for two weeks resolves a substantial proportion of care resistant agitation in dementia, and it is diagnostic as well as therapeutic when behaviour charting shows the change.

options.rationale: Untreated pain is the commonest reversible driver of care resistant behaviour, and a scheduled analgesia trial with an altered routine and structured charting is the recommended first step before any psychotropic (Source: Dementia Australia Clinical Practice Guidelines; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

Risperidone is the only antipsychotic approved for this indication in Australia, but it follows failed non-pharmacological measures and is limited to twelve weeks because of stroke and mortality risk (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).
Benzodiazepines worsen confusion and falls in dementia and are reserved for brief use in severe distress (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

Serotonin reuptake inhibitors have modest evidence in agitation, but there are no depressive features here and the behaviour is confined to one care task (Source: Dementia Australia Clinical Practice Guidelines).

Specialist unit transfer is for severe behaviours that persist despite comprehensive management, and relocation itself often worsens behaviour (Source: Dementia Australia Clinical Practice Guidelines).
